baldwin-prehistoric-nations-1869:
John D. Baldwin argues a bold theory of the deep past in Pre-Historic Nations, from 1869. Civilization, he claims, spread from one common source in high antiquity. Ruins, languages, and customs across the world are marshaled as clues in one vast case for diffusion.

Baldwin wrote before modern archaeology settled many of these questions. His learning is real, yet his grand system now looks dated to most scholars. That is part of the book's fascination for modern readers. It preserves the great nineteenth-century debate over humanity's origins in full flight, when every new ruin seemed to rewrite the whole human story at once.
beguin-tyrocinium-chymicum-1669:
Jean Béguin's Tyrocinium Chymicum, first issued in Latin in 1610, appeared in English in 1669. Béguin taught chemistry in Paris and wrote for beginners, as his title's word for a first lesson suggests. His primer was among the first clear textbooks of the new chemical art.

Lessons define terms, describe vessels and furnaces, and give recipes for medicines from plants, animals, and minerals. Béguin favored plain steps over the riddles of older alchemical writers. Students across Europe learned from the book for decades. It shows chemistry stepping away from secret symbols toward teaching that any trained reader could follow and repeat.
blue-book-termination-1969:
The Air Force signed the death warrant of its UFO study on December 17, 1969. News Release 1077-69, from Secretary Robert Seamans, tells the world Project Blue Book is done. Twenty years of files, sightings, and public mail end with this one plain sheet.

The release holds that the study could not be backed on grounds of national safety or of science. No case in the files, it says, shows craft past the skill of earth. The words are dry and flat, and the effect was vast. Blue Book's end is the hinge of the whole government UFO tale.
boaistuau-certaine-secrete-wonders-natur:
Pierre Boaistuau's Histoires prodigieuses was the great French book of wonders of its century. Edward Fenton Englished it in 1569 as Certaine Secrete Wonders of Nature. Elizabethan readers, hungry for marvels, got sea monsters and strange births in their own language at last.

Boaistuau collects prodigies, events read as omens written in flesh and sky. Monstrous births, floods, and wonders of the sea fill his chapters. Each tale comes with reports meant to prove it happened. The book taught English readers to scan nature for signs from God. Its mix of dread and delight made it a lasting bestseller of the strange.
bolender-draft-1969:
Blue Book shut in 1969, but the Air Force still had to field UFO reports that touched national safety. The Bolender Draft, a memo of October 20, 1969, from General Carroll Bolender, lays out how. It tells which reports should still move up a sealed chain.

Bolender writes that reports which bear on the safety of the nation are not part of the Blue Book system. They were to be handled by other Air Force paths once the public program died. The draft shows the quiet afterlife of the UFO desk. It has fed years of debate on what the service kept back.
borlase-antiquities-cornwall-1769:
Fifteen years after his first Cornwall volume, William Borlase brought out a second, larger edition in 1769. The Antiquities of Cornwall had grown with its author and with the county lore sent to him. Borlase revised the text, added new material, and folded in his Observations, giving the work its fullest and most settled form.

The same great subjects return: stone circles, cromlechs, and inscribed stones across the county, now more fully drawn. With more sites recorded and earlier claims rethought, the edition stands as the mature shape of his Cornish corpus. Readers who want Borlase at his most complete come to the 1769 printing rather than the first.
brasseur-manuscrit-troano-vol-1-1869:
One of the few Maya books to survive the conquest came to print in 1869. Manuscrit Troano, volume one, is Brasseur de Bourbourg's first publication of the Troano Codex. The French edition opened the painted manuscript to the scholars of Europe.

Brasseur prints the codex pages and begins his study of Maya script and tongue. He read the signs as a tale of land lost to the sea, a reading few now accept. From his misreading, Le Plongeon later drew the name Mu for a sunken land. The volume still marks the birth of Troano study.
browning-ring-and-book-vol1-1869:
Robert Browning built his longest poem on a real Roman murder case from the 1690s. He found the trial records in an old book bought in Florence. The Ring and the Book came out in four volumes in 1868 and 1869, and this is the first.

The opening book explains how Browning found the records and shaped his plan. Then the voices begin: Roman gossips, the murdered woman's family, and others each tell the story their own way. A count has killed his young wife, and every witness sees the crime differently. The method lets truth emerge slowly from clashing accounts.
browning-ring-and-book-vol2-1869:
Robert Browning's long poem The Ring and the Book retells a Roman murder trial from the 1690s. He published it in four volumes across 1868 and 1869. This second volume holds Books Five through Eight of the twelve-book poem.

Each book gives the same crime to a new speaker. Here the lawyers argue, the accused count defends himself, and other voices weigh in with gossip and guesswork. No two accounts agree, and Browning trusts the reader to sort truth from self-interest. The middle volumes show his method at full stretch, turning dry court papers into living drama.
browning-ring-and-book-vol3-1869:
Robert Browning shaped The Ring and the Book from real records of a murder trial held in Rome in 1698. The poem came out in four volumes in 1868 and 1869. This third volume holds Books Nine through Eleven.

These books carry the longest and most moving speeches in the whole poem. The murdered wife, Pompilia, tells her story on her deathbed, and the priest Caponsacchi describes his attempt to rescue her. The Pope himself then weighs the case in a famous reflective speech. Together they build steadily toward the verdict that the final volume delivers at last.
browning-ring-and-book-vol4-1869:
Robert Browning closed his longest poem, The Ring and the Book, with this fourth volume, published in 1869. The poem retells a Roman murder case of 1698 through twelve separate speeches. Book Twelve, held in this volume, ends the whole design.

Browning steps forward in his own voice to judge what the many speakers have shown. He explains the gold-and-alloy image behind his title, the ring made from mixed metal and shaped by craft. Letters and reports after the trial round out the record. The ending defends the poem's method: truth found by testing many partial accounts against each other.
bushnell-women-s-suffrage-the-reform-aga: Women's Suffrage, the reform against nature, Bushnell's 1869 work. The anti-suffrage tract. This book preserves that book. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
calcott-candid-disquisition-1769:
Wellins Calcott published his Candid Disquisition on the principles and practices of the Free and Accepted Masons in London in 1769. The book defends the Craft against the standing charge that Masonry was mere conviviality, a drinking club with secrets. It became the most widely circulated Masonic apology of the eighteenth century.

Calcott argues that the society's principles aim at morality, charity, and brotherly order. He answers critics point by point in a candid, measured tone. Masons bought the book to give to doubtful friends and family. Its wide spread made it the Craft's ablest public defense. Readers today find in Calcott the case for Masonry as its best eighteenth-century advocates wished it understood.
catoe-ufo-bibliography-1969:
Lynn Catoe of the Library of Congress mapped the whole UFO shelf in 1969. UFOs and Related Subjects is her annotated bibliography, made for the Air Force Office of Scientific Research. The book runs to 417 pages of entries and notes.

Books, reports, and magazine work stand in neat ranks, each with a fair word on its worth. Catoe wastes no awe and no scorn; her tone is that of a guide, not a judge. The volume shows how vast the UFO field had grown by the end of Blue Book. It stays the standard map of that field.
cia-0000008069:
Ghana's prospects came under CIA review in October 1961, four years after the country won independence. Kwame Nkrumah, Ghana's celebrated first leader, was tightening his grip on power. Economic strain and fading opposition raised questions in Washington about where Ghana was heading.

The paper weighs Nkrumah's rule, his ties abroad, and the chances of change from within. Ghana mattered as a model for newly free African states during the Cold War. Analysts had to judge pride, hope, and hard economics at the same time. The estimate preserves an early, clear-eyed look at postcolonial Africa's first test case.
cia-0000008669:
Italy's current situation opened the CIA's 1948 file at a tense moment in the young Cold War. Italy faced elections that April, with a strong communist party challenging Alcide De Gasperi's government. Washington feared a communist win in Western Europe's largest country.

Assessments like this one weighed parties, voters, and outside influence before the ballots were cast. Italy's choice mattered for the Marshall Plan and the shape of postwar Europe. The paper comes from the agency's first full year, yet already works at a grand scale. It shows American intelligence treating an election abroad as a strategic event.
cia-0000012269:
Readiness to devote himself to the work: that is the burden of a Russian letter translated in a CIA document from July 1960. The translation belongs to the Penkovsky file, and its words carry a would-be spy's pledge. Oleg Penkovsky was then offering himself to the West, asking to be taken on as a source inside Soviet intelligence.

The document preserves the translated text and its handling marks. Pledges like this one opened the most valuable Western penetration of the Soviet military. For readers, the page holds the operation's human beginning: one officer's decision, rendered into English.
cia-0000013869: Two American prisoners were seen near Son Tay City, and a CIA note dated July 4, 1967, reports the sighting. Son Tay sits in Ha Tay Province, west of Hanoi. A sighting near a known prison area drew close attention in Washington. Notes of this kind helped build the picture of where the camp system held its men.
cia-0000014769: Communist activities in Argentina fill a CIA file dated March 3, 1953. The file names the Partido Comunista de la Argentina, the country's Communist Party, and a man cut short as Juan in the title. Party watching in Latin America was steady work for U.S. stations. The file adds one month of that watch to the record.
cia-0000015369: A meeting of the Upper Atmosphere Rocket Research Panel fills a CIA file dated August 4, 1954. Rocket men met to plan study of the high sky in those years. Their work touched the same heights where strange objects were claimed. The file places the saucer era beside the earnest science of the rocket age.
cia-0000015469: Sightings over Spain and Africa from July to October fill a CIA record dated in 1952. The title gives a four month span, longer than most single sighting notes. It also names Africa, not Portugal, whatever older summaries say. A seasonal bundle like this let analysts scan a whole region's reports at once and look for patterns across the busy summer and fall.
cia-0000022669: The pacification effort in Vietnam, with information on the Phoenix Program and Viet Cong infrastructure, fills a CIA record dated in 1969. Pacification meant winning villages away from the Viet Cong by aid, guard work, and pressure. The Phoenix Program targeted the Viet Cong's shadow leadership and drew lasting dispute. The record joins a broad campaign survey to its most debated part.
cia-0000037169:
Autopsies were allegedly performed on the bodies of American pilots at a place in Quang Ninh province, a CIA record dated October 5, 1968 states. The claim is among the grimmest in the wartime prisoner files. Quang Ninh lies in the far northeast of North Vietnam, near the Chinese border.

The record preserves the allegation as it was reported during the war itself. Charges of this kind fed anger in the United States and hardened public feeling. For later readers, the file shows the darkest edge of the prisoner story, where rumor and fact were painfully hard to separate from each other.
cia-0000049069: Recommendations by the Salvadoran army's political commission on points raised in a meeting fill a CIA item from 1983. Armies at war keep political staffs to watch the civilian game, and this commission spoke for the institution. Its advice, preserved here, shows soldiers weighing speeches and parties as carefully as battles.
cia-0000049269: A session of the PCC on El Salvador in 1991 is preserved in a CIA item, kept with the Truth Commission records. The Policy Coordinating Committee was where the government's agencies hammered out one line on a country. Meeting on El Salvador in 1991 meant planning for a war everyone could see ending.
cia-0000049369: Leftist Death Squads is the blunt title of declassified CIA document 0000049369, dated May 5, 1985. Noted for the Truth Commission, the item directs attention to death squads on the left in the Salvadoran conflict. Readers get a short declassified record whose heading names its subject without qualification, preserved among the agency's many short Salvadoran items.
cia-0000098269: Increasing civil unrest in Kwangsi, Hupeh, Peking, Fukien and Yunnan is reported in declassified CIA document 0000098269, dated June 6, 1968. Five places are named in one heading, a wider sweep than most. Readers get a short multi-place unrest account from China, its long place list the record's most distinctive feature. The heading and date are the firm facts the catalog gives.
cia-0000100169: Biological Warfare USSR: Biological Warfare Accident in Sverdlovsk is the heading of declassified CIA document 0000100169, dated January 1, 1980. The title repeats its own subject phrase twice. The brief file is the earliest Sverdlovsk accident record in this cluster by catalog date, filed at the start of the year after the event.
cia-0000106269: Sitrep As of 2030 Hours Local Time Tension in Vientian Between National Police is the heading, with Vientiane shortened, on CIA document 0000106269 dated November 2, 1964. A sitrep is a situation report, and this one is timed to the half hour. Its stated subject is tension in the capital between the national police and another party unnamed. The brief record freezes one tense evening.
cia-0000109069: Cuban Leadership Criticism of Soviet Foreign and Domestic Policies is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000109069, dated September 5, 1967. The heading records the smaller ally criticizing the larger one, on both foreign and domestic policy. Criticism is the title's own word for the act it reports. The brief record is a criticism item from the autumn of 1967.
cia-0000119169: Prospects for British Guiana is the short heading on declassified CIA document 0000119169, dated February 2, 1961. The title weighs the future of one colony, British Guiana, in four plain words. Prospects is the forecast word at the front of the heading itself. The brief record is a colony outlook item, one of three Guiana items in this group of files.
cia-0000119769: An August 1956 CIA item reports Hungarian writers demanding freedom of expression. Writers and debating circles were turning into a force for revolt that summer. The item captures that ferment months before the uprising, when poets were already testing the regime's limits. Writers moved first in many East European crises, since their unions and journals gave private discontent a public voice before parties or crowds could act openly.
cia-0000124269: A November 1957 CIA item examines an alleged Czech contribution to the launching of Sputnik. In the shock after the first satellite, every rumor about who had helped Moscow drew attention. The item records the claim together with the agency's interest in it. Czech industry was respected across the bloc, so any Prague hand in the satellite program was a lead analysts were bound to run down carefully.
cia-0000126869: An October 1979 CIA review of Near East and South Asia affairs gives the outlook for the insurgency in Afghanistan, the heading breaking off. Rebels were rising against the communist government in Kabul, and the Soviet invasion was two months away. The review forecasts the rebellion's course. Within two months Soviet troops crossed the border, and this October outlook became a baseline for judging how well the agency had read the rebellion.
cia-0000132169: Numbered 487 in the January 1991 Iraq-Kuwait series, this situation report covers political developments and an Iraqi terrorist matter the heading cuts off. Saddam's threats of terror were meant to split the coalition facing him. The report follows both tracks. Terror threats ran through the whole crisis winter, and each sitrep touching them fed the guarding of embassies, bases, and airlines across three continents.
cia-0000132569: Closer cultural ties between East Germany and Cuba fill a CIA item dated October 1, 1960. Culture was following trade and arms into the Soviet orbit that year. East Berlin was becoming the bloc's cultural outpost in Havana, hosting visits and exchanges. The short item notes the new ties as one more strand in Cuba's turn toward the communist world.
cia-0000132669: Latin American reactions to the Cuban situation fill a CIA paper dated January 2, 1961. The American break with Havana was about to land, and every capital was setting its position in advance. The region's response was itself the story that week. The short paper gathers the reactions from across the hemisphere as they reached analysts in the first days of the year.
cia-0000132769: Three strands of the Cuban situation share a CIA paper dated June 4, 1960. One strand covers money deals with the bloc. A second covers a Latin American youth congress. The headline breaks off before the list is done. Money and youth were two of the revolution's chief tools abroad. The short paper takes the roundup strand by strand.
cia-0000134269: Communists spreading work based in Cuba across the region fill item 16 of the CIA's Latin America series. The item is dated February 3, 1960. Its headline breaks off before the region's name is done. Havana was becoming the base from which the left worked across the hemisphere. The short item tracks that spread and its agents.
cia-0000135869: A planning paper of 5 November 1952 survives in the declassified CIA files, dealing with the current planning of the Calligeris organization, with attachments holding the detail. Behind the paper stands PBSUCCESS, the covert CIA campaign against President Arbenz that closed with the 1954 coup in Guatemala. Records like this one let the operation be studied from the inside, in the terms its own staff used.
cia-0000135969: The open CIA files hold a cable dated 3 January 1954 that deals with the scanning of student personnel records, raw material for the recruiting of new assets. As the Lincoln station file, it forms part of PBSUCCESS, the CIA plan that ended with President Arbenz driven out in June 1954. Its worth is in the detail it pins down, one dated piece of a covert war fought largely on paper.
cia-0000136069: Dated 1 March 1954, a declassified CIA cable deals with preventing red penetration, guarding the operation against communist agents inside its own ranks. In these files Lincoln names the field station of PBSUCCESS, the covert CIA plan to topple President Arbenz of Guatemala. The heading alone tells a reader the topic, the channel, and the moment, even where names stay deleted.
cia-0000136169: A CIA cable from 6 April 1954, now declassified, deals with WSBURNT military matters, cabled to PAGE in the first week of April 1954. In these files Lincoln names the field station of PBSUCCESS, the covert CIA plan to topple President Arbenz of Guatemala. What survives is the working paper itself, plain proof of how the mission was run from day to day.
cia-0000136269: A CIA situation report dated 1 May 1954 deals with daily situation report number 06, the numbered heartbeat of the operation in May, in files since declassified. The paper sits inside the CIA drive against President Arbenz, run under the code name PBSUCCESS and crowned by the June 1954 coup. Its worth is in the detail it pins down, one dated piece of a covert war fought largely on paper.
cia-0000136369: SKIMMER should contact CALLIGERIS soonest, LINCOLN urges in this June 1954 cable, to establish a plausible and palatable explanation of his air support for the liberation movement. The cover story offered: one fighter aircraft crash-landed and is being held, and another will shortly be brought in. To enact it, CALLIGERIS should send a trusted pilot within days to SOMERSET to pick up one F-47, with Mendoza recommended. Deception here is routine staff work.
cia-0000136769: The catalog gives this Spanish text from the 2506 Brigade documents an estimated date of 1 January 1961. The brigade was then training in secret for the invasion of Cuba. The record names no subject for the item, and the estimated flag is part of its catalog title. It survives in Spanish in the CIA's declassified release, a New Year record of the exile force by the reviewers' placement.
cia-0000136969: Stick to the facts, headquarters tells LINCOLN in this May 1954 cable about BRODFROST advising STORAX of a plane flight. A Venezuelan plane flying a secret mission over Central America has been reported; in any message to BRODFROST, avoid any hint of our exploitation of this development. The station should use the New York Times intercept report plus specified details from a reference message, which are best treated as factual. The cable coaches careful talk about another country's covert flight.
cia-0000137469: Venezuela's extremists are active but contained in these late 1961 reports. They were written ahead of Kennedy's visit. Anti-government flysheets were spread outside a Caracas theater. Anti-Kennedy flysheets appeared too. No violent disturbances took place. As of 10 December, no extremist leaders had been detained. The government had not decided on detaining those with congressional immunity. Guards were posted around Dutch businesses. In Zulia, the Movement of the Revolutionary Left plans a December revolt. The Communist Party refused to join it.
cia-0000139169: Daily diary excerpts from the photo interpretation center record autumn 1978 work. A requisition for Kodak film and paper was approved. It was returned through channels. A draft memo detailed proposed duties for two centers in applications orientation. It was discussed with an Air Force research office. Colonel Burroughs signed a memo on briefing boards. The center would prepare seven boards of coverage photography. They were for the Environmental Protection Agency's monitoring office. Support to an Air Force photo unit in the same building also appears.
cia-0000139369: Terms of reference for National Intelligence Estimate 11-4-61, Main Trends in Soviet Capabilities and Policies 1961-1965, are forwarded in this May 1961 memorandum from Acting Deputy Assistant Director Willard Matthias. Representatives are asked to meet on 12 June in the Administration Building to discuss the terms, covering annexes A and B. The surviving sample is the routing memorandum, not the estimate's judgments themselves. It shows the machinery by which the intelligence community framed its five-year Soviet forecast at the Cold War's Berlin-crisis moment.
cia-06157969: INTELLIGENCE COMMUNITY'S INPUT ON CW USE FOR STUDY ON CBW ARMS CONTROL, a CIA document. The chemical weapons input. This file preserves that declassified paper. The paper lived through the years. It awaits future readers.
cia-06759869: A North Korean publication got the agency's eye on April 24, 1969. The CIB article drew analysis. The Pyongyang press, monitored. The file is now open to the public. This declassified CIA paper is stored. The text is preserved.
cia-06769269: SUSPICION OF COMMANDER OF EXECUTIVE MANSION GUARD BEHIND THE KILLING OF BUCHAN, a CIA document. The Liberian killing. This file preserves that declassified paper. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
cia-06790969: JAMES HAROLD WILSON (UNITED KINGDOM), a CIA document. The prime minister's file. This file preserves that declassified paper. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all. The paper lasts as a quiet witness to its time.
cia-06830669: CENTRAL INTELLIGENCE BULLETIN - 1958/09/04, a CIA publication. The September briefing. This file preserves that declassified bulletin. History keeps its place secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
cosmopolite-ov-novvelle-lvmiere-chymique: Cosmopolite, ou nouvelle lumière chymique, 1669. The French cosmopolite. This book preserves that work. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
cymbeline-pg2269: The wager shames Innogen in this edition: Iachimo's false proof of her infidelity drives Posthumus to order her death. Lost princes, a wicked queen, and Jupiter's descent resolve the tangle. The romance of romances, improbable and enchanting.
die-alchemie-das-ist-die-lehre-von-den-g: Die Alchemie, 1869. The German alchemy history. This book preserves that work. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Future scholars will discover it.
dunraven-experiences-spiritualism-home-1:
Lord Adare kept a log of dark nights in Experiences in Spiritualism with Mr. D. D. Home, out in 1869. Adare, heir to an earl, sat with Home through 1867 to 1869. He writes each night's feats as they came: sounds, moves, forms, and a famed float past the panes of a high room in London town.

His rank and calm tone gave the tales great weight. The log was meant for a small ring, yet soon roamed wide. It is the best guest's eye tale of the top seer at work. Doubt it or not, it grips.
europmc-pmc10244169:
Moliner and a large team report that psychedelic drugs promote brain plasticity by binding directly to a receptor called TrkB, in a 2023 study. Psychedelics can lift depression fast and for a long time, and they help the brain form new connections. Approved antidepressants were recently found to act partly through the same TrkB receptor.

The team shows that psychedelics grip TrkB far more strongly than standard antidepressants do. That binding drives the growth of new connections in their tests. The finding may let chemists design the healing effect without the hallucinations.
europmc-pmc10266069:
Li and colleagues review the crosstalk between ferroptosis and the networks that control mitochondria in a 2023 paper. Ferroptosis is a form of cell death driven by iron and by damage to cell membranes. Mitochondria, the cell's powerhouses, sit close to this process, since their faults raise the same kind of chemical stress.

The review maps how signals pass between the death pathway and the systems that build, split, and clear mitochondria. It shows how each side can hasten or slow the other. The authors discuss what this means for cancer and organ injury.
europmc-pmc10326069:
Meskó and Topol argued in 2023 that large language models in health care need firm rules. Such models, like GPT-4 and Bard, can write text that sounds human. Clinics may use them to draft notes, sum up papers, or chat with patients. GPT-4 can also read text inside images.

Meskó warns that these tools learn in a new way, unlike older medical software. Their answers can vary in quality, which adds risk for patients. Poor use could harm people or leak private data. The authors set out steps for rule makers to take. Their aim is safe use that still lets the tools help care.
europmc-pmc10396969:
Guo and colleagues found in 2023 that a food nutrient helps immune cells fight tumours. The nutrient is glutamine, a common amino acid. One immune cell type, called cDC1, primes killer T cells to attack cancer. The team asked what fuels that priming step.

Tumour cells and cDC1s both grab glutamine through the same gate, SLC38A2. Guo showed that adding glutamine to tumours slowed their growth in mice. It also made blocked immune therapy work again. Inside cDC1s, glutamine signals through a protein called FLCN to a gene switch, TFEB. When FLCN was lost, cDC1s failed and the glutamine gain vanished. The contest for glutamine thus helps tumours hide from the immune system.
europmc-pmc10809869:
Di Cesare and colleagues give a global snapshot of heart and vessel disease in this 2024 paper. Cardiovascular diseases, meaning diseases of the heart and blood vessels, are the top cause of death worldwide. Of 20.5 million such deaths in 2021, about 80 percent were in low- and middle-income countries. The authors pull together the burden, the risk factors, health spending, and policy action by region.

High blood pressure stands out as the leading risk factor, tied to 10.8 million deaths in 2019, they report. Death rates are highest in Central and Eastern Europe and Central Asia. Policy scores vary widely, with parts of Africa scoring lowest. The authors urge each country to study its own risk profile. They back core steps such as tobacco control, steady access to heart drugs, and units in health ministries for these diseases.
europmc-pmc10869269:
van Kempen and colleagues built a faster way to search protein shapes in this 2024 paper. AI tools now predict millions of protein shapes, which are the 3D forms proteins fold into. Searching those vast shape libraries had become a bottleneck for labs. Older search tools were exact but slow.

Their tool, Foldseek, turns a protein's inner contacts into a string of letters from a shape alphabet. Text-style search then finds matches at high speed. The authors report speed gains of ten thousand to one hundred thousand fold over older tools. Measured against three classic tools, it kept 86, 88, and 133 percent of their sensitivity, the authors report. That trade pairs near-classic accuracy with a speed gain of ten thousand fold or more.
europmc-pmc11094169:
Zong and colleagues review failed cell power stations as a therapy target across diseases in this 2024 paper. Mitochondria make most of a cell's energy and run wide information networks. Their failure shows up in heart disease, brain degeneration, metabolic syndrome, and cancer. The failure is hard to pin down, since its effects vary and only show past a threshold.

The review works through concrete diseases to explain how the failure unfolds. It then sums up treatment strategies, from diet supplements to targeted drugs. One advanced plan transplants healthy mitochondria to replace damaged ones, with promise in early animal trials. Parts of mitochondria themselves, including their DNA and small RNAs, may serve as drugs. The authors note many strategies have now reached human trials.
europmc-pmc11645269:
Marsh and a large team show that a standard lab step distorts gene readings in brain immune cells in this 2022 study. Single-cell sequencing starts by breaking intact tissue into a soup of single cells. Protocols were tuned for cell yield, not for keeping gene activity true to life. The team tested what enzyme-based breaking does to brain tissue.

The enzyme step switched on an aberrant set of genes outside the body, most strongly in microglia, the brain's immune cells, they found. That false pattern is widespread in published work and can substantially skew later analyses. The team offers a rigorously tested protocol that keeps in vivo profiles, cell-type mix, and yield, across tissue types and species. A like pattern showed in human brain data taken after death. Heat exposure outside the body induced it in fresh human tissue.
europmc-pmc1240669:
Gubler and co-authors weighed climate effects on insect-borne disease in 2001. Plague, malaria, and dengue once circulated in the United States. Land use, farming, housing, and control efforts pushed most out. Wild animal cycles still carry some infections today.

Most such diseases follow clear seasonal patterns. Rain and heat shape both insects and the germs they carry. Warmth can help or hurt survival depending on species. Global travel adds a steady risk of new imports. Gubler warns forecasts must weigh many factors beyond temperature alone. Zoonotic cycles in wild birds and mammals persist in many areas.
europmc-pmc1266369:
Bendtsen, Kiemer, Fausbøll, and Brunak reviewed odd protein export in bacteria in 2005. Some proteins appear outside cells without the usual export tag. The team compiled all known cases from the literature. Pattern searches hunted for a shared hidden signal.

No signal or motif covered most of the listed proteins. The authors conclude export truly follows a novel route. Still, the proteins differ from stay-at-home proteins in composition. They show distinct structure and disorder patterns. Bendtsen built a prediction method from those traits. Some exported proteins moonlight with second jobs inside cells.
europmc-pmc1513269:
Brain wiring looks wasteful, with long links spanning far regions. Kaiser and Hilgetag tested in 2006 whether brains place parts to save wire. They ran a layout optimizer on wiring data from monkey cortex and a worm's nerve net.

Rearranging parts could cut total wiring by 32 percent in the monkey and 48 percent in the worm. Long links are what make the real layouts costly. But stripped-down layouts with only short links needed far more steps to pass signals. Kaiser argues brains trade wire length for short processing paths. Neural design seems to prize speed of routing over cheap cabling.
europmc-pmc1513569:
A 30-question survey measures how well a hurt arm or shoulder works. Gummesson, Ward, and Atroshi tested an 11-question short form in 2006, the QuickDASH. They pulled short-form answers from full surveys filled by 105 patients before surgery and months after.

QuickDASH scores ran a few points higher than full scores, by 4.2 points at the start. Both forms tracked change after surgery with like strength. Both told apart patients who felt much better from those who did not. Test-retest scores were steady. Gummesson concludes the short form keeps the full form's value while easing the burden on patients and clinics.
europmc-pmc1781469:
Sharif and co-authors mapped in 2007 how immune cells called macrophages respond to a bacterial product named lipopolysaccharide, or LPS. LPS switches on NF-kappaB, a protein that controls genes for inflammation, cell growth, movement, and survival. Losing control of that switch is tied to septic shock and chronic inflammation.

The team treated a lab macrophage line, THP-1, with LPS for one and four hours. Of 465 candidate NF-kappaB target genes, 72 changed clearly, falling into four time patterns. Follow-up tests confirmed 34 of them, including genes not known before as LPS targets. THP-1 cells matched macrophages grown from human blood closely. A second lab line, U937, responded very differently, which warns against trusting that model.
europmc-pmc1794469:
Karakitsos and colleagues ran a randomized trial in 2006 on placing central lines in the internal jugular vein, a large neck vein used in critical care. One group of 450 patients had real-time ultrasound guidance, where the clinician watches the needle on a screen. The other 450 patients had the standard landmark method, guided by surface anatomy alone.

Access time and number of attempts fell sharply in the ultrasound group. Harm was also far more common with landmarks. There, the carotid artery was punctured in 10.6 percent of patients, with blood collections in 8.4 percent and catheter-linked bloodstream infection in 16 percent. Chest complications such as air or blood in the chest cavity also clustered in that group. The authors conclude ultrasound guidance should be the method of choice.
europmc-pmc1878469:
Wu, Skolnick and Zhang extended in 2007 a method that predicts a protein's three-dimensional shape from its letter sequence alone. When a close cousin's shape is known, modeling is fairly direct. For orphan sequences in the structure database, the shape must be built from scratch, and progress there had been slow.

Their I-TASSER method runs an existing threading and refinement pipeline again and again, feeding each round's output into the next. On 16 small proteins under 90 building blocks, its models landed within an average error the authors report in angstrom units, with six models very close to the true shape. Quality matched a leading all-atom simulation while using a tiny fraction of the computing time. A second test on 20 proteins under 120 blocks confirmed the method folds small single-domain proteins well.
europmc-pmc2089069:
May and co-workers presented the Normalization Process Model in 2007, a theory for how complex health interventions become routine. Complex interventions mix behaviour, technology and organisation, making them hard to evaluate and embed. Trial results alone do not explain why a practice sticks or fails. The model focuses on factors that promote or block routine embedding in everyday care.

The authors define the model formally and test whether it is consistent and adequate. It explains normalisation through four factors. Interactional workability covers how people use the intervention together. Relational integration covers trust and accountability, while skill-set workability covers who does the work. Contextual integration covers organisational support. The team argues the model supports process evaluations inside trials and fair comparisons between interventions.
europmc-pmc2124869: A medical paper on the aestivo-autumnal parasite, its sexual cycle in the circulating blood of man. The malaria's romance. This article preserves that parasitology. History keeps its place secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day.
europmc-pmc2124969: A medical paper on pure cultivation of a new spiral organism, Spirochaeta phagedenis. The new germ. This article preserves that bacteriology. Tomorrow's readers will find it. It holds its historical place. Those who study the era will use it.
europmc-pmc2125069: A medical paper contributing to the mechanism of connective tissue growth. The tissue's growth. This article preserves that histology. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. It awaits future readers. Time has kept the file intact through the years.
europmc-pmc2125469: A medical paper with further studies on Treponema pallidum and syphilis. The pox again. This article preserves that venereology. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
europmc-pmc2125769: A medical paper on the cyclic changes in the mammary gland under normal and pathological conditions. The breast's cycles again. This article preserves that histology. The paper lived through the years. It awaits future readers.
europmc-pmc2131669: A medical paper with studies on yellow fever in South America, transmission experiments. The jungle fever again. This article preserves that tropical medicine. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2140769: A biology paper with micrurgical studies in cell physiology, the action of chlorides. The salted cells. This article preserves that cell biology. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
europmc-pmc2180269: A medical paper on the relative reaction within living mammalian tissues, on the course of events. The tissues' chemistry. This article preserves that physiology. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
europmc-pmc2265669:
Wang and a very large team mapped genetic admixture in 2008 across thirteen Mestizo populations in seven Latin American countries. Mestizo populations descend from European, Native American and African ancestors, making them promising for admixture mapping of disease genes. No genome-wide characterisation existed. The team analysed 678 autosomal and 29 X-chromosome microsatellite markers, short repeating DNA stretches used as ancestry signposts, in each population.

Ancestry varied extensively between populations and individuals. Native American and European shares were both large, while African ancestry was generally low. Admixture often involved European men with Native and African women, a sex-biased pattern. Native ancestry within Mestizos matched the pre-Columbian peoples of each local area, showing admixture drew on nearby Native groups. The findings carry direct implications for designing association studies in the region.
europmc-pmc2311269:
Firmann and a large team set out the CoLaus study in 2008, a survey of heart and metabolic risk in Lausanne, Switzerland. Metabolic syndrome is a cluster of risks such as high blood pressure, high blood sugar, and extra body fat. The study also searched for genes linked to those risks.

The team examined 6,188 adults aged 35 to 75, chosen at random from the city. Each person got detailed health checks and gene typing on a chip that reads half a million DNA sites. High blood pressure affected 36.7% of people, and abnormal blood fats affected 34.2%, while obesity affected 15.7% and diabetes 6.6%. Rates were higher in men than in women, and rose with age.
europmc-pmc2323569:
Humphries and Gurney tackled a measurement problem in network science in 2008. Many networks, from brain wiring to social ties, are called small-world. That means nodes cluster tightly, yet any two nodes stay a few steps apart. Until then the label was a yes-or-no call, with no graded score.

They defined a score, S, that balances strong local clustering against short path length. A network counts as small-world when S is above 1, and that claim can be tested with statistics. Across a large set of real networks, S rose in a straight-line pattern with network size. They also showed how to assign one matching standard model, the Watts-Strogatz model, to any real network. That put model comparisons on firmer ground.
europmc-pmc2481469:
Payen and colleagues in the SOAP study, short for Sepsis Occurrence in Acutely Ill Patients, linked fluid overload to death in kidney failure in 2008. The data came from a European snapshot study of 3,147 intensive care patients at 198 hospitals in 24 countries. Of those, 1,120, or 36%, developed acute renal failure during their stay.

Sixty-day death rates were 36% with kidney failure versus 16% without. Patients making little urine died more often, at 41% versus 33%, and those needing dialysis machines died at 52% versus 32% in this cohort. Among kidney failure patients, average fluid balance, how much fluid the body retained, stood as an independent risk factor for death alongside age and illness severity. Patients put on dialysis early fared better than those started late. The authors concluded that positive fluid balance is not a side detail but a driver of worse outcomes.
europmc-pmc2526269:
Canto, Wouterlood, and Witter reviewed in 2008 what the wiring of the entorhinal cortex implies about its job. This small brain region is the main gateway between the cortex and the hippocampus, the structure that supports memory. The standard picture casts it as a simple relay: surface layers pass information in, deep layers send the hippocampus's output back.

New findings strain that picture, including grid cells, neurons that fire in a repeating spatial pattern, found across all its layers. The authors argue the layers differ less in their inputs and outputs than in their internal organisation. Each layer also gets its own very specific input set. On their reading, the entorhinal cortex shapes and computes signals for memory circuits rather than merely passing them along.
europmc-pmc2553769:
Puigbò, Bravo, and Garcia-Vallve introduced a web tool called CAIcal in this 2008 paper. The tool serves the Codon Adaptation Index, a score for how well a gene's codon choices match those a cell prefers. Genes use several equivalent codons for the same building block, and matching the host's favourites usually means the gene is read efficiently.

CAIcal bundles the related calculations in one server, free to use online or download. It computes the index for single genes and plots it along a sequence, or across an alignment of related proteins converted back to DNA. It also calculates the value expected by chance, which helps users judge whether a score is meaningful. The authors offer it as an aid for studying gene adaptation and annotating genomes.
europmc-pmc2559869:
Lu and colleagues analysed in 2008 the collected links between microRNAs and human diseases. MicroRNAs are tiny RNA molecules that tune gene activity, and reports tying them to illness were piling up without a clear overall pattern. The team hand-collected the published associations. They built a network connecting microRNAs to the diseases they are reported to disturb.

Clear patterns emerged from the network. MicroRNAs tended to carry similar evidence for similar diseases and different evidence for different ones. MicroRNAs expressed in many tissues were linked to more diseases than tissue-specific ones. More conserved microRNAs, those little changed across species, also showed distinctive disease links. Groups of microRNAs known to act together kept turning up sharing the same diseases. The authors say that pattern can point to new disease candidates.
europmc-pmc2680969:
Briese and co-authors identified in 2009 a new virus behind a deadly bleeding fever outbreak in southern Africa. Five people fell ill, and four died, after the sickness spread within a hospital. No known virus matched. The team read RNA from patients' blood and tissue with unbiased high-speed sequencing, a method that names whatever germ is present.

Within 72 hours of receiving samples, they had a full picture. The culprit, named Lujo virus, belonged to the arenavirus family, kin to Lassa fever virus, but branched off at the very root of the Old World branch. It was the first new fever arenavirus found in the Old World in thirty years. One of its surface proteins sat oddly between the Old and New World families, hinting it may enter cells by a different door. Its distinctness, the authors warn, shows how much viral diversity still hides undetected.
europmc-pmc2688469:
Spencer, Su, Donnelly, and Marchini set out in 2009 how to design genome-wide hunts for disease genes so the money is well spent. Two choices dominate: which commercial gene chip to buy, and how many patients and controls to type. Vendors advertised chips by coverage, the share of variants captured, but the authors argue coverage is the wrong scorecard.

What matters is statistical power, the true chance of catching a real culprit variant. Because variants travel in correlated blocks, power cannot be computed by formula; it must be simulated. Their simulations of case and control samples, built to mimic real correlation patterns, compared all major chips across effect sizes and populations. Big coverage gaps often shrank to trivial power gaps. Filling in untyped variants by imputation, educated guessing from neighbors, also bought real power cheaply. On a fixed budget, the best buy is often more samples, not the densest chip.
europmc-pmc2688669:
Vaughan and colleagues found in 2009 that malaria parasites need their own fat-making machinery at exactly one step of their life cycle: the jump from liver to blood. The parasite carries a bacterial-style fat synthesis pathway in a small internal organ, long assumed vital in the blood stage that causes disease. The team deleted its key enzymes in a rodent malaria species.

Blood growth, mosquito stages, and the first invasion of the liver all proceeded normally without the pathway, a genuine surprise. Two separate enzyme knockouts agreed. Liver stages grew, but then failed at the last step: they could not form the invasive packets that burst out to seed the blood. Deleting the same enzyme in the human parasite likewise left blood growth untouched. A drug target once aimed at blood malaria, the authors conclude, belongs instead to the liver-to-blood handoff, useful for prevention rather than cure.
europmc-pmc2700969:
Kover and colleagues built in 2009 a new kind of mapping population for the plant Arabidopsis, crossing nineteen wild strains together instead of the usual two. Hunters of trait genes were stuck between two imperfect tools: simple two-parent crosses with little variety, and wild surveys with tangled structure. Their design, called MAGIC, intermates many parents, then inbreeds the mix into stable lines.

The first panel holds 527 lines, each a mosaic of the nineteen founders, typed at 1,260 markers. Simulations say a gene explaining ten percent of a trait's variation will usually be located within about 300,000 letters. The team proved the panel on real traits, pinning known genes for germination timing and flowering with high precision and finding new ones besides. Doubling the lines would sharpen the aim further. It is, they argue, a community resource for dissecting complex traits finely.
europmc-pmc2702369:
Sreeramareddy and colleagues reviewed in 2009 how long tuberculosis patients wait before being diagnosed, a delay during which they sicken and infect others. Reports from single studies varied wildly, so the team systematically gathered the literature from 1990 to 2008 across major databases and specialist journals. Fifty-two studies on confirmed lung tuberculosis qualified.

Total delay, from first symptoms to diagnosis, averaged anywhere from 25 to 185 days across studies. The wait split almost evenly between two halves. Patients themselves delayed about 29 days on average before seeking care. Health systems then took about 25 more days to reach the diagnosis. Poor and rich countries looked surprisingly alike on both halves. With treatment programs already curing most diagnosed patients, the authors argue, the next gains lie in finding cases faster, on both sides of the clinic door.
europmc-pmc2712069:
Singh and co-authors showed in 2009 that Hsp90, a helper protein that shapes other proteins, drives resistance to echinocandin drugs in the yeast Candida albicans. This yeast is a leading fungal cause of severe disease in people with weak immunity. Echinocandins are the newest drug class against it, and they block building of the fungal cell wall.

Weakening Hsp90 by drugs or by gene changes cut drug tolerance in lab strains and resistance in patient strains, and made the drug pairing kill the fungus. The effect ran through calcineurin, a client protein of Hsp90 that helps cells handle stress. Lowering Hsp90 in infected mice also made an echinocandin work better.
europmc-pmc2838869:
Bullard, Purdom, Hansen, and Dudoit compared statistical methods in 2010 for RNA sequencing, the technique that counts gene messages by sequencing them. Their test data came from a quality-control project with matching precision measurements for about a thousand genes, letting them check which methods call real changes and which call noise.

For well-counted genes, the main tests agreed. For genes with very low counts, near ten reads or fewer, the tests split sharply in reliability. Longer genes were more often called changed, a bias the authors show can be eased by weighting for gene length. The usual scaling by total reads per lane also skewed results, and quantile-based scaling, which aligns count distributions, did better.
europmc-pmc2991069:
Moyes and colleagues showed in 2010 that mouth lining cells answer the fungus Candida albicans in two waves, distinguishing its harmless yeast form from its invasive thread-like form. The fungus lives quietly in many mouths yet can turn pathogenic.

The first wave, shared by both forms, follows recognition of the fungal wall and switches on a general defence programme. The second wave arrives only with thread forms at higher burdens, switching on different regulators and inflammatory signals. The authors cast this second wave as a danger response that lets tissue tolerate low burdens yet react hard to damage.
europmc-pmc3076369:
Hajibabaei, Shokralla, Zhou, Singer, and Baird tested in 2011 whether DNA barcoding with high volume sequencing can replace slow species sorting in river health monitoring. Rivers are judged by the small invertebrates living on their beds, but naming those animals under a microscope is slow and often cannot reach species level, especially for young stages. The team compared three approaches on the same samples.

Sequencing short barcode pieces from a pooled mixture correctly found every species present above a small abundance threshold. It missed a few rare species, yet it also detected DNA from species no one had spotted in the sample, a hint it can find the rare ones too. Applied to real rivers, it separated an urban site from a protected one cleanly. The authors say the approach is not yet fully tuned, but it could let monitoring programs survey far more sites at species level.
europmc-pmc3166269:
Catrine Tudor-Locke and colleagues translated activity guidelines into daily step counts for children and teenagers in a 2011 paper in a behavioural nutrition journal. Official advice speaks of minutes of vigorous play, but step counters report steps, so families and researchers need a fair conversion. The team reviewed the world literature on measured youth activity.

Boys typically log several thousand more steps than girls, and totals slide steadily through the teens. An hour of brisk activity corresponds roughly to the low-to-mid teens of thousands of steps in school-age children, and a somewhat lower band in teens. Preschoolers reach their activity target within a lower step range. The authors stress the numbers are early and call for studies tying step counts directly to health outcomes.
europmc-pmc3174969:
Brent Williams and colleagues examined gut tissue from autistic children with digestive trouble in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. Gut symptoms are common in autism and hard to manage, and hints of weak sugar-digesting enzymes motivated a closer look. The team read gene activity and bacterial makeup in intestinal biopsies from autistic children with gut disease and from children with gut disease alone.

Biopsies from autistic children were low in the enzymes that split common sugars and in the transporters that absorb them, a defect tied to a gut control gene's activity. Their gut bacteria were also skewed, with one major group depleted and another overgrown, and the shifts tracked the enzyme shortfall. The findings link host digestion genes and gut microbes in one picture of these children's gut problems.
europmc-pmc3252369:
Elaine Morazzani and colleagues discovered a second antiviral small-RNA system in mosquitoes, reported in this 2012 paper in PLoS Pathogens. Mosquitoes carry many viruses without dying, and a response based on small interfering RNAs was known to keep alphavirus infections in check. The team found infection also triggers another class of virus-derived small RNAs.

These molecules resemble piRNAs, a class previously known from reproductive tissues, where they are made by a ping-pong amplification cycle from repetitive DNA or dedicated clusters. Here they arose in ordinary body cells during infection. Evidence from mutant mosquito cells unable to make the interfering RNAs suggested the piRNA-like molecules can themselves moderate how sick the infection makes the host. The authors propose the pathway works alongside the known system as a redundant antiviral defense.
europmc-pmc3264469:
Chengxiang Wang and colleagues reviewed what governs the sensitivity of metal oxide gas sensors in this 2010 article in Sensors. These conductometric sensors, whose electrical resistance changes on contact with gases, are widely used for detection. Because sensing happens through reactions on the material's surface, anything that changes those reactions changes how strongly the device responds.

The brief review works through five such factors: the chemical makeup of the sensing layer, modifications applied to its surface, the layer's microstructure, and the operating temperature and humidity. Each can be tuned, or can interfere, and the authors explain the direction of the effects. The paper gives sensor designers a compact map of the levers available for sharpening sensitivity and the environmental conditions that can quietly erode it.
europmc-pmc3308069:
Schiff and colleagues pooled safety data for the arthritis drug tocilizumab across its clinical trials, reporting in 2011. The drug blocks signals from a molecule that drives joint inflammation in rheumatoid arthritis. Patients from the main trials could keep taking it in follow up studies, giving the team a long view of side effects in more than four thousand people.

Total time on the drug passed eight and a half thousand patient years. Rates of side effects and serious side effects stayed steady over time rather than climbing with longer use. Serious infections were the most common serious problem, while gut perforations, cancers, heart attacks, and strokes stayed rare. The authors conclude that the longer term safety picture matches what the first year of trials had shown.
europmc-pmc3310869:
Díaz, Zikhali, Turner, Isaac, and Laurie reported in 2012 that extra copies of flowering genes change when wheat blooms. Flowering time decides whether a wheat crop succeeds in a given climate, and breeders have reshaped it for centuries. Two key genes govern the response to day length and the need for winter cold. Yet some varieties with altered timing carried no spelling change inside those genes.

The team found the answer in copy number instead. Varieties carrying extra copies of the day length gene flowered early and ignored day length, a trick that arose at least twice on its own. Extra copies of the cold requirement gene did the opposite, demanding a longer cold spell before flowering. The work shows that counting gene copies is a real force in crop adaptation.
europmc-pmc3328769:
Henderson and fellow members of a validation task force reported the outcome of the group's first meeting, held in 2010 and published in 2012. Electron microscopy now produces three dimensional maps of large molecular machines, and models built into those maps are deposited in public archives. The field lacked shared standards for judging whether a map or model is trustworthy.

The workshop brought together scientists who collect the images, compute the maps, and fit atomic models into them. They discussed how to assess each kind of deposit and what checks archives should require. Their recommendations aim to raise the reliability of deposited data and so increase the value of the technique for biology and medicine. The meeting review records the discussion and the agreed next steps for building validation tools.
europmc-pmc3330269:
Rubio-Perez and Morillas-Ruiz reviewed the role of inflammation in Alzheimer disease, focusing on messenger proteins called cytokines, in a 2012 article. Alzheimer is the most common disease that destroys memory and thinking, and its brain hallmarks include sticky plaques and tangled fibers. The authors argue that inflammation is not a side show but a driver of the damage.

Immune cells in the brain, support cells, and defense proteins all join the process. Certain cytokines fan the flames, with one, interleukin 1, flagged as an early trigger that sets off a self feeding cycle ending in nerve cell death. Others calm the response and protect the brain. Painkillers of the common anti inflammatory kind seem to lower risk when taken for years, yet trials in patients disappointed. The authors point to plant polyphenols as a possible fresh direction.
europmc-pmc3434369:
Baglio, Pegtel, and Baldini reviewed in 2012 the tiny vesicles that mesenchymal stem cells release, and the chance to treat patients with the vesicles instead of the cells. These adult stem cells gather at damaged and cancerous tissue and calm immune responses. Yet few transplanted cells actually settle and survive, so their benefit seems to flow from what they secrete.

Among the secretions, lipid vesicles ferry proteins, fats, and above all varied RNAs between cells, steering repair responses. Early results suggest the vesicles share their parent cells' protective and healing powers and may even fight tumors. A cell-free therapy would dodge many risks of live-cell treatment, from rejection to unwanted growth. The authors map what is known and what must be proven.
europmc-pmc3463569:
Moja and colleagues pooled past studies on hip fracture surgery timing in a 2012 PLoS ONE meta-analysis. Older patients often wait a day or more for their operation, and doctors disagreed on whether that delay costs lives. The team searched several large databases for studies that recorded both timing and survival.

Their pool covered 35 studies with more than one hundred ninety thousand patients. Surgery within about two days was linked with a lower risk of death and fewer pressure sores. Moja's group found no patient trait that explained away the gap. They urge hospital services to operate on most hip fracture patients within one or two days of arrival.
