Microorganisms, including germs, viruses, fungi, and other eukaryotes, play serious roles in human health. Results like these feed the work that turns lab findings into future treatments.
europmc-pmc9925769: This 2023 research paper covers immunotherapy (treatment that boosts the immune system) in breast cancer: an survey of current plans and views. Recent progress in immunobiology has led the way to successful host immunity (immune defense) enhancement against breast cancer. If later work backs it up, the finding could open a new path for treating the illness.
europmc-pmc9988869: Zhu and co-authors published this research paper in 2023 on CD36<sup>+</sup> cancer-linked fibroblasts provide immunosuppressive microenvironment (the tissue surrounding a tumor) for liver carcinoma (a common type of cancer) via secretion. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
finney-character-claims-of-freemasonry-1:
Charles G Finney, a leading revival preacher, published his attack on Freemasonry in 1869. Finney said he had once been a Mason himself, and he wrote as a Christian minister alarmed by the lodge. His target was not one lodge but the whole system.

Finney examined Masonic oaths, claims, and daily practice, and argued that they conflicted with Christian faith and honest public life. He warned that secret pledges could place a brother Mason above church, family, or court. The book became a key text for evangelical critics, and it shows how sharp the clash between revival faith and lodge loyalty could be.
frus-1861-d169:
Carl Schurz wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 15 July 1861. The dispatch is document 169 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Schurz wrote with the flair of the journalist he had been. His Madrid reports mixed court fact with sharp judgment of men. This July letter shows the new minister finding his feet at a proud, formal court in wartime. His flair for phrase later made his memoirs a classic of the German American story. A classic memoir grew from the same pen that penned these wartime pages. The same pen later wrote a classic memoir.
frus-1861-d269:
By the date of 23 November 1861, Seward had new word ready for James Shepherd Pike, the American minister to the Netherlands. Congress received it as Document 269 in the papers printed with the President's message that year. The letter comes from the autumn of the war's first year, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1861-d69:
One of three letters dated 17 August 1861 went from William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams. The letter is document 69 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

The date 17 August opens a cluster of three Seward letters to London in one day. Each took up a point of its own, from notes to claims. Together they show the range of business that crossed the Secretary's desk in the war's first summer. The cluster form of 17 August shows in the printed file as three short papers in a row. Three short papers in a row show the file at its most clerk neat that summer.
frus-1862-d169:
Printed as Document 169, the third Seward dispatch of 25 October 1862 went from Washington to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. Together the three letters show one day's full output from the Secretary of State's desk to his British post.

Short letters, sent often, were how a government without cables ran an embassy in wartime. Each one might carry a single order or a single piece of news. A lone dispatch like this one grows in value when read in its cluster. Set in that stream, it helped keep London and Washington in step. Adams reported home at least once a week, and oftener when the news was hot.
frus-1862-d269:
On 22 April 1862 William L. Dayton sent Secretary of State William H. Seward a report printed as Document 269 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It was one of two Paris papers under that date, the other being a Seward dispatch.

Late April brought the Union flag back over New Orleans, a loss the South felt in every European counting house. Cotton, credit, and sympathy all shifted with such news. Dayton's report from Paris that week belongs to the record of how France absorbed the blow to the Confederate cause it was tempted to aid. Policy at Napoleon III's court was made in private, so an envoy's ear mattered as much as his pen.
frus-1862-d369: A translated paper dated 31 July 1862 stands as Document 369 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Filed in the French section after the Mercier letters. The heading marks it only as a translation, giving no author or reader. So the entry rests on its date, its form, and its place among the French papers of that summer.
frus-1862-d469:
George Perkins Marsh wrote from Turin to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 4 April 1862. His dispatch is Document 469 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, laid before Congress with the annual message.

Spring 1862 found Italy watching France closely, since French troops still guarded the pope in Rome and French ambition was moving in Mexico. Marsh's reports linked those Italian concerns to the American war, which shared the same French question. From Turin he could also report the new kingdom's steady sympathy for the Union. The letter is part of the volume's Italian file, where diplomacy ran on shared national hopes rather than on fear or bargaining.
frus-1862-d569:
Henry Shelton Sanford sent this report from Brussels to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 26 September 1862. It is Document 569 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed with the annual message.

Sanford wrote four days after Lincoln's emancipation order was issued, though the news was still crossing the Atlantic. His report covered the Brussels scene as it stood: the court's connections, the press, and the war's standing in Belgian opinion. Within days he would have the emancipation news to work with, and few ministers used it more eagerly. The letter catches the Belgian file at the hinge of the autumn. The war's new moral shape had not yet reached Europe. When it did, it changed Sanford's brief for the better.
frus-1862-d669:
On 24 December 1861, Anson Burlingame wrote from China to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Burlingame was the American minister there, a former congressman turned envoy. His letter is document 669 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862.

A Christmas Eve date on a letter from the far side of the world hints at the pace of the post. Mail from China took months to reach Washington, so envoys wrote often and covered much ground in each sheet. Burlingame's dispatch is part of that steady flow, the raw stuff from which the State Department built its view of China in the war years.
frus-1862-d69:
Home in Washington, Seward read a fresh report from Charles Francis Adams, dated 22 May 1862. Congress received it as Document 69 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. By then, in the spring of 1862, a year into the war, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Readers get the field report side of the exchange, sent home for Seward to weigh and answer. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1863p1-d169:
Charles Francis Adams closed a three-letter day with this dispatch of 24 April 1863 to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 169 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The last of Adams's three sheets wound up the legation's work for a peak day in the file. His spring letters, read whole, are the story of the Union's cause in Britain told by its keeper. This one ends the 24 April set. It stands in the record as a working piece of the watch that kept Britain's fleet and yards from the South.
frus-1863p1-d269: Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, sent this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 21 August 1863. It is document 269 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, part of the London correspondence on Britain and the Civil War. Letters on this route carried Adams's reading of British policy while Washington worked to keep Britain from backing the Confederacy.
frus-1863p1-d369:
A formal note dated 26 January 1863 passed from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, in Washington. It stands as document 369 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

British subjects caught up in the war, as sailors, traders, or prisoners, gave London steady grounds for protest. Seward's notes answered those complaints one case at a time. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d469:
A 20 April 1863 dispatch from Secretary of State William H. Seward reached Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war? At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral.

The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. The stakes behind this routine mail were high. If Britain had backed the Confederacy, the war could have changed course, so each note helped hold the line of British neutrality. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1863p1-d569:
William H. Seward, Secretary of State received a letter dated 17 June 1863 from Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight.

The formal tone can hide the tension, but the pace gives it away. Notes this frequent mean both capitals were watching each other closely. Much of the mail between the two offices turned on ships: the Union blockade, seized cargoes, and Confederate agents buying vessels in British ports. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1863p1-d669:
Among the day's business on 19 November 1863 was a letter from Charles Francis Adams to William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London, and Seward was Secretary of State in Washington. Mail between London and Washington crossed the Atlantic by steamer, so each reply took weeks to complete the round trip. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight.

From the London end, the work was pressure and reporting. Adams pushed the British government on Confederate shipbuilding and sent home his reading of British politics and opinion. Read in sequence, the London letters show how close the two countries came to open conflict, and how both sides kept stepping back. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1863p1-d69:
William H. Seward sent this letter to Charles Francis Adams on 2 February 1863. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 69 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, opening Seward's February mail in the file.

February brought no rest to the London brief. The South's agents still worked for ships and friends in Britain, and the Union's claims still needed pressing. Seward's letters kept Adams supplied with the government's views and the facts from home. This one opens a run of February sheets that runs thick in the volume, proof of how much of the war was fought with pens.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d169: A second letter from Roosevelt to Hull is dated October 26, 1943, and it stands as Document 169 of the Cairo and Tehran volume, in the Moscow Conference section. Two presidential letters to his secretary in one day, across an ocean and a war, kept the home government's hand firm on the talks. The record names the parties and the date. The letter's text is printed in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d269:
Minutes of the Combined Chiefs of Staff meeting at Cairo on 25 November 1943, at half past two in the afternoon, take up Southeast Asia operations. Admiral Mountbatten reports his meeting of the day before with Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek on the Burma campaign plan.

Chiang had insisted on the larger plan, for which the resources did not exist. It needed 535 more transport aircraft. He settled for the smaller one once the chiefs were formally asked for the planes. He also demanded a seaborne operation alongside the land advance in north Burma. On airlift over the Hump, he held out for the full 10,000 tons a month against a promised average of 8,900. Mountbatten asks for Chiang's agreement to the campaign in writing.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d369:
Minutes of the Combined Chiefs of Staff meeting at Tehran on 30 November 1943 record a morning session at half past nine. The Western staffs were trying to agree a basis for that afternoon's plenary session with the Soviets. Landing craft, once again, decide nearly every question.

Brooke proposes a sequence. Italy comes first, with Eisenhower keeping his landing craft until 15 January to reach the Pisa-Rimini line. Rhodes follows only if Turkey enters the war. Then comes the south of France, with craft from Rhodes returning in time. Leahy answers that the whole knot is Overlord's date: the Russians want it fixed in May, and if that date stands, other operations must fit around it. The British doubt the returning craft can be repaired and their crews trained in time, and ask for American repair facilities.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d469:
President Roosevelt wrote to President Bishara al-Khouri of Lebanon on December 3, 1943, during the conference season at Cairo. Lebanon had just come through a crisis in November, when French authorities arrested its leaders and then released them under pressure, leaving Lebanese independence recognized in fact. The letter appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume.

Roosevelt's message reached a small new state sitting at the center of Allied supply lines and Arab politics. American interest in Lebanon mixed wartime logistics with sympathy for independence from the French mandate. For readers, the letter shows the President tending ties far beyond the Big Three table where the cameras pointed.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d569:
The American consul at Colombo, Ceylon, wrote to Secretary of State Edward R. Stettinius on January 9, 1945. Stettinius had succeeded Cordell Hull at the department the month before. The consul's report appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume, far from the conferences themselves.

Colombo was a working port on the sea roads to Southeast Asia, and consuls there reported on shipping, local politics, and the war's edge in the Indian Ocean. A report from such a post shows how widely the conference volumes cast their net for related records. For readers, it is a reminder that the global war was also administered from small offices in distant harbors.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d69: A second message from Churchill to Roosevelt dated October 29, 1943 stands as Document 69 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Splitting the day's business into two notes was the prime minister's habit when matters differed in kind. The record does not say what set this note apart from its companion. Both are printed in the Foreign Relations series, in the pause between the Moscow Conference and the November summits.
frus-1944-quebec-d169:
The President's Log for the Quebec Conference opens with a foreword by Lieutenant George Elsey. Quebec, he notes, marked the eleventh wartime meeting of Roosevelt and Churchill. The foreword looks back over the road from their first meeting at Argentia in August 1941, where the Atlantic Charter proclaimed their war aims, through Washington, Casablanca, Cairo, and Tehran.

Elsey then describes the war as the leaders gathered in September 1944. Allied armies had swept across northern France and entered Germany, Alexander was cracking the Gothic Line in Italy, and Soviet forces stood at the gates of Warsaw. Rumania and Bulgaria had fallen away from Germany, and the American Navy had just struck Mindanao. Only in China, he writes, were Allied fortunes unfavorable.
frus-1944-quebec-d269:
The combined memorandum on troop movements, forwarded September 13, 1944, examines what Operation Dracula would do to allied shipping. The buildup meant moving six British divisions, 370,000 men, from Europe to India before March 1, 1945. At its peak the movement would absorb virtually the entire British trooping lift, and a decision was needed by October 1 to beat the monsoon.

The costs elsewhere were plain. British help on the Atlantic run would fall to about 25,000 men a month, with only the two Queens sailing it. All British ocean-going troopships would leave cross-Channel work, removing 25 to 30 thousand troop spaces. Indian ports would be fully absorbed, except Calcutta for American troops.
frus-1944-quebec-d69:
Prime Minister Churchill wrote to President Roosevelt on September 14, 1944, in the middle of the Second Quebec Conference. Both men were at Quebec City, and the conference was then deep in its hardest argument, over Germany's future. The message appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

Mid-conference letters carried proposals between the Citadel's sessions, where Roosevelt lodged with Churchill as his guest. September 14 fell in the days when the Morgenthau Plan was accepted, then began to unravel. For readers, a message from that moment catches the summit at its most consequential, in the leaders' own hand-to-hand written style.
frus-1945-50-intel-d169:
The meeting named in the title took place on 25 September 1946, and these minutes are its formal record. The State Department prints it as document 169 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. The National Intelligence Authority, set up in January 1946, oversaw the Director of Central Intelligence and his Central Intelligence Group.

Minutes are the formal record of a meeting: who sat in, what was put on the table, and what the group agreed to do. They rarely give long speeches, but they fix the choices that later memos then carry out. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d269: Dated 4 May 1948, "Policy Planning Staff Memorandum" comes from the top level of the government. Readers meet it as document 269 of the Foreign Relations series volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. It was the CIA's first full year, and the Council was setting the rules for both open analysis and secret work. Inside the government, memos were how business got done between meetings.
frus-1945-50-intel-d369:
A memorandum from the Assistant Director for Reports and Estimates (Babbitt) reached Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter on 17 February 1949. The State Department prints it as document 369 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. While the survey team asked its questions, the CIA's covert arm was growing fast under Frank Wisner.

Such notes moved business along: they told a busy reader what had happened, what it meant, and what should come next. The points are stated once and left to stand; the file around it holds the answer they drew. Its worth lies in the trail it leaves: a dated, signed step in the long build-up of the CIA and the Council.
frus-1945-50-intel-d69:
Harold Smith, the budget director, set down a memorandum on his own part in the settlement on 9 January 1946. Smith rarely wrote without a purpose, and self-recording was among his habits. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

Memoranda written for the file by the men who shaped events are gifts to readers, when read with care. Smith knew his bureau's plan had largely won, and his paper helps explain how. Set beside the secretaries' joint letter of the same week, it shows the two tracks of the settlement. The departments agreeing in public, the budget director noting in private how the agreement was built. The volume's balance of open and office papers is nowhere better shown.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d169:
Bulgaria is a testing ground for the three allies, this briefing book paper warns. “Principal Bulgarian Problems” was prepared for the President's trip and is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. The armistice signed at Moscow on 28 October 1944 had set Bulgaria on a wholly new course.

The United States seeks neither an equal share with Moscow in the Control Commission nor the lead. What it wants is a clearer charter for the commission, with the rights and duties of the American team made safe. Washington also reserves the right to reopen the question, once Germany is beaten, of making the body truly three-sided. One sore point is flagged: Bulgarian reparation and restitution deliveries to Greece need speeding, and Soviet foot-dragging is expected.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d269:
President Roosevelt asked for a war crimes report on 3 January 1945. His memorandum to the Secretary of State is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It wants two things. First, the state of the work before the War Crimes Commission. Second, the American representative's stand on the charges to come.

The charges, Roosevelt directs, should include an indictment for waging aggressive and unprovoked warfare, in breach of the Kellogg Pact. Hitler and the chief Nazi war criminals are the named targets. Perhaps, he adds, that charge and others like it might be joined in a single conspiracy indictment. The short paper is an early sketch of the legal road that ended at Nuremberg.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d369:
Alger Hiss listed the room before the talk in his notes of February 7, 1945: Stettinius, Molotov, and Eden, with aides ranked behind them. Stettinius opened by offering to clear up any open points on Dumbarton Oaks. Molotov thanked him but had no new points ready. Then came the report on France.

The ministers, Hiss records, agreed that France should have a zone of occupation in Germany, held by French forces. Molotov and Stettinius wanted France's seat on the Control Commission studied by the European Advisory Commission. Eden wanted admission agreed at once. Hiss's lines catch a real split between the Western partners.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d469:
Roosevelt was to carry a piece of news to King Ibn Saud, under this draft memorandum of February 11, 1945. At the final foreign ministers' meeting, held after the President left, Eden proposed adding Saudi Arabia to the nations invited to San Francisco. Molotov and Stettinius agreed — subject, a scrawled note says, to Russian refusal being overcome.

The kingdom would qualify if it declared war by March 1. Stettinius judged the move desirable. The President should tell Ibn Saud when they met in the next few days. Colonel Eddy, the American minister traveling with the King to the cruiser Quincy, should also be informed. The draft ties Yalta to Roosevelt's desert meeting.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d69:
Background on the unfinished business of Dumbarton Oaks fills this editorial note in the Malta and Yalta volume. Rather than write a fresh summary, the editors quote the State Department's book Postwar Foreign Policy Preparation, pages 374 and 375. The quoted passage sets up the document group that follows.

When the Dumbarton Oaks Proposals were published on 9 October 1944, six questions were still open, the voting question among them. Work on them began at once under a senior committee chaired by Acting Secretary Stettinius. By 1 November he could report the President's plan: settle the open items at a conference with Churchill and Stalin.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d169:
The British Chiefs of Staff added one item to the staff conference agenda in a memorandum dated June 25, 1945. The paper, C.C.S. 880/1, is document 169 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It builds on their draft agenda of June 15, which had covered the Pacific war from end to end.

The new eleventh item looks past the fighting: Combined Chiefs of Staff machinery after the war with Japan. The British say they will submit a paper on the subject as a basis for discussion. The addition is a small sign that planners on both sides were already thinking ahead. They were asking what would become of the joint war machine once Japan fell. They were also asking whether the Anglo-American partnership that ran the war could outlive it.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d269:
The Joint Civil Affairs Committee warned against home-grown national governments in an undated memorandum printed as document 269 in the Foreign Relations volume on Potsdam. The paper draws a lesson from Soviet sponsorship of the Renner government in Austria and from earlier Soviet experiments with a committee of German officers.

The three powers agree that central agencies will run Germany and Austria for now, and that democratic governments may come one day. But no one has agreed that an occupying power will not recognize, on its own, a body claiming national authority. The United States should urge that no such body be recognized, nationally or in a zone, until all four governments agree and the Control Council has fixed its powers. Local cooperation in each zone would remain allowed.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d369:
Grew cabled Secretary Byrnes, then at sea, on July 7, 1945, to endorse Pauley's Moscow achievement. The agreed recommendations in Pauley's cable of July 6, he writes, conform fully to Pauley's instructions. Those instructions came from the Informal Policy Committee on Germany, were cleared with the Joint Chiefs, and were approved by the President.

Winning the agreement of his Russian and British colleagues, Grew adds, was a considerable achievement for Pauley. He recommends that the Secretary send Pauley a message of concurrence and gratification. The short cable is Washington's pat on the back, sent while the Secretary sailed toward Potsdam.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d469:
Premier Parri is sized up in Kirk's strictly confidential cable from Rome, sent at midnight on July 6, 1945. Kirk had talked with Parri the previous evening. The gist of the Premier's remarks was the necessity of material aid to Italy, with stress on the immediate need for coal to prevent further unrest in the north. He stressed, too, the difficulty of reconstruction under the armistice regime's restrictions.

Personal contact, Kirk writes, confirms the general impression of Parri's seriousness, simplicity, and intellectual distinction. Yet he showed none of the vitality, alertness, or assurance even Bonomi displayed, and no sign of dynamic leadership. With such a cabinet, Kirk judged, speculation about Italy's course was nearly useless.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d569:
From Caserta on June 24, 1945, Ambassador Alexander Kirk sent an urgent secret extract to Washington. It is document 569 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Kirk explains how news of the Yugoslav reservation on article 3 reached his staff late.

Kirk says General Morgan reported the signing of the Duino deal with no word of any exception. Belgrade learned of it first, since a British officer, Colonel Clarke, sat in on the talks. Morgan then held back the text until he could explain it at a meeting. Only there did he name the reservation. The extract shows the top Allied staff in Italy learning of a key flaw in their own deal from the side lines.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d669:
Thomas Wasson, acting chief of the African Affairs desk, recorded a talk on Tangier dated July 6, 1945. His memo is document 669 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The French embassy's counselor, Lacoste, had called on Loy Henderson in Washington.

Lacoste raised the question of Soviet delegates in the Paris talks. Henderson said the Department knew the development well. Soviet ambassador Gromyko had called on Acting Secretary Grew on the morning of July 2. Gromyko expressed surprise that Moscow had not been invited to exchange views on Tangier. He said his government was interested in the zone's future and asked that the Paris talks be put off. A Soviet expert, he said, should be arranged to take part before they went on.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d69:
Secretary of State Edward Stettinius cabled President Truman from San Francisco on June 16, 1945. The urgent top secret telegram is document 69 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Stettinius had just heard that the State Department had sent Truman a tentative list of staff for the Big Three meeting.

Stettinius stresses that the list is only tentative. He wants to talk with Truman while both are in San Francisco about the size and make-up of the party, so the number of State Department people matches the President's own thinking. He asks for a few minutes to settle it before the list becomes final. The short cable shows the staffing of the American delegation still open a month before the conference.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1069: George Allen sent James Dunn this memorandum extract at Potsdam on July 25, 1945. It lists his understanding of the final decisions on five Near Eastern and African items meant for the closing Protocol. Only the Greece passage is printed here. Allen records that the Soviet delegation declined the American and British invitation to help supervise the coming Greek elections. Their stated ground was that such supervision would mean interference in Greece's internal affairs. The other sections of the memorandum appear in separate documents elsewhere in the volume.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1169:
General Arnold, chief of the Army Air Forces, wrote to Ambassador Harriman in Moscow on 20 July 1945. Arnold commanded American air power across the world. Harriman was the president's envoy to the Soviet Union and a key voice on Soviet affairs.

A letter between the air chief and the Moscow envoy links two worlds: the war in the air and the talks about the peace. Air bases, routes, and Soviet ties all touched both men's work. This message shows that wiring in use during the summit. It reminds readers that Potsdam's paper trail ran far beyond the town in Germany where the leaders sat.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1269:
The British Chiefs of Staff issued this memorandum on 20 July 1945. It follows their paper of two days before in the volume's run. The British staff kept its own steady pace of advice as the first week closed.

Each note took up the military questions as London's chiefs saw them: forces, fronts, and the means to hold what the talks might win. This one continues that series. Together the British memoranda form a staff diary of the summit from the soldiers' side. They let readers trace how the military view held or shifted as the bargaining moved.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1369:
The Soviet delegation presented another proposal at Potsdam on 22 July 1945, one of a run of Soviet papers in the volume's last section. Each proposal fixed Moscow's wording on a point under dispute. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

Reading the Soviet papers in order shows a method: state a claim in full, then bargain down only as far as needed. This proposal came as the conference moved past first speeches into hard drafting. For students of the talks, the value lies in contrast. Readers can set what the Soviet side tabled beside what all three leaders signed at the end. The gap between those texts is the story of Potsdam in brief.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-69:
Charles Bohlen's minutes record a private Byrnes-Molotov meeting on July 23, 1945, at 9:30 a.m. They are an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. The Secretary had asked for the meeting out of deep concern over German reparations.

Byrnes restated the U.S. aim first. America had always favored an overall policy treating Germany as an economic whole. But Soviet positions heard at Potsdam, he said, could not be reconciled with any overall reparation plan. Handing a large part of 1937 Germany to Polish administration was one such position. Maisky's wide definition of war booty was another working against the plan. Byrnes then made the U.S. limit very plain. The United States did not intend to pay out money to finance imports to Germany, repeating the last war's pattern of American funds paying reparations.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d769:
The Soviet delegation tabled this proposal at Potsdam on July 24, 1945, as document 769. Soviet texts arrived through the conference's middle days in steady number. Each marked a position Moscow meant to defend. The proposal was printed among the numbered papers of the second Potsdam volume.

A Soviet draft mid-conference shows aims after a week of testing. The other sides had revealed their limits. Readers can judge what Moscow still pressed and where it had softened, if at all. The document keeps the three-sided shape of the talks in view. Potsdam was a triangle, and each side's paper matters.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d869: General Lucius D. Clay, deputy military governor of the American zone, wrote to the Secretary of State from Berlin on July 21, 1945. Clay explains that General Eisenhower, after meeting the President, asked him to draft a directive for the zone commanders. The draft is attached and appears next in the volume. Clay says Eisenhower believed the directive would help the commanders and the Control Council work.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d969: J. Howard Marshall wrote this one-sentence memorandum at Babelsberg on July 31, 1945. Marshall was general counsel to the American delegation on the Allied Commission on Reparations. The note answers a drafting question: how should the proposed reparations plan enter the final conference agreement? His answer is simple. The most satisfactory way is to attach the plan to the Economic Principles as Annex I. Section 16 of those principles already refers to such an annex. The brevity of the note is itself the record of a settled drafting point.
frus-1964-68v06-d169: A 1964-1968 FRUS editorial note from the early 1968 Vietnam volume. The Tet year. This note provides that background. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years.
galton-hereditary-genius-1869:
Francis Galton published Hereditary Genius in 1869, his first book on inherited ability. He collected the family histories of judges, statesmen, scientists, and other eminent men. Patterns in those pedigrees drive his whole argument.

Galton claims that talent clusters in families because nature outweighs training. He ranks relatives by closeness and counts how eminence fades with distance. The inquiry launched the nature-versus-nurture debate in modern form. It also launched eugenics, whose harms readers must keep in view. The statistical ambition was real; so were the blind spots. Galton later expanded its methods into the statistical study of human differences generally.
gao-gaoreports-b-295569: Scot filed a March 2005 twin protest — two dockets — and GAO's combined ruling answers both. The firm's double claim got one careful response. Both filings faced the same referee. The referee was even-handed. The response was careful. The twin was answered.
gao-gaoreports-b-299369: AMS Group took its April 2007 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the call. The firm challenged the award as unfair; the ruling tests the claims in full. Short names get the same long, careful hearing in the protest process as the big players.
gao-gaoreports-b-299469: Knight's Armament Company took its April 2007 weapons-contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the call. The arms maker challenged the award; the ruling tests the claims in full. Even gun deals go through the same bid-law mill as everything else.
gao-gaoreports-b-308969: Parking money in open-ended deals drew GAO's fiscal eye in 2007 — could funds be obligated this way under the interagency pact? The ruling reads the purse law against the contract vehicle. The call decides where the budget lines really sit.
gao-gaoreports-b-309869: KIC Development cried foul on a 2007 federal award, and GAO's ruling is the final word. The firm said the bid contest was run unfairly; the call tests each charge and rules. gao-gaoreports-gao-05-169: AWACS spare parts buying needed fixing in 2005, and GAO's report says the Air Force should improve its purchasing. The review writes the shopping list. The radar planes deserved the parts. The buying had to improve. The radar planes deserved the parts.

The military kids deserved a fair look. The assessment had to continue. The military kids deserved a fair look.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-669: The Army's battlefield internet hit snags in 2005, and GAO's report says the build risks had to be solved soon. The findings demand the solutions. The report warns that the battlefield net deserved doing right. The battlefield net deserved doing right.

gao-gaoreports-gao-06-169: The Bureau of the Public Debt's schedules got a GAO audit in 2005, and the report examines the federal debt figures for 2005 and 2004. The findings grade the accounting. The report shows the nation's IOUs were checked. The schedules had to be sound.

The findings demand the upgrade. The report warns that the secrets deserved better locks. The policies had to be improved. The secrets deserved better locks.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-669: The air toxics program needed better management in 2006, and GAO's report says EPA should improve its handling. The findings demand the upgrade. The report warns that the poisons in the air deserved serious management. The program had to be managed well.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-769: Unemployment insurance financing spread the burden in 2006, and GAO's report says states' tax systems allowed costs to be shared among industries. The findings explain the mechanics. The report shows the safety net's funding was a team effort. The sharing had to be fair.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-869: Checked-bag screening oversight needed strengthening in 2006, and GAO's report says TSA's watch over the procedures could improve. The findings target the gaps. The report warns that the luggage line was a security line too. The oversight had to be strong.

grettir-saga-magnusson-morris-1869:
Grettir the Strong killed a ghost, outlived a curse, and held out as an outlaw for nineteen years in Iceland. His saga, translated by Eiríkr Magnússon and William Morris in 1869, tells of strength wasted by temper and fate. Grettir could beat any man or monster, yet could not master his fear of the dark.

Hauntings, wrestling matches with the undead, and lonely winters on a sea-girt rock fill the tale. Morris loved the sagas and helped give them their English shape in versions like this one. The Story of Grettir stands as the greatest of the Icelandic family sagas in outlaw form, grim and human at once.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lubliner-hugo-p:
Hugo Lubliner (1846– ), who wrote under the name Hugo Bürger, was a German dramatist born at Breslau. A Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906 by Isidore Singer and Newell Dunbar profiles him. He studied at Berlin’s industrial school and managed a cotton and woolen mill. Playwriting drew him from business, first as a sideline, then full time.

The article lists dozens of his plays from 1865 to 1899, mostly comedies for German theaters. Successes include the one-act “Nur Nicht Romantisch,” which still held the stage, and “Der Frauenadvokat” of 1873, performed at all the principal German theaters. Later titles include tragedies, dramas, and two novels in a cycle on Berlin under the empire. Four volumes of his dramatic works appeared at Berlin in 1881–82. The entry works as a full play list for a popular stage writer.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-manissa-the-anc:
Manissa, the ancient Magnesia ad Sipylum in Turkey, is given a community entry in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. The town stands twenty-eight miles northeast of Smyrna. Of its forty thousand people, some 1,800 were Jews. The community is said to be older than Smyrna's own.

The article draws on travelers' reports and local detail. Pococke, visiting about 1733, found its Jews rich exporters and calico makers. Tournefort counted three synagogues in 1702; by 1904 there were five. Their names include Shalom, Mayorca, and Toledo, a map of the community's roots. Charities dowried brides, aided mourning families, and shod the poor. A small hospital opened in 1869. Alliance schools for boys and girls arrived in the 1890s, teaching Hebrew, French, and Turkish. The entry records a complete Ottoman Jewish community at the moment modern schooling reached it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mannheimer-magy:
Gustav Mannheimer, called Magyar, a Hungarian painter, gets a very short entry in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Born at Budapest on February 27, 1854, he trained at drawing schools in four cities. Budapest came first, then Munich, Vienna, and Rome. The entry names no teachers and gives no account of his later career.

What the article does give is a short list of his best-known canvases. On Flowery Mead and Italian Evening Landscape show his landscape work. Procession at Anacapri points to time spent painting in Italy. Young Tramps turns to figure subjects instead. The notice rests on a single source, Singer's general artists' lexicon. For a period reference, the entry still has value. It fixes a painter's training and chief works in a few lines, keeping a minor artist from vanishing altogether.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-masseket-or-mas:
"Masseket," the word for a tractate of the Talmud, is defined in a short Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906 by Solomon Schechter and S. Mendelsohn. The term literally means "a web," from a Hebrew verb for weaving, much like the Latin "textus" behind the English word text. In practice it names any gathered collection of rabbinic teaching on a subject, whether a treatise of the Mishnah alone, a set of baraitot, or Mishnah together with its Gemara.

The article then does the counting. The Mishnah holds sixty-three tractates, though ancient authorities said sixty, because they reckoned the three Babas as one tractate and Sanhedrin with Makkot as one. The Babylonian Gemara covers thirty-seven tractates and the Palestinian thirty-nine. It ends with the so-called minor tractates printed with the Babylonian Talmud, seven of which Kirchheim edited in 1851.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meir-ben-eliaki:
Meir ben Eliakim was a German liturgist who probably lived at Posen toward the end of the seventeenth century. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn give him a short entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His known work is “Meir Elohim,” printed without place or date. It gathers the biblical passages a worshiper should recite on entering the synagogue. It adds ethical directions for prayer, instructions on how to pray as much as what to say.

In that book Meir mentions two further collections of prayers he called “Menorot,” lamps. Steinschneider, whose catalogue is the only authority of the entry, thought a “Menorah” printed at Prague in 1696 might be one of them. The whole notice is three facts deep. Yet it fixes a name, a probable city, and a shelf of devotional books. Without it they would be anonymous.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meza-christian-:
Christian Jacob Theophilus de Meza was a Danish physician and author born in Copenhagen on November 26, 1756. Richard Gottheil and Frank Cramer profile him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was the son of the physician Christian de Meza. Father and son embraced Christianity together in 1783. That same year he took his medical degree at Copenhagen.

From 1784 until his death in 1844, Meza practiced medicine at Elsinore. He published essays in the medical journals on mixed pregnancy, an epidemic fever, and a rare abnormal twin birth. One paper was reprinted in French and American journals. He also wrote a drama staged at Copenhagen's Royal Theater in 1796. His son Christian Julius became a Danish general in the 1864 war with Germany.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-miracle-lit-won:
Miracle, defined as an event no ordinary natural agency can explain and therefore an act of a higher power, opens a theological Jewish Encyclopedia article by Kaufmann Kohler, published in 1906. Kohler's first move is a distinction: a miracle is not a myth. Myths personify nature's powers as gods; miracles subject all nature to one higher will working out holier designs.

Miracle is thus, for Kohler, essentially monotheistic, even where an old myth has been recast as a prophet's or saint's wonder. In the Bible the category is broad: whatever breaks the ordinary course counts as a wonder, preeminently the wonders in Egypt by which God's power was made known. He alone does wonders, the psalmists say, and nothing is too wonderful for him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-montpellier-heb:
Montpellier, capital of the Hérault in Languedoc, held one of southern France's most important Jewish communities from the later eleventh century, as Isidore Singer and S. Kahn write in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its Jews, trading with coreligionists worldwide, built much of the city's commerce. In Hebrew letters the town was simply Har, the Mountain.

Their second gift was medicine: Montpellier's famous medical school grew with Jewish help, and in 1180 Guillem VIII granted Jews the right to practise. Aragonese kings later required them to pass the regular examinations like everyone else — a proviso that tells how far they had risen. The article traces their standing as physicians on into the year 1300.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-cordovero:
Moses Cordovero was a physician who lived at Leghorn in the seventeenth century. The Jewish Encyclopedia entry, by its editorial committee and Meyer Kayserling, rests chiefly on the praise of Conforte. Conforte calls him a good physician and praises his scholarship and his giving.

One habit of his is singled out. Cordovero was always eager to free prisoners, working through his own influence where he could and paying ransom where he could not. He died at an advanced age. The brief notice keeps the name of a doctor remembered as much for charity as for medicine.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mosessohn-marke:
Miriam Mosessohn, born Wiersbolowsky, was a Russian Hebrew writer born at Kovno in 1841. Herman Rosenthal and A. S. Waldstein wrote her Jewish Encyclopedia entry. At thirteen she moved with her parents to Suwalki, where she kept up her Hebrew studies. She also devoted herself to German and French language and literature.

Mosessohn translated German novels into Hebrew, starting with Philippson's The Refugee from Jerusalem, which stayed in manuscript. Family troubles kept her from giving herself fully to the work. Only one book of hers reached print: Ha-Yehudim be-Angliya, printed at Warsaw in 1869. It is a Hebrew version, in pure and elegant style, of Francolm's work on the Jews and the Crusaders.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nagawkar-benjam:
Benjamin Shalom Nagawkar was a Beni-Israel soldier born at Bombay before 1830. Joseph Jacobs and J. Hyams wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He enlisted in the Twenty-fifth Regiment of Bombay Native Light Infantry in 1848. He rose step by step to subahdar-major in 1879.

The entry is a service record, battle by battle. Nagawkar fought at Dhar, Jhansi, the Betwa, Calpee, and the capture of Gwalior, winning medal and clasp. He served through the Abyssinian campaign as well and took its service medal. He retired in 1881, a senior Indian officer of the Bombay army.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nathan-moses-b-:
Moses b. Solomon b. Nathanael was a Provençal writer of verse for worship. Gotthard Deutsch and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His dates and birthplace are not known. Even his homeland is given only as Provence. What survives of him is his poetry. One poem is didactic, teaching through verse.

His teaching poem is called Toze'ot Hayyim, or Results of Life. It runs to fifty-eight sections in all. Menahem di Lonzano printed it in Shete Yadot at Venice in 1618. Dukes later reprinted part of it in 1844. Moses is also thought to have written a Sabbath hymn. That hymn, Ahabah be-Ta'anugim, appears in most prayer-books.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-neumann-carl-fr:
Carl Friedrich Neumann was a German scholar of the East. Isidore Singer and Newell Dunbar wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Reichmansdorf on Dec. 22, 1798. His parents bore the name Bamberger. He died in Berlin on March 17, 1870.

Neumann began in business, then studied at Heidelberg and Munich. He taught at Speyer, but religious words cost him his post. He learned Armenian at Venice and Chinese in Paris and London. In China in 1830 he gathered ten thousand books. Munich made him keeper and professor of Chinese. Progressive views cost him that post in 1852. His works span Armenia, China, Russia, and America.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-no-amon-11569:
No-Amon is the Bible's name for Egyptian Thebes. The entry was written by the Editorial Board's Executive Committee and J. Frederic McCurdy for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The name means No, city of the god Amon. Nahum and Jeremiah both use it of Thebes. Egyptian speech made it the city above all.

Thebes stood at the center of Nile traffic. Ethiopia's trade passed through it as an emporium. It first headed the fourth nome of Upper Egypt. The eleventh dynasty took its seat there early. After the Hyksos fell, it stayed the capital. Thothmes and Rameses raised Karnak and Luxor there. Assurbanipal's captures hastened its long decline afterward. By Ptolemaic days it was Egypt's great ruined city.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-offenbach-jacqu:
Jacques Offenbach made French comic opera a form of its own. Isidore Singer and Joseph Sohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Cologne on June 21, 1819. He died at Paris on October 5, 1880. His father was cantor of the Jewish flock at Cologne.

Offenbach went to Paris at the age of thirteen. He read the cello at the music school there. He then played in the band of the Opéra Comique. Tours as a solo player brought him little fame. So he turned to the stage and to song. In 1855 he opened a house of his own. It was the Bouffes Parisiennes, in the Passage Choiseul. Many of his best loved works were first sung there.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-orleans-or-1176:
Orleans is the chief city of Loiret, in France. Richard Gottheil and S. Kahn wrote its long entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its Jewish group dates from the sixth century. Church councils met in the city in that age. Those councils set harsh laws against the Jews there.

In 533 a council barred wedlock of Jews and Christians. A Christian who broke that rule faced casting out. In 538 Jews were barred from the streets at Easter time. Clerks were told not to eat with Jews at all. In 541 a new set of rules came down. A Jew who made a convert lost all his slaves. King Gontran came to Orleans in the year 585. Jews in the crowd hailed him with a Hebrew speech. He met their words with scorn, the piece says.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pe-ah-corner-or:
Pe'ah is a treatise of the Mishnah about gifts to the poor. Its name means corner, the corner of the field. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The treatise stands second in the order Zera'im.

The laws rest on verses in Leviticus and Deuteronomy. A farmer must leave the field's corner for the poor. The treatise runs eight chapters with many fine points. It defines which fields count as one field. It sets the time and manner of giving. It also lists good deeds that earn reward in this world.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-peter-of-alessa:
Peter of Alessandria was an Italian monk of the fourteenth century. Crawford Howell Toy and Joseph Jacobs wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Alessandria, in Italy. His fame rests on two Latin translations. He worked daily between the Hebrew and Latin worlds.

About 1342 Pope Clement the Sixth asked for his work. Peter rendered Levi ben Gershon's treatise into Latin. The treatise described Gersonides' new star-measuring tool. That tool later bore on the finding of America. Peter also translated Gersonides' forecast on Saturn and Jupiter.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pinkhof-herman-:
Herman Pinkhof was a Dutch physician based in Amsterdam. Isidore Singer and E. Slijper wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Rotterdam on May 10, 1863. He took his degree at Leyden in 1886. His practice served Amsterdam for many years.

Pinkhof wrote on medical ethics for a Dutch journal. In 1895 he founded a society for Judaism's interests. From 1898 he led the fight against Neo-Malthusian teaching. He argued that cause in many printed articles. He also served on the seminary board at Amsterdam. His learning joined medicine, ethics, and Jewish life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pontremoli-esdr: Esdra Pontremoli was an Italian rabbi, poet, and teacher born at Ivrea in 1818. Isidore Singer wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was the son of Eliseo Pontremoli, rabbi of Nizza. A street in that town later bore his father's name. In 1844 Esdra became professor of Hebrew at Vercelli. For fifteen years he helped edit the Educatore Israelita. He turned a Hebrew work of Luzzatto into Italian verse. That poem came out at Padua in 1879. He died in 1888.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-priority-12369:
Priority in Jewish law means whose claim on goods comes first. The Editorial Board and Lewis N. Dembitz wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Part of the rules deal with deeds and bonds on land. Those rules are told in another article of the set. What is left is the case of a wife's claim.

A widow or a parted wife claims her marriage sum first. Plain creditors of the husband claim the same goods too. The Talmud gives its rules in Mishnah and Gemara. The husband's marriage writ binds him to pay back her dowry. That writ is the root of the wife's strong claim. The article works out who is paid first, and why.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-raba-b-joseph-b:
Raba ben Joseph ben Hama was a Babylonian teacher of the fourth set. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Mahoza in about the year 280. His father was a rich and noted scholar there. Raba died at Mahoza in the year 352.

As a youth Raba went to Sura for his learning. He heard the lectures of Hisda in that town. He kept company with Rami ben Hama as well. Years after Rami's death, Raba wed his widow. She was a daughter of Hisda, his old teacher. The entry traces his teachers and his ties of blood and marriage.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rapa-portrapa-s:
Simhah ben Gershom ha-Kohen Rapa was a Talmudic scholar born at Porto, Italy. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and A. S. Waldstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was a younger cousin of Menahem Abraham Rapa. He later called himself Portrapa.

The article says Simhah studied at Venice in his cousin's house. His teacher was Samuel Judah Katzenellenbogen, rabbi of Venice. In 1593 he settled at Prossnitz in Moravia. He then moved to Vienna and stayed until his death. His one named work is Kol Simhah, from 1602. It is a hymn acrostic for Saturday. The entry follows a scholar across Italy and central Europe.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-reland-adrian-1:
Adrian Reland was a Dutch Christian Hebraist born on July 17, 1676. Crawford Howell Toy and Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Ryp near Alkmaar. He died at Utrecht on February 5, 1718.

The article says he studied Hebrew and rabbinics at Amsterdam. In 1699 he took the chair of Oriental languages at Utrecht. His works include Analecta Rabbinica from 1702. He wrote on ancient Hebrew coins as well. His Sacred Antiquities went through five editions. His Palestine, from 1714, carried eleven maps. Both books long stood as standard authorities, they say. The entry honors a Christian scholar of Hebrew antiquity.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-riparian-owners:
Riparian owners are landowners along a river bank. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Lewis N. Dembitz wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. The Holy Land had little river navigation. So the Mishnah says little about bank owners' rights.

The article finds one rule about irrigation for peace. Upper owners may draw canal water before lower owners. On the Euphrates, river traffic was heavy, they note. Men walked the shore dragging boats by long ropes. Rabbis ordered all trees cut along both banks. That cleared room for the boatmen's shoulders at the ropes. Trees fell with or without the owner's consent. No notice to the owner was even required. The entry shows public need trimming private rights.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosenthal-jacob:
Jacob Rosenthal was a Polish physician at Warsaw, a son of David Rosenthal. Herman Rosenthal and Max Rosenthal wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He studied medicine at Berlin and at Warsaw, his home city.

In 1870 Rosenthal joined the Jewish Hospital at Warsaw as a staff physician. He gave himself to the diseases of women, then a growing field. Through his efforts a women's section opened at the hospital in 1894. He directed that department for more than a decade afterward. He also described the hospital in print and wrote a medical handbook for women.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sammter-asher-1:
Asher Sammter was a German rabbi born at Derenburg on January 1, 1807. Isidore Singer and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. From 1837 to 1854 he served as rabbi and preacher in Liegnitz.

At Liegnitz Sammter introduced German preaching and the confirmation ceremony to his congregation. From 1869 he lived in Berlin, writing to the end of his life. He published the Babylonian Talmud's Baba Mezia with German translation and notes. His Mishnayyot gave all six Mishnah orders in Hebrew with German renderings. The plan ran to forty parts, but only the first numbers appeared.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sancho-sandje-o:
M. Seligsohn and M. Franco wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, issued with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board in 1906. It treats Sancho as a family name. The name occurs often among Oriental Spanish Jews. Several writers bore it. The entry gives short lives of each, one by one.

Abraham ben Ephraim Sancho was a Turkish physician and Hebrew poet at Constantinople. He wrote poems praising other men's books. Eliezer ben Sancho, a rabbi of the late seventeenth century, lost most of his works in a fire. His commentary Dat wa-Din survived. Another Ephraim ben Sancho debated religion before the king of Aragon. A third Ephraim served as court physician in Portugal. He then won the same post with Sultan Maḥmud II at Constantinople.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schiffer-feiwel:
Herman Rosenthal and Peter Wiernik wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Feiwel Schiffer. He was a Russian Hebraist and poet. Schiffer was born at Lasezow, in the government of Lublin, about 1810. He died sometime after 1866. He lived at Josefov, Brody, Szebrszyn, and Warsaw in turn. He ranked among the best-known early Maskilim of Russian Poland.

Schiffer's Ḥaẓerot ha-Shir, from 1840, is an epic poem on the patriarch Jacob. His Maṭṭa' Leshem treats farming and country life. He wrote a life of Prince Paskewitsch in 1845. His Toledot Napoleon, a history of Napoleon, came out in two parts. He also turned Knigge's book on dealing with people into Hebrew. That translation appeared at Warsaw in 1866.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-secchi-pablo-ma:
Isidore Singer and Isaac Broydé wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Pablo Marini Secchi. He was an Italian Christian merchant. Secchi lived at Rome in the sixteenth century. He made a strange wager with a Jew named Samson Ceneda. The bet was whether Santo Domingo would be conquered. The terms shocked even that age.

If Ceneda lost, he owed Secchi a pound of his own flesh. If Secchi lost, he owed the Jew 1,000 scudi. The Jew lost the wager. Secchi then demanded the penalty in full. Word reached Pope Sixtus the Fifth. The pope punished both men for making such a bet. The article notes that Shakespeare used the tale in The Merchant of Venice. He reversed the characters there, making the Jew the creditor.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shabbat-shubah-:
Shabbat Shubah falls between New Year and the Day of Atonement. Cyrus Adler and Wolf Willner wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on it. Its name comes from its prophetic reading, opening, Return, O Israel. People also call it the Sabbath of Repentance.

The day sits within the ten days of penitence each autumn. Its reading comes from Hosea, with verses from Micah added. Polish custom inserts a passage from Joel as well. In medieval times the rabbi himself preached on this Sabbath. That sermon called hearers to repent before the fast. The entry links a calendar date, a reading, and a yearly call to change.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-solomon-ben-jud:
Solomon ben Judah of Châteaulandon was a French Talmudist of the thirteenth century. Wilhelm Bacher and A Peiginsky wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He lived at the end of that century in France. He debated a case about an antedated document with colleagues. His partners were Samson of Chinon and Eliezer ben Joseph.

The same question was also laid before Solomon ben Adret. Solomon of Châteaulandon was reputed an eminent Talmudist of his day. Among his pupils was Eliezer, father of a known author. Bible glosses by Solomon are quoted in Minhah Yehudah. Some of his responsa appear in the collection of Rashba. The entry preserves his name from a handful of citations.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-spitz-abraham-n:
Abraham Spitz, called Naphtali Hirsch ben Moses ha-Levi, was a Moravian rabbi. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born about 1628 and died at Worms in 1712. In 1663 he became rabbi of a Moravian congregation.

In 1692 he became dayyan at Nikolsburg for twelve years. In 1704 he was called to Worms, where he died. His Male Razon held novellae on forty-five Talmud tractates. It appeared at Frankfort-on-the-Main in 1710 in print. An appendix explained the hardest Tosafot passages in the Talmud. Before death he told his sons to study his work daily.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-strasburg-14069:
Strasburg is a German commercial city in Alsace-Lorraine on the Rhine. Isidore Singer and A. Ury wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about it in 1906. Legend says fugitive Jews reached Alsace after the Temple fell. Records place Jews there under Charlemagne in fair conditions. They held property rights and their own courts then.

The Crusades ended that calm for Strasburg's Jews. In 1095 about 1,500 Jews were burned alive there. Violence flared again during the Second Crusade in 1146. Yet in 1160 the city held Jewish schools with famed scholars. Benjamin of Tudela noted them on his visit that year. Later sections trace privileges granted to the community. The entry gives a long, harsh civic history in brief form.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-syrkin-maximili:
Maximilian Syrkin was a Russian jurist and editor born in 1858. Herman Rosenthal and George D. Rosenthal wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He was born at Ponjewezh on October 27. He descended from the family of Joel Sirkes. He studied law at the University of St. Petersburg.

By 1905 Syrkin practiced at the St. Petersburg bar. He helped edit a registry of Russian Jewish documents. That work appeared in 1899 under a culture society. Since then he has edited the journal Voskhod. In 1900 he published a book on plastic art. It came out at St. Petersburg in Russian. The brief entry joins courtroom work with Jewish letters. Readers meet a lawyer who also guarded his people's records.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tauwitz-eduard-:
Eduard Tauwitz was a German composer born at Glatz in 1812. Isidore Singer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He was born on January 21 of that year. At Breslau he studied law at the university. He died at Prague on July 26, 1894.

At Breslau, Tauwitz chose music over a legal career. He directed the academic singing society there. In 1837 he left to lead Wilna's theater orchestra. Riga hired him in the same role in 1840. He returned to Breslau, then settled at Prague in 1845. There he taught music and later led the Sophien Academy. He wrote songs in very large numbers. Two operettas and soldiers' song sets stand out. Sets for four and five male voices survive. The entry follows a conductor across five cities.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-theudas-14369:
Two men named Theudas share this entry on Jewish life under Rome. Wilhelm Bacher and Schulim Ochser wrote it for the Jewish Encyclopedia, published in 1906. The first Theudas claimed to be the Messiah. He promised to split the Jordan River by his word alone.

Rome read the gathering as open rebellion. Cavalry under Cuspius Fadus crushed the followers. Theudas was beheaded, and his head reached Jerusalem as a trophy. The second Theudas taught law at Rome under Hadrian. He funded teachers hit by persecution there. He also brought Jerusalem's Passover lamb custom to Rome. Palestinian sages nearly banned him for that step. His sermons urged martyrdom over loss of faith.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-trachtenberg-he:
Herman Trachtenberg was a Russian jurist born at Jitomir in 1839. Herman Rosenthal and J. G. Lipman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He studied law at the University of St. Petersburg. He then entered government service in the capital. He died in his home town in 1895.

His fine service won two imperial orders. Those awards made him a hereditary citizen. He was known for compilations of criminal-case briefs. In the late 1870s he became an honorary justice of the peace. That honor was rare for a Jew in Russia. He stayed active in St. Petersburg Jewish affairs. In 1891 he worked hard for the Starodub Jews. They had suffered in anti-Jewish riots there.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ulla-called-rab:
Ulla was a leading Palestinian teacher of law around the year 300. Schulim Ochser wrote this article with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He studied under R. Eleazar II in his youth. Nine of his teacher's rulings survive through Ulla. Babylonia's exilarch often invited him to lecture there.

His travels to Babylonia were frequent and sometimes dangerous. On one journey a companion threatened his very life. He ruled on blessings and on the new moon's reckoning. His rulings were announced in Babylonia when he visited. He interpreted religious law with notable strictness. One sharp retort to R. Huna became famous. Only before R. Nahman did he hold back opinions. His sayings passed through many named students.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ventura-rubino-:
Rubino Ventura was an Italian soldier of fortune. He was born at Finale, Modena, in 1795. Isidore Singer and Umberto Cassuto wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. At seventeen he joined the militia of the kingdom of Italy. After Napoleon's fall he had to flee Italy. A quarrel with a policeman forced him out in 1817.

Ventura first served Persia as an army officer. He rose to the rank of colonel there. English rivals then pushed him out of the shah's service. He moved on to Lahore, in India. There he fought for Ranjit Sinh and won hard campaigns. His victories enlarged the Lahore kingdom. He died at Toulouse in 1858.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wertheimer-solo:
Solomon Aaron Wertheimer was a Hungarian rabbi and scholar. Isidore Singer wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Bösing on November 18, 1866. In 1871 his family moved to Jerusalem. He was educated in that city. In 1890 he lived at Cairo, collecting old Jewish manuscripts.

His many books edit rare texts from manuscripts. Batte Midrashot gathers short midrashim in four parts. Ginze Yerushalayim prints treatises with his notes. Kohelet Shelomoh collects geonic legal answers. He translated their Arabic parts into Hebrew. A commentary on the Jewish prayers appeared in 1902. His first work mourned Sir Moses Montefiore in 1885.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wohllerner-jett:
Jetty Wohllerner (1813-1891) was a Galician woman who wrote fine Hebrew letters. Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn wrote her entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Lemberg, she worked in her father's office from the age of eight. She sat in on the Hebrew lessons given to her brothers.

Her wish to learn Hebrew grew with time. At last her father hired a teacher for her alone. At fourteen she was engaged to a young man from Brody. Their letters won praise from a top scholar of the day. He called them an echo of the Song of Songs. Her groom died, and she later wed Samson Wohllerner. She kept writing, and her letters reached print in Hebrew journals.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yates-benjamin-:
Benjamin Eliakim Yates was the first minister of the Liverpool Jews. Joseph Jacobs and Isidore Harris wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He died at Liverpool in the year 1798. His father came from Strelitz in the German lands.

Yates came to England as a seal cutter on the road. He then settled at Liverpool as a gold worker. He joined that trade with the work of a minister. He led prayer, slew beasts by rite, and cut male babes. His house is thought to be the first synagogue there. Its small yard served as a grave yard for the group. Yates was the last man laid to rest in that yard. His brother Samuel then came to run the shop and shop kin.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zappert-george-:
George Zappert (1806-1859) was a Hungarian scholar of the Middle Ages. Isidore Singer and Newell Dunbar wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Alt-Ofen, he was the son of rich kin. He schooled at Pesth and at the school of Vienna.

He began the study of drugs and cures at first. In 1829 he left the Jewish faith for the Roman one. He then took up the study of church thought in earnest. In his second year a hard ill made him deaf. That blow forced him to quit that path for good. He gave his life to the study of the Middle Ages. He led a lone life at Vienna from that time. Men note that he told the hour of his death in advance. He told it three days ere it came, to the minute.
jim-davis-pg7369:
John Masefield's Jim Davis is a novel of a boy's early life, told in the first person. Jim Davis was born in 1800 in Newnham-on-Severn, Gloucestershire, as the century turned. He remembers masons shaping the two bows of a great house near his home. His nurse stopped to watch them on the green strip by the river, where gypsies camped.

His mother died in 1805, on Trafalgar day, and his father in 1809, after shutting himself away in grief. His uncle fetched him to Devonshire, and the coach journey made a deep mark on him. At Bristol he first saw big ships and spoke with sailors. The book, long loved as a boys' classic, grows from these beginnings toward the smuggling coast.
krylov-krilof-and-his-fables-1869:
Some two hundred verse fables by Ivan Krylov appear here in W. R. S. Ralston's English translation of 1869, Krilof and His Fables. Crows and foxes, wolves and lambs act out the vanities of Krylov's Russia in brief, quotable scenes. Russians call him their La Fontaine, and children there still learn the fables by heart.

Satirical and wise, the poems aimed at officials, flatterers, and fools of every rank. Krylov's lines entered everyday Russian speech the way proverbs do, detached from their stories. Ralston's version carried that national treasure to English readers early. The fables remain the most beloved poems in the Russian language by common consent. Their animals have been judging human beings for two centuries now.
lecky-european-morals-1869:
W. E. H. Lecky published History of European Morals in 1869, a classic Victorian study of moral ideas. Lecky traces how standards of right and wrong changed from the Roman Empire to his own century. He treats slavery, charity, chastity, and the treatment of animals and enemies. Pagan and Christian morals are weighed in turn.

Lecky writes with calm learning and wide reading in primary sources. He credits Christianity with raising charity, yet faults its record on tolerance and the intellect. The book became the standard history of morals for generations. Its method shaped later work on the history of ideas. It remains clear, fair, and absorbing.
leger-histoire-eglises-vaudoises-1669:
Jean-Paul Léger, a Waldensian pastor, wrote the general history of the evangelical churches of the valleys of Piedmont in 1669. His own people, the Vaudois, had kept their faith in the Alpine valleys since long before the Reformation. The book is in French. Léger wrote as pastor, witness, and exile after the massacres of 1655.

The first book sets out the doctrine and discipline of the valley churches. The second tells the persecutions, rising to the Piedmontese Easter of 1655, when ducal troops slaughtered the Vaudois and Milton's sonnet cried out across Europe. Léger prints the papers and the names. His history is the founding archive of the Waldensian memory.
macoy-general-history-freemasonry-1869:
Robert Macoy published his General History, Cyclopedia and Dictionary of Freemasonry in 1869 in New York. Macoy was a major American Masonic publisher and organizer. He meant the volume as a single reference work that a lodge member or curious reader could keep at hand.

Entries cover symbols, degrees, officers, and terms, while longer sections trace the order from early guilds to modern lodges. Biographies of noted Masons and accounts of rites in many lands fill out the survey. Macoy wrote as a supporter of the craft, not a critic. The book remains a handy record of how American Masonry described itself in the nineteenth century.
marriage-pg12669:
Marriage is a novel by Susan Ferrier, in Bentley's 1881 Edinburgh edition. A prefatory note boasts that later editions had cut the text. This reprint restores the whole from the original editions. Sir Walter Scott and Sir James Mackintosh praised Ferrier's novels.

An epigraph from Johnson sets her theme of ordinary life. Life, it says, passes in daily duties and petty pleasures. Ferrier builds her tale on two girls raised in opposite ways. Scotland and England, sense and folly, meet in their marriages. Her wit made her the Scottish Jane Austen of her day. The Noctes Ambrosianae thought her worth discussing. This edition gives her first novel complete at last.
memoirs-of-louis-xiv-and-his-court-and-o:
Volume ten of Saint-Simon's memoirs opens at chapter seventy. The reign of Louis XIV draws toward its last month of life. Plans form round the man who must lead in the young King's youth.

That man is the Duc d'Orleans, next head of affairs in the realm. Saint-Simon draws him in full: of middle height, full bodied, and easy in manner. His voice charms, his words flow, and his memory never drops a name. Grace marks even his most plain acts, by this close account. He skimmed books, yet forgot no name or date he once heard. That mix of ease and sharp recall marks the Regent's portrait.
mill-subjection-women-1869:
John Stuart Mill published The Subjection of Women in 1869, a founding text of liberal feminism. Mill argues that the legal subordination of women is wrong in itself and bad for society. What is called women's nature, he says, is an artificial product of forced repression. No one can know women's capacities until they are free.

He demands equal education, equal access to work, and the vote. The argument proceeds from utility and justice together. Mill credited many ideas to his wife, Harriet Taylor Mill. The book scandalized many Victorian readers. It remains a model of clear, principled argument for equality.
morgagni-sedibus-alexander-vol1-1769:
Giovanni Battista Morgagni founded pathological anatomy in De sedibus, first printed in Latin in 1761. Benjamin Alexander translated the work into English in 1769, and volume one begins the set. Morgagni compared the symptoms of the sick with the lesions found after death. His records drew on some seven hundred autopsies.

Letter by letter, he matches bedside stories to damaged organs. That matching created clinicopathological reasoning, still the core of diagnosis. Volume one opens a three volume English set. Doctors learned from it to ask where disease sits in the body. The change in thinking was enormous. Modern pathology starts on these pages.
morgagni-sedibus-alexander-vol2-1769:
Volume two of Alexander's 1769 English Morgagni continues De sedibus, the seats and causes of diseases. The first volume began Morgagni's letters matching symptoms to organ lesions. This volume carries the survey through the middle of his five Latin books. Its last page ends book three, as the original note records.

Autopsy reports pile up, each tying a case history to findings in the body. Chest, belly, and the organs between them receive their share of cases. Morgagni's method stays steady: observe, open, compare, and record. The volume forms the center of a three part set. Pathologists still honor the discipline shown here. It is heavy reading with heavy rewards.
morgagni-sedibus-alexander-vol3-1769:
Alexander's English Morgagni ends with volume three, printed in 1769 like its fellows. The Latin De sedibus of 1761 reshaped medicine by rooting disease in organs. This closing volume finishes the remaining books of cases. A general index ends the set, marked by the words The End.

Morgagni's letters complete their long survey of the body's seats of illness. Symptoms recorded in life stand matched with lesions found in death, case after case. The full English set runs to three volumes. Together they founded pathological anatomy for English readers. Few medical works of the century carried more weight. The index alone shows the scope.
neue-sammlung-von-einigen-alten-und-sehr:
