Printed in German in 1769, this set holds old and very rare writings on philosophy and alchemy. Its title page calls it a new sequel to the well known German Theatrum Chemicum. The catalog record counts six volumes in all. No editor or author is named for the set as a whole.

Volume one, per the record, reprints Raymond Lull's Codicil, or Vade Mecum. It adds his general practice of the great work of the quintessence. Such sets saved scarce alchemy texts from loss by putting them in one place. Readers of early chemistry and its lore can trace old claims about changing metals here.
openalex-w2047299569:
Sijia Wang, Nicolas Ray, Winston Rojas and colleagues mapped mixed ancestry across Latin America. Their paper appeared in PLoS Genetics in 2008. Latin American populations descend from several source groups. Native American, European and African roots combine there. No genome-wide map of that mixture existed yet.

Such a map can help find genes behind complex traits. The team measured ancestry in mestizo populations across the region. They compared patterns between countries and areas. Ancestry shares varied widely across Latin America. The results reflect each region's distinct history. The data form a resource for medical genetics studies. They also help correct for ancestry in disease research. The study set a baseline for later admixture mapping.
openalex-w2055698469:
Dan Stein, Wai Tat Chiu, Irving Hwang and colleagues studied links between trauma and suicidal behaviour across countries. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2010. Surveys and clinic data had suggested a connection. Few studies had separated the roles of different traumas. The team used World Mental Health Surveys.

They asked which traumas predict the first onset of suicidal thoughts. They also studied suicide plans and attempts separately. Data came from household surveys in many countries. The analysis compared people with and without trauma histories. It adjusted for mental disorders and other factors. Knowing which traumas carry the highest risk matters. Prevention can then focus on the people most affected. The study gives a global baseline for that work.
openalex-w2109730769:
Dong-Gill Kim, Rodrigo Vargas, Ben Bond-Lamberty and Merritt Turetsky reviewed gas bursts from soils after wetting or thawing. Their paper appeared in Biogeosciences in 2012. Dry soils release gas pulses when rain returns. Frozen soils do the same when they thaw. These brief events can sway yearly totals.

The review gathers studies on carbon dioxide and other gases. Microbes wake quickly when water returns. Stored gases also escape from thawing ground. Pulse sizes vary with soil and climate history. Models often miss these short events entirely. The authors suggest standard ways to measure them. Better coverage would improve global carbon budgets.
openalex-w2119690969:
G. Aad and colleagues in the ATLAS Collaboration published this search in Physical Review D in 2014. Working at the Large Hadron Collider, they asked whether very heavy new particles exist. Such particles might break down into pairs of electrons or pairs of muons. Several ideas that try to fill gaps in the standard model predict them.

The team studied proton collisions recorded by the ATLAS detector. They looked for a sharp bump in the mass of the lepton pairs. No such new particle was confirmed. Instead, the results set firm lower limits on how heavy these particles could be. A standard-model-like heavy Z boson was ruled out below a few trillion electron volts.
openalex-w2159464369:
Jean-François Flot, Jean Blanchot, Loïc Charpy, and colleagues published this study in BMC Ecology in 2011. They tested whether coral shapes match true species in the genus Stylophora. Coral form often predicts diversity poorly, and this genus looked richest in the western Indian Ocean and Red Sea, contrary to most sea life.

The team sampled corals in Madagascar, Okinawa, the Philippines, and New Caledonia. Two genetic marker sets agreed on three species in their samples, though the shapes suggested otherwise. One species lumped together several named shell forms, while look-alike shapes hid distinct species. Shape plasticity and frozen form best explain the mismatch, not cross-breeding. The genus likely arose in the western Indian Ocean.
openalex-w2191139669:
Sara Pires, Christa Fischer-Walker, Claudio Lanata, and colleagues published this study in PLoS ONE in 2015. They estimated worldwide illness and death counts for diarrheal diseases caused by nine germs commonly spread through food. Diarrhea burdens children most, yet no full estimates existed split by the germ responsible.

Working for the World Health Organization's foodborne disease group, the team drew on systematic reviews. Depending on each country's overall death rates, they applied one of two estimation routes. One built up from national incidence figures, the other adapted a child health reference method. The result is a germ-by-germ account of cases and deaths, by region, for foodborne diarrhea planning.
openalex-w2797097369:
Jorge Ovalle, Roberto Casadio, and R. da Rocha, with colleagues, extended their gravitational decoupling method to black holes in this 2018 paper in the European Physical Journal C. Black holes are prized laboratories for strong gravity and tests of general relativity. The classic Schwarzschild solution describes an empty black hole exactly. Real black holes, though, sit inside matter, and this paper asks how surrounding fluid changes the picture.

The authors couple a spherical fluid to the Schwarzschild source without energy exchange between them. Using minimal geometric deformation, they prove the surrounding fluid must push unevenly, that is, be anisotropic. They then work through several explicit cases. The method manufactures new, physically interpretable black hole solutions from the classic one. Such solutions give theorists fresh test beds for gravity in extreme conditions. They also model more realistic settings for the black holes now heard through gravitational waves.
openalex-w2895779069:
Samuel Treviño, Alfonso Díaz, and Eduardo Sánchez-Lara lead this review of vanadium in biology, published online in 2018 in Biological Trace Element Research. Vanadium compounds have been tested as candidate treatments for cancer, atherosclerosis, and diabetes. Yet none has reached routine clinical use. The missing piece, the authors argue, is basic pharmacology: what the body does to these compounds.

The review traces vanadium's path through living systems in detail. It covers dosage, the physiological environment, and interactions inside cells. Metabolic transformations and signaling pathway effects follow. Toxicology, transport, and tissue distribution get full treatment. Animal and human evidence is reviewed side by side. Without this groundwork, trial results stay hard to interpret and compare. The authors map what must be understood before vanadium drugs can be judged fairly.
openalex-w2941857669:
Fabien Lombard, Emmanuel Boss, Anya Waite, and colleagues wrote this 2019 review in Frontiers in Marine Science. Their topic is how scientists observe plankton, the tiny drifting organisms that support ocean food webs. The authors argue that plankton counts and measures need to be consistent across the globe.

Plankton are sampled by many teams, ships, and instruments, and unlike methods can make results hard to compare. The review sets out what globally consistent, quantitative observation would require. It surveys current tools and practices for measuring plankton in numbers rather than rough presence alone. The goal is data that can be pooled worldwide to track how ocean ecosystems change over time.
openalex-w3132257869:
Joanne Bennett, Jennifer Sunday, Piero Calosi, and colleagues published this study in Nature Communications in 2021. It traces how the critical thermal limits of life, the heat and cold edges species can bear, evolved across Earth. Those edges help set where species can live.

Cold tolerance varies hugely between species, families, and places. Heat tolerance, by contrast, is strikingly steady across latitudes, heights, and family trees. That steadiness is odd, since fitness curves suggest heat should bite harder than cold. Species also tend to keep the climate tastes of their ancestors, which may block quick adaptation to warming. The authors test explanations for the frozen heat ceiling at a global scale, with stakes for forecasting climate losses.
openalex-w3200279669:
Martin Prince, Daisy Acosta, Mariella Guerra, and colleagues test a World Health Organization idea called intrinsic capacity, in PLOS Medicine in 2021. The term covers a person's combined physical and mental abilities, across movement, energy, senses, thinking, mood, and continence. Health care for older people is being reframed around keeping that capacity up, to delay dependence on others.

The team used population studies from Latin America, India, and China run by the 10/66 Dementia Research Group. They measured how common declines in capacity were and who had them. They also tested whether such declines predicted later dependence and death, as the approach assumes. The results matter most for poorer settings, where broad screening must prove its worth.
openalex-w4366264269:
Aaron Eger, Ezequiel Marzinelli, Rodrigo Beas-Luna, and colleagues value the services that kelp forests give people worldwide, in Nature Communications in 2023. Kelp are large brown seaweeds that form underwater forests along cold and mild coasts. Travellers in the Americas relied on them for food twenty thousand years ago. Cultures in Asia and Europe have farmed, eaten, and used kelp for centuries since.

Today kelp forests shelter major fisheries and yield alginate, a thickener used in food and medicine. Countless species depend on them for habitat and food. By pricing and weighing these services together, the study makes kelp's worth visible to policy makers. Such accounting can steer protection toward forests that quietly support coastal economies.
openalex-w4389086869:
Shahida Siddiqui, Zeki Erol, Jerina Rugji, and colleagues overview fermentation in the food industry, in Bioresources and Bioprocessing in 2023. Fermentation likely began in the Fertile Crescent, and nearly every culture now keeps fermented foods. Microbes transform milk, grain, vegetables, fruit, and meat into products that keep longer and taste richer. Fermented foods also carry helpful bacteria and break down toxins, and research links them to better health.

The review looks back over this history with fresh eyes. It covers how fermentation improves safety, nutrition, and flavour in dairy foods, beer, and wine. It also examines a newer use: turning food waste into enzymes, pigments, and fuels. As chronic diseases rise, fermented diets draw interest as one practical defence.
openalex-w4409743169:
Takako Konoike, Shinya Uji, Yuya Hattori, and Taichi Terashima control electronic states in an organic conductor using strain. Their paper appeared in the Journal of the Physical Society of Japan in 2025. The material, an organic crystal, changes its electronic phases under pressure. Ordinary pressure squeezes from all sides at once.

Squeezing along one chosen direction reveals which direction actually drives the changes. The authors apply both tensile and compressive strain along single axes. That directional control is hard in fragile, tiny organic crystals. The work shows how strain can tune an organic conductor's electronic state on purpose. Such control helps physicists map phase changes and test ideas about organic superconductors.
openalex-w7204234769: Brazil's 2021 bidding law moved government buying onto online platforms. This study checks whether e-procurement made public buying cleaner and quicker. The authors test if the reform cut waste and sped up deals paid with public money. A nuts-and-bolts look at whether digital rules made the state's shopping better.
openalex-w7205015369: Microgreens are tiny young vegetable and herb plants, and they pack a lot of nutrition into a few inches. This review covers how they are grown: their health perks, farm methods, useful traits, and market trends. Drawing on Brazilian and world research, the authors map a crop that rose from restaurant garnish to serious farming. Handy for growers eyeing a high-value niche and eaters curious about the hype.
openalex-w7206168469: Cattle sometimes eat things they should not, soil, bones, plastic, a condition called depraved appetite or pica. This veterinary paper reviews the causes, signs, and consequences of feeding disorders in cattle, aiming to help ranchers prevent and manage them. It gathers what is known about triggers and herd-level impacts. Practical and farm-focused, it treats animal nutrition as both a welfare and an economic issue.
openalex-w7206170569: Hidradenitis suppurativa, also called acne inversa, is a painful chronic skin disease marked by recurring lumps, abscesses, and tunnels under the skin. It affects roughly one percent of the population and can be deeply debilitating. This narrative review pulls together current knowledge on how doctors diagnose it and what treatments help. Written for clinicians and patients alike, it offers a clear update on managing a condition that is often misunderstood.
openalex-w7207549069: A school's walls, wiring, and plumbing shape what happens inside its classrooms. This article surveys the physical state of rural and urban schools offering the final years of elementary education in Bahia's Piemonte Norte do Itapicuru region. It documents gaps between what the law promises for the right to education and what the buildings actually provide. The result is a detailed portrait of unequal conditions across one territory.
penn-no-cross-1669: No Cross, No Crown, William Penn's 1669 Quaker classic on self-denial. Written in the Tower of London, it urges Christians to bear suffering patiently. This edition preserves that early Quaker testimony. Its pages add to the record of the past.
plos-pbio-0000069:
Unnur Styrkarsdottir, Jean-Baptiste Cazier, Augustine Kong, and others mapped an osteoporosis risk region in PLOS Biology in 2003. Their search ties weak bones to chromosome 20 and to BMP2, a gene known for helping bone form. Osteoporosis thins bone and raises the risk of breaks in older people.

The team used family data to find where the risk sits in the genome, then narrowed it to a gene that fits the biology. That link matters because bone density runs in families, yet the genes behind it were mostly unknown. Naming a region and a likely gene gives drug and diagnosis work a place to start. It also helps explain why some people lose bone faster than others.
plos-pbio-0020069:
Martin Wu, Ling V. Sun, Jessica Vamathevan, and a big team sequenced a parasite genome for PLOS Biology in 2004. Wolbachia pipientis wMel lives inside fruit fly cells and bends the fly's reproduction to spread itself. Its whole genome runs to about 1.27 million DNA letters.

For a free-living bacterium that genome is small and stripped down. Yet it is packed with mobile DNA elements that copy and move within the genome, an odd trait for so compact a genome. The full sequence lets researchers compare Wolbachia strains and track how it manipulates hosts. That knowledge may aid pest control, since Wolbachia infects many insect species of concern.
plos-pbio-0020369:
Olaf Sporns and Rolf Kötter analyzed patterns in brain wiring in PLOS Biology in 2004. Brain networks can be read as maps of nodes and links. Small recurring link patterns, called motifs, appear more often than chance would suggest, much as common words recur in a language.

The authors catalogued motifs in brain maps from several species and compared them with random networks. Certain motifs stood out, hinting at design rules for how brains are wired. Motif counts give a compact way to compare healthy and disordered brains, or brains across species. The paper helped bring network math into neuroscience, where it now shapes how brain maps are read.
plos-pone-0000069:
Lester M. Shulman, Yossi Manor, Danit Sofer, and a large team searched sewage for poliovirus in PLOS ONE in 2006. In places where most people are vaccinated, the live polio vaccine itself can, on rare occasions, change back toward a harmful form. Those vaccine-derived viruses can pass through the gut and out into sewage.

Finding them in sewage is an early warning that they are circulating. The team reports such neurovirulent strains in a highly immune population, where few would expect them. Sewage testing thus acts as a silent sentinel for polio control. It can spot risk before any child falls ill, which is exactly what the endgame of polio eradication needs.
plos-pone-0000169:
Roderick Nigel Finn and Børge A. Kristoffersen published this evolution paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Vitellogenin is the protein that stocks fish eggs with yolk. The authors examine how this gene was duplicated in vertebrates, testing the so-called 3R hypothesis of genome doublings. They link the copies to the floating pelagic egg and to the great spread of teleost fishes in the oceans.

Teleosts make up most fish species alive today, so their egg strategy matters at scale. The authors connect gene duplication timing to the rise of the buoyant ocean egg. The paper ties a DNA-level event to one of the biggest radiations in vertebrate history.
plos-pone-0000269:
Doris Estrugo, Alexander Fischer, Franziska Hess, and colleagues published this leukemia study in PLOS ONE in 2007. Integrins are the anchors cells use to grip their surroundings, and beta1 integrins sit on leukemia cells. The authors report that when these anchors are bound to their ligands, they inhibit procaspase-8, a starter protein of cell death. In doing so they mediate resistance to drugs and radiation that depends on cell adhesion.

Leukemia cells hiding in the bone marrow can survive chemotherapy by gripping their niche. This paper names the molecular brake that grip applies to the death machinery. Blocking that protective signal could make standard treatments work on cells that currently outlast them.
plos-pone-0000369:
Daryl Wile and Evan Balaban explored how the brain hears pitch, in a paper published in PLOS ONE in 2007. When people hear a musical note, they sense one whole pitch even when the sound is built from many parts. The authors looked for a brain signal that matches that whole-note sense of pitch.

Their study reports an auditory neural correlate, a pattern of brain activity that tracks pitch as a single quality rather than piece by piece. Work of this kind helps explain how the hearing system builds a simple sensation out of complex sound. It also bears on how people perceive music and speech, where pitch carries much of the meaning.
plos-pone-0000469:
Claude Sadis and colleagues found a protective side to nicotine in kidney injury, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. The injury model is ischemia/reperfusion, where blood flow to the kidney stops and then returns, paradoxically causing extra damage through inflammation. The team showed nicotine protects the kidney from this injury through the cholinergic anti-inflammatory pathway.

That pathway is a nerve-based brake on inflammation, triggered through the same receptors nicotine acts on. The finding does not make smoking safe; it isolates one drug-like action worth copying without tobacco. Separating nicotine's anti-inflammatory effect from its harms is the kind of lead that can seed new medicines for transplant and shock patients.
plos-pone-0000569:
David Liska and colleagues compared how body fat is distributed among obese teenagers of different backgrounds, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The team measured interethnic differences in fat partitioning in obese adolescents. They looked at muscle, liver, and abdominal fat. Where fat is stored matters as much as how much there is.

Fat in the liver and deep abdomen drives diabetes and heart risk far more than fat under the skin. If ethnic groups partition fat differently at the same weight, risk screening by weight alone will misjudge many teens. Studies like this argue for measuring the dangerous depots directly in high-risk youth.
plos-pone-0000669:
Gilles Mirambeau, Sébastien Lyonnais, Dominique Coulaud and co-authors watched two HIV enzymes shape the virus's inner shell, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The HIV-1 nucleocapsid forms as the virus matures, a process directed by the viral protease. After infection, reverse transcriptase copies the viral genome, and the nucleocapsid transforms into pre-integration complexes in the cell's cytoplasm.

Using transmission electron microscopy in detail, the team examined the nucleocapsid's architecture. Their title states that protease and reverse transcriptase together control that structure. Both enzymes are already drug targets. Showing they also act as architects adds a new way to think about blocking the virus.
plos-pone-0000769:
Joern Kamradt, Volker Jung, Kerstin Wahrheit and colleagues scanned prostate cancer cell lines for newly amplified genome regions, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Their purpose was to prove a longmer oligonucleotide microarray platform can profile gene copy number alterations. Amplicons are stretches of DNA copied many times in cancer cells. A genome-wide screen of such changes can quickly indicate novel candidate genes.

Candidates flagged this way may play a role in carcinogenesis, the making of cancer. Comprehensive profiling replaces one-gene-at-a-time searching with a single sweep. Each new amplicon is a lead: somewhere inside it may sit a gene whose extra copies drive tumor growth, and which drugs could target.
plos-pone-0000869:
Britta Eickholt, Aminul Ahmed, Meirion Davies and co-authors studied a single enzyme form called p110 delta in nerve growth, for PLOS ONE in 2007. The enzyme belongs to the PI 3-kinase family, which has eight forms whose roles in the nervous system were unclear. The p110 delta form was mostly known from white blood cells.

The team asked what this form does in sensory neurons, the cells that carry signals from skin and muscle. They focused on how axons, the long fibers of nerve cells, grow and regrow after damage. Knowing which enzyme form drives regrowth could guide later work on nerve repair.
plos-pone-0000969:
Eleonora Castelletti, Sergio Lo Caputo, Louise Kuhn and colleagues studied a mucosal signal chemical in HIV infection, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The chemical, CCL28 or MEC, draws antibody making cells into moist body linings. Those cells release IgA, the antibody that guards mucosal surfaces.

HIV specific IgA shows up both in infected people and in some exposed people who stay uninfected. The team analyzed the CCL28 circuit across infected, exposed and unexposed groups. Mucosal defense is where HIV usually enters, so its local signals matter. Work of this kind may help explain why a few exposed people resist infection.
plos-pone-0001069:
Sacha Genovesi, Liviana Leita, Paolo Sequi and colleagues directly detected prions bound in soil, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Scrapie in sheep and chronic wasting disease in deer are contagious prion diseases. Spread through the environment seems important in keeping these epidemics going, with contaminated ground as a reservoir.

Detecting prions in soil, rather than inferring them from sick animals, was the missing step. The team present a direct detection method for soil bound prions. Land where deer or sheep gather could then be tested before animals are moved there. Environmental control of prion disease depends on exactly this kind of tool.
plos-pone-0001169:
Building a brain means first making many progenitor cells, then having them stop dividing and become neurons. Barbara Hämmerle and Francisco Tejedor describe a new role for the Delta-Notch signaling system in that switch, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The transition from proliferation to neurogenesis is a crucial step in development.

The authors report a novel function of Delta-Notch signaling that mediates this transition in neural progenitor cells. A complete account of neurogenesis needs the molecular processes that govern each such step. Their finding adds a control point that other researchers can probe when development goes wrong.
plos-pone-0001269:
Hutchinson-Gilford progeria is a rare disorder of accelerated aging, caused in most cases by a specific mutation in the LMNA gene. Dayle McClintock and colleagues report that the mutant protein appears in ordinary aging skin too, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Progeria patients age fast and often die early, frequently from stroke or heart disease.

The authors show that the mutant form of lamin A acts as a biomarker of cellular aging in human skin, detectable beyond the disease itself. In other words, the progeria mechanism leaves traces in normal aging. That widens the relevance of studying this rare disease.
plos-pone-0001369:
Christopher Kanakry and co-authors published a 2007 PLOS ONE study on a growth factor called neuregulin-1. The gene for this factor has been linked to a higher risk of a severe mental illness. The same factor also plays a part in how the brain grows and how cancer spreads through the body.

Using blood cells grown in the lab, the team traced how the factor helps cells stick to each other. They found a chain of signals inside the cell that drives this effect. The findings tie one gene to both brain growth and cancer spread. That link may guide new work on both fields.
plos-pone-0001469:
Jun Cui and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE model of the switch that tells a cell to die. A family of proteins acts as a checkpoint for this death program, called apoptosis. How its parts interact was still in dispute. The team's past models had backed one account of the switch over others.

Here they show the switch holds two self boosting loops that can lock it in two states. Such a lock makes cell death a firm, one way choice once it flips. A clear model helps labs test drugs that flip the switch in cancer. It also explains why half measures tend to fail in this system.
plos-pone-0001569:
Yanjun Jiang, Dongsheng Xu, and Yong Zhao published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on two cancer viruses in one tumor type. Both viruses, tied to Kaposi's sarcoma and to mono, belong to one virus family. Most cases of a rare AIDS linked lymphoma carry both. Each virus can wake and copy itself via a starter protein.

The team show the two starters hold each other back when both viruses share a cell. That mutual brake may keep both viruses quiet in the tumor. It is a neat case of rivals checking each other. It also shapes how drugs that wake one virus might act on the pair.
plos-pone-0001669:
Laurent Gillet, Susanna Colaco, and Philip G. Stevenson studied how a mouse herpesvirus first grabs hold of cells, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The first contact a virus makes largely decides which cells it can infect. Murid herpesvirus-4 depends heavily on glycosaminoglycans, long sugar chains on cell surfaces, for binding.

That dependence pointed to one of the virus's own surface glycoproteins as the sugar-binding part. The authors tested the gH and gL protein pair and report that this complex binds glycosaminoglycans. The full text gives the binding assays and the mutants they used to confirm the contact. A virus's first grip on a cell is a natural drug and vaccine target, since blocking it can stop infection before it starts.
plos-pone-0001769:
Sylvane Desrivières, Kristina Krause, Anne Dyer, and their co-authors linked a signaling gene to teenage drinking behavior in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The PI3K pathway usually regulates cell growth and survival. Growing evidence tied it to behavioral responses to addictive drugs, which made its genes candidates for addiction risk.

The team reports that sequence variation in the PI3K p85 alpha gene associates with alcohol risk drinking behavior in adolescents. The full text gives the teen sample and the variant statistics. A gene in a drug-response pathway showing up in teenage drinking supports the view that addiction risk is partly hard-wired. That could one day guide early prevention for high-risk youth.
plos-pone-0001869:
Hiroshi Ageta and co-authors published a brain study in PLOS ONE in 2008 on activin, a hormone that helps cells grow and change type. Activin was already known to shield brain cells from harm when blood flow fails. The team asked what else activin does inside the brain. They focused on mood, and on the growth of new brain cells in adult animals.

The authors report that activin in the brain shapes acts linked to fear and stress. It also shapes adult neurogenesis, the birth of new neurons in grown animals. Readers get a clear case that a growth hormone can sway both behavior and brain repair. That link matters for work on mood disorders and on how the adult brain renews itself.
plos-pone-0001969:
Michael Forbes and co-authors compared ear infection strains of a common bacterium in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The bacterium, Streptococcus pneumoniae, causes both local ills, such as ear infection, and body-wide disease. How much of that variety comes from the strain's genes, its serotype, or the host's response was not fully clear.

The team used a chinchilla model of otitis media, infection of the middle ear, to score each strain's virulence under the same host conditions. Holding the host fixed lets strain traits stand out. Such scores help predict which strains cause the worst disease, and which a vaccine must cover.
plos-pone-0002069:
Paloma Alonso-Magdalena and co-authors studied how estrogen shapes insulin stores in the pancreas, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Pancreatic beta cells make and release insulin, the main hormone that keeps blood sugar in balance. Estrogen receptors, in two forms called alpha and beta, play a part in glucose control, yet their role inside beta cells was still grey.

As the title states, the team report that the alpha form, ER alpha, regulates how much insulin the pancreas holds. A hormone better known for reproduction thus also tunes the insulin supply. That link may help explain sex gaps in diabetes risk.
plos-pone-0002169:
Omar Salim, Ian Clarke, and Paul Lambden examined the front end of the genome of a cattle virus, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Jena virus is a bovine norovirus that causes gut disease in cattle. It serves as a workable model for the noroviruses that infect the gut of people, which are hard to study directly.

The virus carries a single strand of RNA with sections that code first for building proteins, then for its shell. The team analyzed the 5 prime end of that genome to see how its parts are arranged and controlled. Details at this level guide work on how noroviruses copy themselves.
plos-pone-0002269:
Mahomed Patel and co-authors built a framework for judging how ready family doctors are for a flu pandemic. Their paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Primary care, and general practice above all, will stand at the frontline when pandemic influenza hits. Yet no framework existed to guide systematic planning for that task or to compare the plans countries had drawn up.

The authors aimed to create such a framework and to test it against plans from five countries. A common yardstick lets health systems spot the gaps in their own plans before a crisis exposes them. General practice is where most patients will first turn.
plos-pone-0002369:
Liao and co-authors published a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Anne P. Liao, Elaine O. Petrof, Sumalatha Kuppireddi, among others. Its subject is salmonella Type III Effector AvrA Stabilizes Cell Tight Junctions to Inhibit Inflammation in Intestinal Epithelial Cells. Salmonella Typhimurium is a major cause of human gastroenteritis.

The Salmonella type III secretory system secretes virulence proteins, called effectors. Effectors are responsible for the change of tight junction (TJ) structure and function in intestinal epithelial cells. The paper sets out the problem first and then the line of work the team chose to take. That makes the article a clear record of one research question, the path taken to test it, and the limits the authors faced.
plos-pone-0002469:
Karkan, working with fellow researchers, published a study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Delara Karkan, Cheryl Pfeifer, Timothy Z. Vitalis, among others. Its subject is a Unique Carrier for Delivery of Therapeutic Compounds beyond the Blood-Brain Barrier.

The piece walks readers through the question, the setup, and the steps that came next. The result is a compact record of the work, of use to readers who study the same problem or teach it to others. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002569:
Pérez-Mancera and fellow authors published a research article through PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Pedro A. Pérez-Mancera, Camino Bermejo-Rodríguez, Manuel Sánchez-Martín, among others. Its subject is fUS-DDIT3 Prevents the Development of Adipocytic Precursors in Liposarcoma by Repressing PPARγ and C/EBPα and Activating eIF4E. FUS-DDIT3 is a chimeric protein generated by the most common chromosomal translocation t(12;16)(q13;p11) linked to liposarcomas.

The paper sets out the problem first and then the line of work the team chose to take. As a record, it keeps the focus on facts and method, and lets readers judge the claims for themselves.
plos-pone-0002669:
In 2008, Joenna Driemeyer and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE about changes in gray matter induced by Learning—Revisited. Authorship is credited in the record to Joenna Driemeyer and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Recently, activation-dependant structural brain plasticity in humans has been demonstrated in adults after three months of training a visio-motor skill. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state.
plos-pone-0002769:
Ulrich Meinzer and others wrote for PLOS ONE in 2008 on the subject of nod2 mediates susceptibility to yersinia pseudotuberculosis in mice. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Ulrich Meinzer, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Nucleotide oligomerisation domain 2 (NOD2) is a component of the innate immunity known to be involved in the homeostasis of Peyer patches (PPs) in. A further point appears in the abstract. However, little is known about its role during gut infection in vivo . Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002869:
Nasir Salam, Shashank Gupta, Sachin Sharma and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on protection against tuberculosis. Their focus was dendritic cells, a type of immune cell that helps start T cell responses. They asked how two signal proteins, RANTES and IP-10, shape that protection when cells are treated with the bacterial protein CFP-10.

The work looks at how treated dendritic cells prime T cells and guide immune responses to mycobacteria. It links chemokine and cytokine signals to the strength of the response. Readers get a lab-based view of one route the immune system may use to fight Mycobacterium tuberculosis, the germ that causes tuberculosis.
plos-pone-0002969:
Cathrin Bruederle, Robert Hnasko, Thomas Kraemer and co-authors tested whether prion-infected meat-and-bone meal stays infectious after biodiesel production in 2008. The BSE epidemic had collapsed markets for beef by-products such as meat-and-bone meal, a protein-rich feed supplement. Normal rendering did not remove all concern about prions.

A key question was whether turning the fat into biodiesel also destroys infectivity in the remains. The title gives the answer: the meal is still infectious afterward. Published in PLOS ONE, the finding sets a hard limit on one proposed safe use for risky material. The full text gives methods, results, and references for readers who want to check each step.
plos-pone-0003069:
Jean-Marc Melgari, Patrizio Pasqualetti, Flavia Pauri and co-authors mapped upper limb muscles in motor cortex together in 2008. Past work with transcranial magnetic stimulation focused on the cortical representation of a limited group of muscles. No attempt had recorded hand, forearm, and arm at once to disentangle a functional topography.

Their concert metaphor means muscles mapped as an ensemble, not soloists. Published in PLOS ONE, a joint map shows how the primary motor cortex organizes coordinated limb control. That matters for stroke rehabilitation, where recovery is about combined actions, not single muscles. The complete article sets out the methods and data behind each claim in full.
plos-pone-0003169:
Hugo Merchant, Wilbert Zarco, Ramon Bartolo and colleagues examine how timing tasks relate to each other in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. They measured performance links among ten different tasks that involved judging time intervals below one second, using multidimensional analyses. Twenty human subjects carried out explicit timing tasks such as interval categorization.

The authors argue that the context of temporal processing shows up in the pattern of links between tasks. Readers learn that timing is not one single skill but a set of related abilities. That view matters for brain research on time, music, speech, and movement control.
plos-pone-0003269:
Petra Vetter, Brian Butterworth and Bahador Bahrami test a classic claim about counting small sets in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Traditionally, visual enumeration of a small number of items, from one to about four, called subitizing, has been thought of as a parallel, pre-attentive process distinct from serial counting of larger numbers. The team tested this hypothesis by modulating attentional load.

The title reports that attentional load affects numerosity estimation, as evidence against a pre-attentive subitizing mechanism. Readers see a neat textbook split challenged by experiment. How we judge number at a glance matters for models of basic cognition.
plos-pone-0003369:
Jeremy R. Sanford and co-authors published this genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was SF2/ASF, a protein that helps cut and paste gene messages before use. The protein also moves back and forth between the cell nucleus and the outer cell body. The team set out to list which messages it binds in each place.

Inside, the authors explain how they pulled the protein from cells and read the RNA tied to it. They report separate target lists for the nucleus and for the outer cell body. Those lists link one protein to splicing, message export, and protein building. The work helps explain how a single factor can guide a message from gene to finished protein.
plos-pone-0003469:
Virginia Tirino and co-authors hunted stem-like cells in solid tumors for this 2008 paper. Osteosarcoma is the most common primary tumor of bone. Solid tumors mix many cell types with unlike roles. A small subset may hold stem cell powers and drive growth.

The team detected and characterized cells marked by CD133 in human tumors. Such cells may gain aggressiveness and resist treatment. Killing the root cells could stop tumors from regrowing. This survey helps define what those cancer stem cells look like. Bone tumors strike the young most often, raising the stakes of relapse.
plos-pone-0003569:
Xinjiang Cai and David E. Clapham traced a sperm channel's evolution in this 2008 paper. CatSper channels are calcium channels found only in sperm. They drive the hyperactive swimming sperm need to reach the egg. Four subunits plus an auxiliary part form the channel complex.

Across mammals, the family showed lineage-specific gene loss. It also showed rapid evolution in the lines that kept it. Such restless history is common in reproduction genes. Sperm competition may drive that fast, uneven change. Male fertility has few drug options, so channel biology draws steady interest.
plos-pone-0003669:
Rocio G. Urdinguio, Lidia Lopez-Serra, Pilar Lopez-Nieva, and colleagues published this neurology study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Rett syndrome is a severe disorder that mainly affects girls and is tied to faults in the MECP2 gene. Mice that lack Mecp2 are a standard model of the disease.

The team searched these mice for changes in neurons that could serve as new treatment targets. Finding fresh targets matters because no cure yet exists for this disorder. Their results add candidate points where future drugs might act to ease a lifelong condition that takes skills away after early growth.
plos-pone-0003769:
Jialiang Wang, Hui Wang, Zhizhong Li, and colleagues published this brain cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Malignant gliomas are among the most lethal cancers known. Their cells form a hierarchy, with cancer stem cells at the top that can regrow the tumor. The team asked what keeps those stem cells going.

They found the gene c-Myc is required for the maintenance of glioma cancer stem cells. Without Myc's support, the self-renewing core of the tumor falters. The result points to a weak spot in the hierarchy that makes gliomas so hard to kill.
plos-pone-0003869:
Ruchi Jain, Bappaditya Dey, Neeraj Dhar, and colleagues published this vaccine study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The BCG vaccine protects against tuberculosis unevenly, with efficacy from zero to eighty percent against adult disease. Better vaccine candidates are needed. One route is recombinant BCG that overproduces strong antigens of the TB bacterium.

The team built a recombinant BCG expressing the antigen Ag85C. It gave enhanced and enduring protection against tuberculosis in their tests. The stronger protection was associated with a changed cytokine profile in the lung, linking the vaccine's effect to the local immune mix. A stronger first shot could protect more of those at risk.
plos-pone-0003969:
Andrew W. Horne, John A. Phillips, Nicole Kane, and co-authors measured a receptor in ectopic pregnancy in 2008. Ectopic pregnancy happens when an embryo lodges in the Fallopian tube. It is a major cause of illness in early pregnancy. In mice, silencing the CB1 cannabinoid receptor traps embryos in the tube.

Their PLOS ONE article measured CB1 in women's Fallopian tubes and decidua. CB1 levels were lower in samples from ectopic pregnancies. That parallel with mice suggests the same system guards embryo travel in humans. The finding may help predict or prevent tubal pregnancies. The article came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for science and health research.
plos-pone-0004069:
Thomas Fischer, Falko Nagel, Stefan Jacobs, and co-authors rechecked a cancer receptor measure in 2008. CXCR4 is a chemokine receptor that steers cell migration. It guides cancer cells toward specific sites where they seed metastases. Knowing a tumor's CXCR4 status could predict its course.

Earlier attempts to locate the receptor in tissue proved unreliable. Their PLOS ONE article validates a new rabbit antibody called UMB-2. With it, they reassessed normal and tumor tissues. A trustworthy stain is the first step toward CXCR4-guided therapy choices. The paper came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for work in science and health.
plos-pone-0004169:
John Heidelberg and colleagues published this genomics study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Many bacteria and archaea carry CRISPR arrays, stored snippets of DNA from past invaders, together with cas genes. Together they give the microbes a form of acquired immunity against viruses.

The team read genomic data from two heat-loving Synechococcus microbes living in a microbial mat, a layered community of microbes. By comparing host CRISPR records with viral genomes from the same mat, they traced an arms race in action. The study shows germ warfare at the gene level, with hosts and viruses changing together over time.
plos-pone-0004269:
Patrick Reeves and Christopher Richards published this genetics methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2009. Spotting genetic breaks between populations is key to studies of biodiversity and evolution, and to association genetics. Small genetic breaks can hide inside one named population. The most widely used inference methods are model-based Bayesian tools that can be slow and assumption-heavy.

The authors present an approach based on principal coordinates, a statistical way to summarise genetic distances. They show it can detect subtle population structure and other genetic breaks. A lighter method for spotting fine divisions helps researchers working with large, complex samples.
plos-pone-0004369:
John Castle and colleagues published this metabolism study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Acetyl-CoA carboxylases ACC1 and ACC2 catalyse the conversion of acetyl-CoA to malonyl-CoA, controlling how fats are made and burned. They are potential targets for treating metabolic syndrome. In rodents, ACC1 is expressed in fat-making tissues and ACC2 in oxidative tissues such as muscle.

The team report that ACC2 is expressed at high levels in human white adipose tissue, contrary to the rodent pattern. They also found an isoform with a novel N-terminus. Human fat tissue breaks the rodent rule. A human-specific pattern warns against designing obesity drugs from mouse maps alone.
plos-pone-0004469:
Newborn eyes are not set at birth, and Raji Varghese, Vishnubhatla Sreenivas, Jacob Puliyel, and co-authors measured how vision at birth tracks body size and age, in PLOS ONE in 2009. It is known that babies born early tend to be shortsighted, and that this fades as the due date nears. Full-term babies are usually longsighted.

The study compared refractive status, how the eye focuses light, with birth weight and gestational age in both early and full-term babies. Such numbers help doctors know what is normal for a newborn of a given size and age. They also guide checks for babies at risk of eye problems. A clear baseline at birth makes later changes easier to spot and treat.
plos-pone-0004569:
A malaria drug is failing in northern Tanzania, and a new resistance mutation has appeared, report Samwel Gesase, Roly Gosling, Ramadhan Hashim, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The drug pair is sulphadoxine-pyrimethamine, long used for uncomplicated malaria. It was also recommended to protect pregnant women, and was being studied for protecting infants.

The team found high resistance of Plasmodium falciparum, the deadliest malaria parasite, to the drug pair in northern Tanzania. They also report the emergence of a resistance mutation in the dhps gene at a position called codon 581. Mutations at new positions signal a drug losing ground. The findings argue for changing treatment policy before the drug fails completely in the region.
plos-pone-0004669:
John Reich, Mark Snee, and Paul Macdonald studied the fruit fly ovary for a PLOS ONE study in 2009. The ovary is a tissue where genes are often controlled after their messages are made. Past work had found many protein factors that do this control through gene screens.

More recent work found tiny RNAs called microRNAs that seem to block message use in other animals and tissues. The team asked how much this kind of block matters inside the fly ovary. Their work helps show how egg cells tune gene use without changing the genes themselves. That tuning is a core part of how eggs form and mature.
plos-pone-0004769:
Arne Egesten and colleagues showed that a strep enzyme alters both germ killing and signaling powers of human chemokines, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Chemokines are signals made by surface cells when inflamed. Some of them can also kill Streptococcus pyogenes, the bacterium that causes strep throat and deeper infections, in direct tests.

An enzyme from the bacterium cuts a wide range of chemokines. The team studied how that cutting changes both killing and receptor action. Cutting may help the bacterium evade local defense. The work shows a tug of war at infected sites. More work in larger samples can confirm how general the effect proves to be.
plos-pone-0004869:
Jonathan Scholz and colleagues showed distinct regions of right temporo parietal junction are selective for theory of mind and attention, in PLOS ONE in 2009. In fMRI studies, a cortical region in right temporo parietal junction is recruited when participants read stories about thoughts. Lesion and imaging studies also suggest a nearby region assists exogenous attention, raising the question whether one area serves both social cognition and attention reorienting.

Neighboring subregions separate the two functions cleanly. Overlap in earlier scans reflected coarse resolution. Social and attention networks remain distinct. Autism and neglect research benefit. Taken together, the findings mark a useful step for research in this area.
plos-pone-0004969:
Many insects host bacteria that live inside their cells. These primary endosymbionts cannot survive outside. Trapped in tiny populations, they should pile up harmful mutations. That doom spiral is called Muller's ratchet. Julie Allen and colleagues tested whether the ratchet runs unchecked. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009.

They found that selection still limits the ratchet. The worst mutations get weeded out despite the small populations. The spiral is braked, not unstoppable. That braking helps explain an old puzzle. These ancient partnerships survive their own decay for millions of years. The finding sharpens how evolution works in the smallest genomes.
plos-pone-0005069:
Depression clusters among people with lower socioeconomic status. Genes, circumstance, or both could explain the pattern. Sandra López-León and colleagues tested the genetic thread in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their study included over two thousand participants. They asked whether shared genetic factors explain the clustering. They also examined neuroticism and intelligence as possible pathways.

The results weigh how much genes contribute. Depression and low status may partly descend from common genetic roots. That does not make circumstance irrelevant. It makes the pattern harder to read. The work untangles nature from circumstance in mental-health inequality. Policy that ignores either thread will miss part of the cause.
plos-pone-0005169:
In AL amyloidosis, faulty antibody light chains fold the wrong way and pile up as amyloid in tissues. The deposits kill cells and wear organs down over time. Poshusta and colleagues wrote in PLOS ONE in 2009 about patients with this rare disease, where each person carries a distinct light chain.

The authors linked changes in set parts of the light chain to the level of free light chains in the blood. That tie between protein shape and blood level may help doctors track how the disease is moving. It also gives drug hunters a clearer view of which chain forms do the most harm.
plos-pone-0005269:
Entamoeba histolytica is a parasite that causes amoebic dysentery, and calcium signals are thought to drive its attack. One of its calcium-binding proteins, EhCaBP1, is essential for the parasite to grow. Jain and colleagues dissected that protein in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The protein has two ends, the N-terminal and C-terminal domains. Using its crystal structure and tests, the team showed the two ends carry distinct functions. A protein the parasite cannot live without is a tempting drug target, and knowing its parts helps aim at it. A drug that hits just one end of this protein might stop the parasite and spare the host, since our own cells use a form of their own.
plos-pone-0005369:
Helicobacter pylori lives in the harsh stomach and must fight oxidative stress to survive there. Its defense enzyme SodB is repressed by a regulator called Fur. Carpenter and colleagues reported in PLOS ONE in 2009 that one DNA letter changes that control.

A single nucleotide change affected Fur-dependent regulation of the sodB gene. Small changes in a control region can retune a pathogen's stress defense. The finding shows how H. pylori fine-tunes survival in the stomach, one letter at a time. A stomach germ that lives in half the world must tune its shields hour by hour as acid. Food shift, and one small change in its DNA can tilt that tune for good.
plos-pone-0005469:
Camilla Rathcke and colleagues studied a gene linked to diabetes in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. The gene CHI3L1 makes a protein called YKL-40, which rises with inflammation in the body. People with type 2 diabetes tend to have more of it in their blood, in step with how resistant they are to insulin.

The team checked whether common forms of the gene track with diabetes or with related traits such as weight and blood sugar. Testing the gene itself helps show whether YKL-40 is a cause of disease or just a sign that disease is present.
plos-pone-0005569:
Monika Zochowska and co-authors tested a virus shell as a drug carrier in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Bleomycin is a drug used against several cancers. Its use is limited because it can scar the lungs, an effect that can be fatal in a few patients.

The team loaded the drug into hollow protein shells built by a virus, shaped like a twelve-sided ball. Carrying the drug inside a shell could steer it toward tumours and away from the lungs. Early work like this tests whether such carriers are safe and practical.
plos-pone-0005669:
Gwen Robbins and co-authors reported in 2009 on a skeleton from ancient India that shows signs of leprosy. The bones date to about 2000 B.C., making them among the oldest direct proof of the disease. Leprosy is a long-lasting infection that still affects many thousands of people each year.

The team reads the damage in the bones against what is known about how and when leprosy spread. Genes from the modern germ point to a long shared past with humans, but hard dates have been scarce. A dated case from India helps pin down where the disease was, and when, early in its history.
plos-pone-0005769:
Teruhisa Hirai and Sriram Subramaniam compared two ways of picturing a light-driven protein in 2009. Bacteriorhodopsin pumps protons across a membrane when light hits it, changing shape as it works. Over thirty structure sets, from X-ray and electron methods, claim to show its steps.

The pair checked where the two methods agree on the protein's movements, and where they clash. Clash points may be artifacts of how crystals were made or frozen. Sorting real motion from artifact matters for all membrane protein work. Bacteriorhodopsin is the test case for methods used across drug target research.
plos-pone-0005869:
Colleen Novak and co-authors argued in 2009 that stamina, not body size, sets how much an animal moves each day. Some people stay lean despite pressure to gain weight, and lean people tend to be more active. Where that extra activity comes from was unknown.

In lean and obesity-resistant models, leanness could not be explained by eating less for their weight. Instead, a muscle enzyme, PEPCK, tracked with higher endurance and spontaneous activity. Muscles built for stamina may drive a generally restless, lean life. The finding reframes leanness as partly a muscle trait, not only an appetite trait.
plos-pone-0005969:
Our first line of defense spots germs by their foreign look, not by their name. Benjamin Greenbaum, Raul Rabadan and Arnold Levine asked in 2009 which short word-like patterns in RNA give that foreign look away. Their PLOS ONE paper compares letter patterns in viral RNA with those in the RNA of host cells.

Patterns that differ between virus and host can flag the mediators the innate immune system uses to tell self from non-self. Those flags also push both sides to evolve, as germs hide their patterns and hosts learn new ones. The study gives vaccine and drug work a sequence-level view of the body's oldest alarm system.
plos-pone-0006069:
Methane-making microbes form a deep and varied branch of life. Haiwei Luo, Zhiyi Sun, William Arndt and colleagues sorted their family tree by a fresh route in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper uses gene order, the sequence of genes along the genome, to build a phylogeny of methanogens, members of the Euryarchaeota.

Earlier trees, built from large gene datasets, split methanogens into two classes but left some deep branches unclear. Gene order offers an independent witness, since it changes more slowly than single genes. A firmer tree helps explain how methane making evolved, a question with weight for both early Earth history and modern climate science.
plos-pone-0006169:
Standing still looks easy, yet the body must keep correcting its balance the whole time. In a 2009 PLOS ONE study, Yoshiyuki Asai and colleagues built a model of quiet standing in humans. Their model starts from two hard facts: ankle stiffness alone is too weak, and nerve signals arrive with a long delay.

The authors compare two kinds of feedback control for keeping the body upright. One works all the time, while the other switches on only in short bursts. The burst style holds up better against the delay that would otherwise tip the body over. Readers get a clear picture of how small, timed corrections keep balance steady.
plos-pone-0006269:
Some patients cannot make enough antibodies and suffer repeated bacterial infections. Karina Melo and colleagues studied that condition, common variable immunodeficiency, in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Alongside weak antibody output, patients show faults in their T cells, the immune system's coordinators.

Regulatory T cells, which calm immune responses, occurred at decreased frequency in the patients. Too few regulators could let immune activity swing out of balance. The finding adds a cellular detail to a mixed and puzzling syndrome. It may help sort patients into groups that need different care. The work adds one more piece to the search for the roots of this illness.
plos-pone-0006369:
Most adult humans lose the ability to digest milk, but some populations keep it for life. Pascale Gerbault, Celine Moret, and Mathias Currat modelled the spread of lactase persistence in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The trait persists at high frequency in Europe and some nomadic populations; two hypotheses compete to explain that map.

One credits natural selection favouring milk drinkers; the other credits population movements. Their model weighs selection against demography in the trait's diffusion. Lactase persistence is a flagship case of recent human evolution. The verdict informs how culture and genes co-evolve.
plos-pone-0006469:
Louisa Hooven and co-authors asked whether the time of day changes pesticide effects, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Circadian clocks drive daily rhythms in body and molecular processes. Genes that break down foreign chemicals, called xenobiotic metabolizing genes, may rise and fall with those rhythms. Such rhythms could change the outcome of chemical exposure at different hours.

The team examined responses to pesticides across the daily cycle. Their title poses the question of whether the clock makes the poison. If timing matters, safety tests done at one hour may mislead. Farmers, workers, and regulators may need to think about when exposure happens, not just how much.
plos-pone-0006569:
Tomasz Leski and co-authors validated a chip for detecting biothreat agents in PLOS ONE in 2009. Rapid and effective detection of emerging microbiological threats and potential biowarfare agents is very challenging with traditional culture-based methods. Culture takes days and misses organisms that grow poorly. The team tested a high density resequencing microarray for broad range detection.

Resequencing chips read the DNA of many pathogens at once. Validation shows how accurate and sensitive the chip is across agents. A broad, fast detector serves both public health and biodefense. The study is a benchmark for replacing slow culture with DNA-based screening.
plos-pone-0006669:
Marcus Claesson and co-authors compared two ways to profile gut microbes in PLOS ONE in 2009. Shifts in the mix of microbes in the human gut are linked to many health states. New high-throughput tools had just begun to reveal that mix in fine detail. The team ran a head-to-head test of pyrosequencing, a fast DNA reading method, and a phylogenetic microarray, a chip that spots known microbe groups.

Both tools profile which microbes are present, but each has its own bias and cost. A fair test tells labs which tool to trust for which question. Gut microbe science was growing fast at the time and needed such checks. Their study helped set shared ways of work for the young field.
plos-pone-0006769:
Laurent Demougeot and his team tested if picturing a move stirs the body's autonomic nerves in PLOS ONE in 2009. Picturing strong, repeated acts does stir those nerves. Heart rate and breath rate rise with the image in mind. A single short move was a less clear case. It was also unclear if the stir matched the move that was pictured.

The team had people picture single, hard moves. Sensors tracked heart and breath while they did so. The title gives the result in plain words. Such imagery did not stir those nerves in a way tied to the move. That limit helps mark when mind drills can stand in for real strain. It counts for rehab plans built on pictured movement.
plos-pone-0006869:
Kenji Nishide and colleagues grew a brain tumor from cells lacking a stem cell marker in PLOS ONE in 2009. Prominin1, also called CD133, marks cancer stem cells widely. Those cells self-renew and seed tumors, including glioblastoma. Glioblastoma is the most malignant brain tumor type. Yet other evidence showed marker-negative cells can also form tumors.

The team depleted prominin1-expressing cells from the population. Glioblastoma still formed from the remaining cells. That result challenges a strict cancer stem cell hierarchy. Tumor-seeding ability is not confined to marked cells. Treatments aimed only at marked cells may therefore miss the real reservoir.
plos-pone-0006969:
Evgeny Mavrodiev drew a bold link between plant form and algebra in PLOS ONE in 2009. Classical invariant theory is a branch of mathematics about algebraic forms. Structural chemistry had long shown a curious match with it. In that view, a binary form of a given degree matches an atom with the same valence.

Mavrodiev argued that classical plant morphology fits the same pattern. Plant structures, he proposed, form an elementary case of invariant theory. The claim is theoretical rather than experimental. It invites mathematicians and botanists to test whether one formal system truly describes both molecules and plant shapes.
plos-pone-0007069:
Hiroto Nishizawa, Takeshi Suzuki, and Takao Shioya imaged heart cells from guinea pigs in PLOS ONE in 2009. Diseased heart muscle often shows abnormal calcium pulses. Such pulses appear in conditions like ventricular tachycardia, a dangerous rhythm disorder. The cause could be faulty electrical signals or faulty calcium handling. Telling the two apart was the challenge.

The team imaged calcium and action potentials at the same time, cell by cell. That paired view assigns blame more precisely. Knowing the source of abnormal pulses guides better drug choices. It also sharpens models of how arrhythmias start.
plos-pone-0007169:
Katy Hanlon, Claudius Rudin, and Lorna Harries investigated two microRNAs in leukemia in PLOS ONE in 2009. MicroRNAs are short RNAs that tune the expression of many genes. Their deregulation is common in human cancers. The pair MIR-15a and MIR-16-1 sit in a chromosome region often lost in chronic lymphocytic leukemia. Most patients show them turned down.

The team hunted the target genes these microRNAs control in patients. Losing a brake on those targets may help leukemia cells survive. Knowing the targets explains what the missing microRNAs normally hold in check. It also suggests genes that treatment might target instead.
plos-pone-0007269:
Etienne Maisonneuve, Adrien Ducret, Pierre Khoueiry, and colleagues studied selective protein damage by oxidation in 2009. Carbonyl groups form on certain amino acids when metals catalyze oxidation attacks. The affected amino acids include proline, arginine, lysine, and threonine in many proteins inside living cells.

For unknown reasons, only some proteins are prone to this carbonylation damage. The authors use mass spectrometry to identify damaged proteins and sites. They derive rules governing which proteins get selected. Their work helps explain how oxidative stress marks proteins for breakdown during aging and disease. The rules come straight from the measured damage patterns.
plos-pone-0007369:
Ngo Duc Thang, Annette Erhart, Niko Speybroeck, and colleagues trialed insecticidal hammocks against forest malaria in Vietnam in 2009. Malaria persists in remote areas along Vietnam's borders and in the central highlands. Local vectors live mainly in forests and are less vulnerable to standard control measures such as indoor spraying and bed nets.

The authors test long-lasting insecticidal hammocks in a community-based trial. Hammocks suit forest workers who sleep outdoors. The trial covers a rural area of central Vietnam. Their PLOS ONE results show whether hammocks can control forest malaria where houses-based tools fall short.
plos-pone-0007469:
Jason Ernst and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how growth signals shape developing blood cells. The growth factor IL-3 keeps early blood progenitors alive and growing. A cancer-causing form of the Abl protein drives similar effects in leukemia. Both were thought to act mainly by switching genes on or off. The team tested a different layer of control.

They found that IL-3 and oncogenic Abl reshape the myeloblast's message pool by changing how long messenger RNAs survive. Altering message stability changes which proteins get made, without touching the genes themselves. That lever turns out to be powerful in deciding a blood cell's fate. Leukemia appears to exploit the same mechanism. The study widens the view of how signals rewrite a cell.
plos-pone-0007569:
Lance Martin, Austin Che, and Drew Endy published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on tools for synthetic biology. Engineers of living systems need standard parts whose behavior is measured precisely. Reporter proteins supply the readouts: some produce color through enzyme activity, others glow. Each kind has strengths and blind spots. The team built a reporter called Gemini that does both jobs in one molecule.

Gemini is bifunctional, acting as an enzymatic and a fluorescent reporter of gene expression at once. Two readouts from one part cross-check each other. That makes part characterization cleaner and more quantitative. Standardized, well-measured parts are the foundation of serious bioengineering. The study contributes a versatile instrument to that foundation. It is a tool paper, aimed at everyone building with genes.
plos-pone-0007669:
Christina Roland and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on what anti-VEGF cancer drugs do besides starving tumors. Blocking VEGF cuts off the growth of blood vessels in solid tumors. Its effects, though, extend into the tumor's immune landscape. No study had compared mechanistically different anti-VEGF inhibitors on tumor growth and environment together. The team ran that comparison in preclinical mouse models of breast cancer, tracking cytokines and immune cell infiltration.

Cytokine levels correlated with how many immune cells entered the tumors. Different blockers shifted that landscape in their own ways. So these drugs are partly immune drugs, whether intended or not. That matters for combining them with immunotherapy. It also gives doctors possible markers for whether the drug is working. The study widens the frame around a well-known class of cancer medicine.
plos-pone-0007769:
Luke Meredith and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It describes a mutant protein that strongly blocks HIV replication. The protein is Tat, which HIV normally needs to copy itself at full speed. The mutant is named Nullbasic.

The team built Nullbasic by swapping Tat's arginine-rich basic region for simple building blocks. The mutant does not just fail to help the virus. It actively inhibits several steps of the viral cycle. A blocker drawn from the virus's own machinery is an appealing drug idea. Proteins like Nullbasic could anchor a new class of HIV therapy.
plos-pone-0007869:
Bo Bai and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It studies the brain's resident immune cells and their effect on T cells. The central nervous system is often called an immune-privileged site. Which cells present antigens there, and how, was largely unknown.

Microglia are the brain's own immune sentinels. The team also made microglia-like cells from dendritic cells in the lab. Both cell types inhibited the proliferation of CD4 T cells. That brake may help keep the brain's immune activity in check. Understanding it matters for brain inflammation and autoimmune attacks on the nervous system.
plos-pone-0007969:
Yudi Pawitan and colleagues asked how many gene variants are still out there to find, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Genome-wide hunts had turned up many variants, but each explained only a sliver of disease risk. The open question was how much more the same approach could yield.

Using the math of what had been found so far, the team forecast the likely haul ahead and the study sizes it would take. Most variants left to find have tiny effects, so the sample sizes must grow very large. The forecast helped funders and teams set honest hopes for the gene-hunting era.
plos-pone-0008069:
Sheila Vinton and colleagues read old plant remains to see how empire changed dinner in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their sites sit in Chile's Atacama Desert, drawn into the Inka empire centuries ago. Studies of conquest often track disease and hunger; this one tracked the household table.

Seeds and other plant traces from homes showed diets shifting as Inka rule took hold. New crops and state demands changed what families grew and ate. The humble seed record thus tells a political story: empire reaches all the way into the cooking pot.
plos-pone-0008169:
Kathryn Whetten and colleagues compared the lives of orphans in institutions and in community care across five poorer nations in PLOS ONE in 2009. The world holds well over a hundred million orphans and abandoned children. Policy had swung toward moving children out of institutions into family settings fast, on thin proof.

Children aged six to twelve were compared on health, feelings, learning, and behavior in both settings. The gaps were smaller, and more mixed, than the policy swing assumed. Care quality, the authors stress, may matter more than the label on the door, a call for proof over fashion.
plos-pone-0008269:
Nina Bosch and colleagues studied a flipped DNA segment in humans in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. A region on chromosome 8, called 8p23.1, can sit in two orientations. This inversion spans several million DNA letters and varies among individuals. Finding markers tied to the orientation helps track who carries which form. The team examined the inversion at several levels.

They assessed its effects on DNA sequence, cell structure, and gene expression. A large inversion can shuffle how nearby genes behave. Knowing its impact helps interpret genome scans for disease. It also adds to the map of human structural variation.
plos-pone-0008369:
Ping-Pui Wong, Adam Pickard, and Dennis J. McCance studied skin cell growth in a PLOS ONE paper from 2010. The protein p300 acts as a transcriptional co-activator in cells. It regulates responses such as growth, transformation, and differentiation. p300 affects the tumor suppressor p53, which controls the cell cycle brake p21. The role of p300 in keratinocyte behavior was their focus.

They found p300 alters keratinocyte growth and differentiation through p21 regulation. Keratinocytes are the main cells of the outer skin. Balancing their growth and maturation keeps skin healthy. The findings link a general co-activator to skin-specific outcomes.
plos-pone-0008469:
Raymond Chan and co-authors revisit brain signs in schizophrenia in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Neurological soft signs are mild flaws in movement or senses. They are common in schizophrenia, as are flaws in thinking skills. Past studies linked the two sets of flaws. But the links were based on simple correlations. The team use a stronger modeling design.

Structural equation modeling lets them test how signs and skills relate. They sort which thinking skills track with which signs. The results give a cleaner map of the links. Such a map may help track illness and sort patients for care and research.
plos-pone-0008569:
Lynda Li Song and co-authors study a protein induced by interferon in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The protein is called IFI16. Its levels rise in normal prostate cells as they enter senescence. Senescence is the state where old cells stop dividing. IFI16 also slows cell growth. The team ask how it does so at the gene level. They focus on the gene for telomerase, called hTERT.

IFI16 lowers expression of the hTERT gene. Telomerase keeps chromosome ends intact and is switched back on in most cancers. Lowering it helps lock in the growth stop of old cells. The work links an interferon signal to a key cancer gene.
plos-pone-0008669:
Michael Cusimano and co-authors map violent injury in a city in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Injury related to violent acts is a problem in every society. Some authors examined the geography of violent crime. Few focused on spatio-temporal patterns of violent injury. None had used an ambulance dataset to explore its spatial characteristics. The team analyze ambulance records for urban violent injuries over time.

They find violent injury clusters in specific places and times. Hot spots concentrate on certain streets, nights, and hours. Ambulance data reveal patterns police reports may miss. Prevention resources can target those hot spots for greatest effect.
plos-pone-0008769:
Jim Sun, Xuetao Wang, Alice Lau, and colleagues found how the tuberculosis germ stalls its own digestion. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Macrophages swallow germs into sacs called phagosomes. A mature sac fuses with acid-filled lysosomes and kills its cargo. Mycobacterium tuberculosis blocks that fusion and survives inside. The blocking tool was the mystery addressed here.

A germ enzyme, nucleoside diphosphate kinase, proved able to block maturation. Mouse macrophages carrying the germ showed stalled sacs. Removing that block could let macrophages finish the kill. The enzyme becomes a candidate target for new tuberculosis drugs.
plos-pone-0008869:
Nagore Puente, Izaskun Elezgarai, Mathieu Lafourcade, and colleagues mapped cannabis receptors in a small brain hub tied to stress and reward. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The bed nucleus of the stria terminalis helps drive reward seeking and stress responses. The body's own cannabis system influences both behaviors. Yet the system's anatomy inside this hub was barely described. The CB1 receptor is its main brain docking site.

Detailed mapping showed where CB1 sits in the hub's front-side division. Functional tests matched the wiring to behavior circuits. A precise map supports work on addiction and anxiety. It shows where cannabis-like drugs act in this hub.
plos-pone-0008969:
Elvir Becirovic and co-authors traced what one spelling error in a gene does to its message, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Retinitis pigmentosa is an inherited disease that slowly destroys the eye's light sensors. Vision fades over years and can end in blindness. Some cases come from faults in CNGB1, a gene for a channel protein in rod cells.

The team studied one CNGB1 mutation found in patients. The fault sits at a spot where the gene's message is cut and rejoined. Because of it, a whole section, exon 32, is skipped in the finished message. Losing that piece explains how the mutation breaks the channel and harms sight.
plos-pone-0009069:
Weibin Zha and co-authors tested a plant compound against a side effect of HIV drugs, in PLOS ONE in 2010. HIV protease inhibitors save lives but inflame blood vessels over time. That inflammation feeds the lipid problems and heart risks seen in patients. Berberine, a traditional herbal medicine, was the candidate remedy.

In mouse macrophages, berberine calmed the drug-triggered inflammation. It worked by tuning stress signals inside the cells' protein-folding compartment. Those ER stress pathways link the protease inhibitors to the inflammatory response. A plant compound easing drug side effects could widen HIV treatment options.
plos-pone-0009169:
Bob Zimmermann and co-authors watched a molecular fishing contest round by round with deep sequencing, in PLOS ONE in 2010. SELEX is a lab method that evolves DNA strands binding a chosen target. Genomic SELEX fishes such binding strands straight out of a genome. Until now, only the final winners of the contest got read and studied.

Fast, cheap sequencing let the team check the pool after every round. Their neutral version of the method watched strands without forcing a contest. Families of binding strands appeared and faded across the rounds in full view. Tracking the whole process turns a black-box hunt into something observable.
plos-pone-0009269:
Arthur Samuel and co-authors published this virus genome study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Avian paramyxoviruses are bird viruses divided into nine serotypes. By 2010, every serotype's genome had been fully read except type 5. The team filled that last gap.

They sequenced the complete genome of the APMV-5 prototype strain, taken from a budgerigar in Kunitachi in 1974. With it, the set of all nine serotypes is complete. Type 5 turned out to have the longest genome of the group. A complete set lets virologists compare the whole family and trace how these bird viruses evolved.
plos-pone-0009369:
Jonathan Zuccolo and co-authors published this gene family study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The MS4A family includes CD20, a famous target of lymphoma drugs. At least thirteen related genes sit together in the human genome. Most make membrane proteins that span the cell surface four times. A second family, TMEM176, is closely related.

The team traced the evolutionary history of both families. Family trees show when each gene arose and how they spread across species. Such history helps guess what the lesser-known members do. It also explains why some of these proteins became such useful drug targets.
plos-pone-0009469:
Cheryl Carling and colleagues tested how wording shapes a health choice in PLOS ONE in 2010. Blood pressure drugs cut the risk of heart attacks and strokes. The same benefit can be stated in more than one way. The team ran an online trial with people who had just learned they had high blood pressure. Each person saw one of three ways of framing the benefit.

Which framing people saw changed how many chose to start the drug. The trial shows that words at the point of prescribing carry real weight. Doctors can use the results to present benefits in a fair, clear way. Good wording may help more patients take a drug that can save their lives.
plos-pone-0009569:
Jason Bragg, Stephanie Dutkiewicz, and Oliver Jahn modeled ocean microbes in PLOS ONE in 2010. Phytoplankton are tiny drifting plants that base the ocean food web. New tools had revealed far more kinds of them than anyone expected. Making sense of that flood of data is hard. The team built a model of which forces shape these microbes across the world ocean.
