Their model weighs forces such as nutrient supply, light, and grazing in each region. It shows how the balance of forces differs from sea to sea. That helps explain why the same group thrives in one place and not another. The work brings order to a fast growing picture of ocean life.
plos-pone-0009669:
Ines Samengo and Marcelo Montemurro modeled a code change in nerve cells in PLOS ONE in 2010. Neurons can fire in bursts, and the timing within a burst carries information. That timing is called phase information. Downstream cells, though, may simply count spikes. The team asked how bursting neurons convert phase information into a spike count code. Their model follows that translation step by step.

The conversion shows how the brain can repack the same message in a new format. A count code is simpler for some readers, while timing is richer. Knowing the translation helps decode real recordings from the brain. It may also inspire computing designs that switch codes as neurons do.
plos-pone-0009869:
Even a tiny worm must decide how much fat to store. Bin Liang and colleagues studied a receptor that helps run that decision in Caenorhabditis elegans. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. C. elegans is a millimeter-long worm used in labs worldwide.

The receptor is NHR-64, a nuclear receptor, a protein that switches genes on from inside the cell nucleus. Nuclear receptors in people help manage fat and metabolism. The team traced the role this one plays in fat storage regulation. Worm findings often preview pathways that matter in human obesity research.
plos-pone-0009969:
Computers can predict webs of working partnerships between proteins, but predictions include false links. Beatriz García-Jiménez and colleagues used machine learning to judge which links are real. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Protein networks map thousands of partnerships at once.

Inference of functional relations means deciding which predicted partners truly work together. A machine learning approach trains on known cases, then scores new ones. Predicted protein networks guide experiments toward promising pairs. Cleaner networks make systems biology far more useful. False links waste months of bench work.
plos-pone-0010169:
Guennadi Kozlov and Kalle Gehring solved how two proteins recognize each other in 2010. The first, PABPC1, binds the tail end of RNA messages and promotes their translation. It also helps control how long those messages survive in the cell. Beyond its RNA-binding parts, the protein carries a unique interaction domain called MLLE.

Their PLOS ONE study showed the molecular basis for MLLE recognizing a protein called eRF3. eRF3 helps end protein production at the right point. Structural detail like this explains how the start and finish of translation stay coordinated.
plos-pone-0010269:
The authors were Léon Plaghki, Céline Decruynaere, Paul Van Dooren, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study modeled how heat pain switches on. Heat stimuli always rise gradually, unlike a sudden touch or pinprick. A painful heat also fires two types of nociceptor, or pain sensor. Their fibers carry signals at medium and slow speeds.

From those two speeds, the authors describe pain thresholds as a double alarm system. One alarm arrives fast, the other slower, and together they fine-tune the threshold. The model helps explain timing quirks in heat pain that single-sensor accounts miss.
plos-pone-0010369:
Chiara Lambertini, Serafino Pantano and G. Paolo Dotto studied control of the Notch1 gene in skin cells for PLOS ONE in 2010. In skin, Notch signals push cells to mature and can suppress tumors. When Notch1 is turned down, cancer becomes more likely. Apart from one known controller, p53, little was known about who sets its level. The team compared normal skin cells with cancer-derived ones.

Two factors, Klf4 and Sp3, handled the gene differently in the two cell types. That difference may help explain why cancer cells lose Notch1's protection. Gene control is often where cancer begins, long before visible change. Naming the controllers gives drug research new targets. It also shows the same gene can obey different masters in health and disease.
plos-pone-0010469:
Irina Lyadova and colleagues followed tuberculosis in mice to see how lung inflammation tracks with disease course for PLOS ONE in 2010. TB infection ends many ways, from quiet containment to rapid, fatal illness. What decides the path in otherwise healthy hosts was unclear. The team infected mice and watched their lungs over time. They measured inflammation and the cells gathering there.

As disease advanced, inflammation grew intense rather than protective. A particular cell type, marked Gr-1 dim, piled up in the lungs. Heavy inflammation may itself drive damage in progressing TB. That flips a simple view where more immune response is always better. The study helps explain why some hosts lose control of the infection.
plos-pone-0010569:
Philippe Halfon and colleagues asked whether semen can still carry HIV when blood treatment works well in PLOS ONE in 2010. Effective therapy can drive blood virus to undetectable levels. Whether the male genital tract matches that clearance was uncertain. The team studied men on therapy in France over several years. They tested semen for HIV despite good blood control.

Finding virus in semen would mean a residual transmission risk remains. Male-to-female transmission risk per act is low but not zero. The study's answer informs counseling for couples where one partner has HIV. It also probes the idea of body compartments where drugs reach poorly. Residual risk questions are central to treatment-as-prevention policy.
plos-pone-0010669:
Sibo Tian, Robert Haney, and Martin Feder traced the history of heat-shock gene switches in fruit flies, in PLOS ONE in 2010. When cells overheat, heat-shock genes switch on within minutes. Short DNA motifs in front of each gene, called heat-shock elements, trigger that response.

Comparing species on the fly family tree cleaned up a confused picture. Some motif arrangements were old, while others arose recently in single lineages. Family history, not guesswork, separated true shared patterns from look-alikes. The cleaned history helps explain how a life-saving stress response stays fast while still evolving.
plos-pone-0010869:
Cedar Chittenden, Michael Melnychuk, David Welch and co-authors published this salmon study in PLOS ONE in 2010. A coho salmon population in British Columbia's Thompson River is endangered, and managers did not know where its young fish were dying. The team fitted juvenile salmon, called smolts, with tiny acoustic tags and followed them downstream.

Tracked over three years, the smolts took between ten and sixteen days to reach the lower Fraser River, but very few were ever detected on ocean tracking arrays. Freshwater survival was near zero in the first year and rose sharply by the third. Return rates of adults followed the same pattern. Chittenden and colleagues conclude that many young fish die before ever reaching the sea, shifting conservation focus onto the river itself.
plos-pone-0010969:
Gabriele Möller, Bettina Husen, Dorota Kowalik and co-authors published this enzyme study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Some breast cancers and endometriosis feed on estrogen made locally by an enzyme called 17beta-HSD1, and blocking it is a promising treatment idea. The team tested new blocker candidates built on a hormone scaffold, checking carefully what else they might hit.

They measured the compounds against five related human enzymes and against the target enzyme from marmoset, pig, mouse, and rat, the species used in drug screening. Susceptibility differed profoundly: rodent versions of the enzyme were much less sensitive to the blockers than the human one. Möller and colleagues warn that a candidate can look weak in a mouse and strong in a person, or the reverse, distorting preclinical decisions.
plos-pone-0011069:
Ann Moore, Mary Biggs, Amy Matteini and co-authors published this aging study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Frailty, the syndrome of weakness, slowness, and shrinking that leaves older adults vulnerable, has been linked to failing mitochondria, the cell's power plants. The authors tested whether inherited variation in mitochondrial DNA helps decide who becomes frail.

Drawing on a long-running population study of older Americans, they compared mitochondrial variants between frail and non-frail participants and explored links to muscle strength. Frailty was scored from five standard indicators at the study's baseline examinations. Moore and colleagues bring mitochondrial genetics into the frailty question. That matters for a clear reason. A genetic link would point to energy use in cells as a lever for prevention. Exercise, or drugs that support mitochondria, could pull that lever.
plos-pone-0011169:
Hlevnjak, Zitkovic and Zagrovic proposed a binding rule in PLOS ONE in 2010. For two proteins to form a working pair inside a cell, many traits must match. The authors argued that matching love of water, called hydrophilicity, may be a basic first requirement for pairing.

If partner proteins share similar water affinity, they may meet and stick more readily in the watery cell interior. A simple rule like this could help predict which proteins work together. Such predictions speed the mapping of cell networks, which is slow to test one pair at a time. The idea now invites tests in real protein data.
plos-pone-0011269:
Gawecka, Griffiths, Ek-Rylander and colleagues traced melanoma movement in PLOS ONE in 2010. For skin cancer to spread, its cells must grip surfaces and crawl. The team studied a small switch protein and its handshake with a scaffolding protein that shapes the cell's inner frame.

That interaction regulated how melanoma cells migrate. A defined motility circuit gives drug designers specific points to jam. Stopping crawl would not kill the first tumor, but could halt the spread that makes melanoma lethal. The study adds molecular detail to the search for anti metastasis drugs.
plos-pone-0011369:
Rudy Jonker and co-authors asked in 2010 why barnacle geese had shifted the timing of their spring migration. The geese travel from wintering grounds to Arctic breeding sites, and their departure and stopover dates had moved over recent years. Food and weather were the usual suspects, but the team tested another pressure: the danger from predators along the route.

Their analysis found that predation risk fits the new timing well, as if geese adjust travel to dodge the most dangerous places and moments. Safer timing can mean arriving when predators are scarce, even at some cost to feeding. The result broadens how migration change is explained. Climate is not the only moving force; a shifting map of danger may redraw flyways just as strongly.
plos-pone-0011469:
Marta Szajnik and co-authors showed in 2010 how tumors recruit the immune system's peacekeepers by mail. Regulatory T cells calm immune attack, and cancers thrive when these cells gather around them. Tumors shed tiny packages called microvesicles into their surroundings, and the team tested what those packages do to human regulatory T cells.

The tumor packages induced new regulatory cells, expanded existing ones, and raised their suppressive activity. In effect, the tumor mails out instructions that build and arm its own bodyguard force. Exposing that trick matters because it names a step that treatment could interrupt: block the packages or their message, and the tumor's shield thins. The study also explains a long-noted puzzle, why regulatory cells are so plentiful and active in people with cancer.
plos-pone-0011569:
Caterina Scoglio and co-authors modeled in 2010 how to fight epidemics where help is far away. Rural regions face outbreaks with few hospitals, long distances, and thin staffing, so strategies copied from cities waste their scarcest resource, time. The team built models of epidemics in rural settings and compared mitigation strategies for efficiency: which measures slow spread most per unit of effort.

Their simulations give public health planners a playbook for the places pandemics hit hardest and help reaches last. Efficient choices might mean protecting transport hubs and clinics first, rather than spreading effort evenly across a map. Modeling before an emergency is the only way to have such answers ready, since mid-outbreak there is no time to compute them. The study treats distance and scarcity as design constraints, not as afterthoughts.
plos-pone-0011669:
Phing-How Lou and co-authors engineered mice that make extra amounts of a hormone-binding protein, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Leptin is a hormone that reports the body's fat stores. Its soluble receptor, OBRe, floats in the blood, binds leptin and adjusts how much of the hormone stays in circulation.

Mice overproducing OBRe weighed less and burned more energy than normal mice. That leaner, faster-burning profile was notable because simply mopping up a hormone might have been expected to blunt its signal instead. The result reveals an unexpected dial on body weight that could inform obesity research.
plos-pone-0011769:
Darius Moharregh-Khiabani and co-authors tested a hopeful multiple sclerosis drug in mice, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Fumaric acid esters were being studied as a pill treatment for the relapsing-remitting form of the disease. One proposed action was direct protection of nerve tissue, beyond calming the immune attack.

The team used cuprizone, a chemical that strips the myelin coats from mouse nerves, to model both the stripping and the repair. They then checked how fumaric acids changed the damage and the regrowth. The test probes whether this drug family can help nerves rewrap, a goal current MS drugs barely reach.
plos-pone-0011869:
Rakel Carpintero and co-workers showed in 2010 that HDL, the so-called good cholesterol particle, can calm a route to inflammation. Small vesicles shed by activated T cells can bind to monocytes, another immune cell type, and trigger them to release inflammatory cytokines. Direct cell contact of this kind is thought to feed diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis.

HDL interfered with that binding, and the monocytes then produced less of the inflammatory output. The finding adds an immune role to a particle known mainly for carrying cholesterol. It also suggests a specific step, vesicle binding, where the calming effect of HDL could be studied for use in inflammatory disease.
plos-pone-0011969:
Ernesto Bernal-Mizrachi and co-workers showed in 2010 that pushing a calcium-driven enzyme too hard in insulin-making cells backfires. Glucose raises calcium in beta cells, and calcium switches on growth pathways that maintain beta cell mass. One key effector is calcineurin, an enzyme activated by calcium and calmodulin.

In mice engineered for extra active calcineurin in beta cells, beta cell mass fell and blood sugar rose, the opposite of the intended growth effect. More signal is not always better; the pathway appears tuned to a middle range. That caution applies directly to diabetes drug ideas built on boosting this pathway.
plos-pone-0012069:
Prasad Burra, Lajos Kalmar, and Peter Tompa found in 2010 that germs fit for great heat run plainer proteins than their mild-weather kin. Such germs grow well at heats from chill to the boil. Much past work told how their stiff proteins hold up in the heat. What had been missed is the floppy side of proteins: the loose parts with no fixed shape that many proteins carry.

Reading gene sets across the full range of growth heats, the team found less of that floppy build. The heat-fit kinds also ran a plainer set of jobs. Loose parts pay off in mild climes but cost too much when heat shakes all parts hard. The trend shows life's slow hand trimming give and flex as the price of a hot home.
plos-pone-0012169:
Colleen O'Rourke, Todd Pitlik, Melissa Hoover, and co-authors compared how day-hunting raptors scan for prey, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Hawks and their kin often hunt from a perch. They watch the ground below for movement. With eyes set on the sides of the head, each bird must move its head in a set pattern. That pattern keeps the scene covered. Yet how the patterns differ between species was little known.

The team measured head movements across raptor species as they scanned from perches. The gaps in rhythm and sweep may match each bird's prey and habitat. Such details show how sight and hunting style evolve together. They can even inform the design of scanning sensors on machines.
plos-pone-0012269:
Gustavo Gómez and Vicente Pallás reported foreign messages traveling into plant chloroplasts, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Chloroplasts, the green engines of plant cells, descend from captured bacteria, and most of their ancestral genes long ago moved into the cell's nucleus. Traffic between nucleus and chloroplast is therefore constant and vital, carried mostly by proteins.

Their finding adds a new courier: noncoding RNA can escort a foreign RNA message into chloroplasts. A signaling route nobody had charted changes how plant scientists think the cell's compartments negotiate. It may also give crop engineers a way to deliver instructions into the chloroplast, a prized target for improving photosynthesis.
plos-pone-0012369:
Nadezhda Tikhmyanova, Alexei Tulin and Fabrice Roegiers studied a fruit fly protein called Dcas in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper on development. Cas proteins in mammals guide cell movement, division, and survival, and they often go wrong in cancer. With four similar Cas proteins in mammals, their jobs blur together, so the team turned to the fly, which has just one.

In fly tissues, Dcas helped cells keep their orientation and supported the adhesion complexes that hold cells to each other. Losing it disrupted growing structures. Because the fly version is simpler, these results clarify what the whole Cas family does, knowledge that feeds back into cancer and development research in humans.
plos-pone-0012469:
Cristina Cellurale, Claire Weston, Judith Reilly and colleagues tested a stress pathway in a mouse breast cancer model, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The pathway centers on JNK, a kinase switched on by cell stress, and it had been implicated in mammary tumor growth. Their model removes Trp53, the mouse version of the p53 tumor guard, in breast tissue.

By also removing JNK in that setting, the team measured how much the pathway matters for tumors to start and grow. Dissecting one pathway inside a defined cancer model shows whether blocking it could ever help patients. JNK blockers exist, so a clear answer guides drug development for breast cancer.
plos-pone-0012569:
Christian Scherling, Christiane Roscher, Patrick Giavalisco and colleagues used metabolomics to read how plant diversity affects individual species, in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Diverse grasslands usually produce more total biomass, yet for any single plant species the effect of neighbors can swing from help to harm. Yield totals hide those private fortunes, so the team profiled plant chemistry instead.

Metabolic fingerprints showed contrasting effects of biodiversity on different species sharing the same plots. Chemistry reveals stress and prosperity that weighing plants cannot. The approach may explain why diversity helps fields and meadows overall while individual species rise and fall within them.
plos-pone-0012669:
Feliziani, Lujan, Moyano and co-authors tracked how a lung bacterium changes during long cystic fibrosis infections. Pseudomonas aeruginosa settles into the airways of these patients for years. To survive, it mutates in set genes, gaining traits such as a slimy coat and drug resistance.

Their 2010 study links slime production, cell-to-cell signalling, DNA repair faults and resistance in bacteria taken from chronic infections. The mix shows adaptation is a package, not single changes. Knowing the package helps doctors expect how infections will evolve under treatment and why late-stage infections are so hard to clear.
plos-pone-0012769:
Fuss, Ben Abdallah, Hensley and co-authors reversed a common story about running, new brain cells and anxiety in mice. Running spurs the growth of new neurons in the hippocampus, a brain area tied to mood. Some evidence had cast that growth as calming, yet their 2010 study reports the opposite pattern.

When they used radiation to erase the running-induced new neurons, the anxious behaviour that running produced also disappeared. So in their setup the new cells were needed for anxiety, not against it. The surprise warns against simple claims that more new neurons always mean better mood.
plos-pone-0344869:
James Arinaitwe and colleagues tracked three respiratory viruses circulating together among adults with acute respiratory illness around Kampala, Uganda, from March 2023 to April 2024. More than twelve hundred outpatients gave nose and throat swabs tested for the COVID virus, influenza A and B, and RSV, a virus better known for infecting children. Records also captured symptoms and vaccination status.

RSV turned up most often, slightly ahead of the COVID virus, with influenza A behind and influenza B rare. The individual shares look modest, but together they mean a steady viral load on clinics year-round. Knowing which virus dominates, and when, helps a low-income health system aim vaccines and plan staffing for seasonal surges.
plos-pone-0345769:
Noa Krawczyk and colleagues outline a study of what happens to people with opioid use disorder in the year after a hospital encounter. Effective medicines exist, yet many patients never start or quickly drop them. Their 2026 protocol describes linking administrative records across New York City and mapping each person's path through treatment, gaps, and returns, using a cascade-of-care framework.

Sequence analysis will group the common trajectories, which the team will relate to personal and neighbourhood traits and to later overdose, hospitalisation, and death. As a protocol, the paper reports design rather than results. The findings are meant to show hospitals and policymakers where the chain of care most often breaks.
plos-pone-0346269: Vélez de Lachica and three co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on a knee injection for athletes. The shot combines hyaluronic acid with sorbitol and targets pain at the kneecap joint. The team also checked whether body mass index changed how well the shot worked. Athletes and team doctors need such detail to weigh injections against rest and therapy.
plos-pone-0347669:
Richard Vogg and colleagues present PriMAT, software that tracks individual primates in wild video footage, a job deep learning usually does well only in tidy laboratories. Forest light shifts, animals hide behind each other, and backgrounds change constantly. PriMAT learns from simple labelled boxes around animals rather than detailed body points, making training data far quicker to prepare.

With only a few hundred labelled frames, the system tracked Assamese macaques and red-fronted lemurs robustly, and transferred to baboons, chimpanzees, and gorillas. An added identification branch named individual lemurs with eighty-four percent accuracy. Code and models are public, offering field researchers automated behaviour watching.
plos-pone-0347769:
Jianwei Hu, Hanyu Song, and Wanwan Peng asked what parts of town life make folk glad to live there. They used forms from near eleven thousand folk in Wuhan, China. Their score card held eight parts and fifty-four gauges of space, aid, and green life. A smart net, tuned by a search trick, then guessed glad scores from the card.

Health and ease of life weighed most. Safe streets and tough homes came next. Shops close by, ease of car space, fire care, and new life for old halls all counted a lot. The tuned net beat plain tools by a clear edge. The team says towns should fund aid, safe streets, and homes folk can pay for.
plos-pone-0347869:
Lina Yuan and three co-workers wrote a smarter plan for beaming power to small tags by radio. Such tags log heat, motion, and sights on farms and in stores. Fixed power plans waste juice and treat tags in an unfair way. The team mixed a forward-looking control with a fair rota for charge time. A shared solver split the hard sums into small ones.

In tests the plan hit a much higher peak rate than the old style of control. Power swings fell by more than half. Each tag got a near fair share of charge, at ranges from half a metre to five. The team sees uses in mobile gear of all kinds.
plos-pone-0348069:
Ulvhild Helena Færøvik and Karsten Specht asked more than a thousand people online to judge the feelings carried by short pieces of music. The pieces were played at different speeds and in major or minor keys. Five original tunes were each reshaped into eight versions, and listeners rated every clip for feelings of wonder, unease, and lively energy, alongside control sounds such as noise and spoken voices.

Faster music was steadily rated as more energetic and less wondrous in both keys, and fast major-key music felt less uneasy than slow. Training, gender, and schooling nudged ratings only slightly, though age mattered more in places. The results confirm that speed and key together steer the mood listeners hear, and they matter for anyone choosing music to set a feeling.
plos-pone-0348269:
Juliette Bih Nkarenbi, Erhabor Idemudia, and Lawrence Ejike Ugwu survey African students at South African universities. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. It covered seven hundred eighty-one students at four public universities. Students abroad often face bias and exclusion. The team asked if such treatment links to post-traumatic growth. They also asked if student stress carries that link.

Standard scales measured bias, stress, and growth. Growth meant gains like personal strength and richer ties to others. Models traced how bias fed stress, and how stress fed growth. The work treats bias as neither pure harm nor hidden gift. Its path to growth runs through the strain it creates.
plos-pone-0348369:
Courage Siame and co-authors tested garlic compounds against breast cancer targets using only computer simulations. Garlic's sulphur-rich chemicals have shown anti-cancer hints in earlier work, but whether they can hit several cancer proteins at once was unclear. Their 2026 study docked six garlic compounds into proteins that help tumours survive and multiply, then screened the compounds for drug-like behaviour and safety.

One compound, Z-ajoene, latched strongly onto three separate targets, and another touched five. All six passed basic rules for medicines taken by mouth, with no predicted cancer-causing risk. The authors are careful: these are predictions, and they call for laboratory tests, especially for cancers that resist current drugs.
plos-pone-0348569:
Haiyan Lu and colleagues built a model that flags listed companies likely to be committing financial fraud. Their training data covered more than seven thousand Chinese non-financial firms, including firms punished for fraud in the years from 2007 through 2022. Each firm carried eighty-seven measures of governance, finances, and operations. Rare fraud cases were oversampled so the model could learn their pattern.

A convolutional network first extracts higher-level features from the indicators, and a support vector machine then makes the final call. The hybrid scored far above standard logistic regression and random forest models on accuracy measures. For regulators and investors, an early-warning score like this could focus audits where the risk of cooked books is highest.
plos-pone-0348669:
Huda Kutrani and colleagues asked whether simple bedside data can sharpen a widely used frailty score. The Hospital Frailty Risk Score, built from diagnosis codes, flags patients likely to stay long in hospital or die there, but it was designed mainly for older people. The 2026 study used ten years of admissions at a large Portsmouth hospital, covering everyone aged sixteen and up.

Adding routine vital signs or a lab-based early warning score improved predictions of both stay length and death at every age. The lab score helped most for longer stays and later deaths, while vital signs helped most for early deaths. All the added data are already collected, so hospitals could adopt the combined approach cheaply.
plos-pone-0348769:
Sylvia Kusemererwa and co-workers measure new HIV infections inside a Ugandan group gathered to prepare for vaccine trials. The volunteers, adults living along a major highway and Lake Victoria shores in Masaka district, faced high exposure risk by design. Their 2026 study follows more than fourteen hundred initially HIV-negative adults with testing every three months across four years.

Twenty-four people acquired HIV during follow-up, a rate the authors report for planning trials. Being female carried much higher risk, as did living in a fishing community and recent recreational drug use. Knowing which subgroups seroconvert fastest helps trial designers recruit where prevention benefit and study power are greatest, and points services to the same people first.
plos-pone-0348869:
Xiaoxiong Zhou and colleagues upgraded a vision model so drones can spot tiny flaws in electrical insulators, the ceramic stacks that keep power lines safe. Standard detectors miss small defects against cluttered skies and towers. Their version, RDA-YOLO, widens how the model gathers context, replaces its decision stage with an attention-based one, and judges box overlap in a way that treats small targets more fairly.

On the team's own inspection dataset the model reached precision above ninety percent, beating rival detectors they tried, while adding only modest computing cost. Extra tests under harsh conditions showed it held up better than the base model when weather and lighting turned nasty. The authors aim the tool at routine grid patrols, where early flaw spotting prevents outages and fires.
plos-pone-0348969:
Juliana Osorio-Marulanda, Juliana Lopez-Jimenez, and Juan Alzate wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article about a plant virus. Hydrangea ringspot virus infects hydrangeas, popular garden shrubs. The authors study its genomic diversity, which hosts it infects, and which plant tissues it prefers, a property called tissue tropism.

Their view is both global and regional, comparing virus samples across places. Knowing how much the virus varies and where it concentrates in the plant helps growers and inspectors track its spread. Ornamental plant trade moves viruses worldwide in symptomless stock, so a map of this kind supports nursery biosecurity.
plos-pone-0349169:
RETRACTION NOTICE: The PLOS One Editors issued this 2026 notice withdrawing an earlier case-control study from Belgrade on workplace solvents, pesticides, gene variants, and bladder cancer risk. Readers should not rely on the original findings. Serbia's health ministry and national ethics board asked for the withdrawal over approval concerns.

The ethics board said the study used patients and samples from a major hospital without that hospital's own ethics approval. The first author pointed to a faculty ethics approval and a clinic director's letter instead. Hospital officials answered that their board never reviewed the study and that this route did not meet the needed standard. Faced with that dispute, the journal retracted the article.
plos-pone-0349669:
Fatemeh Rastekar and three colleagues test an unusual cleaning crew in this 2026 museum study. Natural history museums need animal skeletons that are clean yet undamaged. Standard methods are slow, risky, or harsh on delicate bones. The team tried superworms, the larvae of a darkling beetle, which eat dead tissue. Trials covered several vertebrate groups and body sizes.

The key turned out to be the ratio of worms to specimen weight. Too many worms damaged fragile bones. Too few made cleaning drag on. A ratio between ten and fifteen worked best, stripping tissue within hours to days. Bird skulls cleaned at that ratio came through thoroughly cleaned with no visible damage. Superworms could give small museums a cheap, safe alternative to beetle colonies and chemicals.
plos-pone-0349869:
Benjamin Chaffee and colleagues developed a short questionnaire for dry mouth aimed at young adults, a group the standard tools were never built for. Dry mouth harms comfort and oral health at any age, yet research had concentrated on older and high-risk people. Two hundred seventy-eight students at two California public universities answered a fourteen-item draft inventory mixing new and borrowed questions.

Statistical analysis trimmed the draft to five items that held together well and behaved soundly in this age group. Scores lined up sensibly with other oral health problems and known dry-mouth risk factors, supporting the short scale's validity. A five-question tool makes it practical to screen students and young patients, and to study causes of dry mouth earlier in life.
plos-pone-0350169:
Marco Vinicio Alban-Paccha and colleagues lay out the protocol for ADVANTAGE, a study hunting for new painkillers for chronic gut and pelvic pain by studying extreme cases. More than one in five adults live with such visceral pain, yet its mechanisms are poorly understood. The project recruits three groups: people with extreme pain, people who strangely feel almost none, and healthy volunteers.

Participants give genetic samples and immune profiles, map their pain, wear sensors, and log daily pain in a phone app. Conditions range from endometriosis to chronic pancreatitis. Comparing the extremes can reveal protective and risk factors invisible in average patients. This paper is the plan, registered before results, for the consortium's search for drug targets.
plos-pone-0350269:
Junnan Song and colleagues studied heart artery narrowing in Chinese adults. The team used two hundred and eighteen patients. Care took place at one large hospital. Visits ran from mid 2023 to early 2024. Pulse pressure was read at arm and ankle sites. Readings were set beside artery imaging grades.

All site readings ran higher in severe narrowing. Mild narrowing showed lower readings. Left arm readings stayed linked after adjustments. The link held in both sexes. Ankle strength swapped sides by sex. A cheap cuff test could sort urgent cases. High readings may flag who needs imaging first.
plos-pone-0350669:
Alhusseini and colleagues profiled drug resistance across more than a thousand genomes of an opportunistic hospital germ in a 2026 study. The germ infects weakened patients and resists many drugs. Public genomes spanning over a century and forty countries were filtered to a clean confirmed set.

Resistance genes were catalogued by type, place, host, and era, alongside strain family labels. Patterns of genes appearing together were also mapped. A genome atlas like this helps hospitals anticipate which drugs will fail and tracks how resistance travels. The century-long span shows resistance building as antibiotic use spread.
plos-pone-0350969:
Liz Ignowski led a team of five authors studying off-season farming in Cambodia, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Growing vegetables against the normal season can fetch higher prices, since supply is scarce, but it carries more risk from weather and pests. The team measured the impact of that gamble on Cambodian farmers.

Ignowski's group assessed whether bucking the calendar pays off, which farmers benefit most, and what risks they carry. Such evidence helps extension services advise farmers with real numbers instead of slogans. Off-season success can lift incomes a great deal, but a failed crop hurts more when inputs cost more. Knowing who wins and who loses guides credit and support toward those who can use them.
plos-pone-0351069:
Tamara Scharf and colleagues ran a trial in Swiss primary care on shared choice for bowel cancer screening. Doctors there usually book a colon camera test directly, without offering the stool test choice. Clinics were split by chance. Trained clinics got decision aids, evidence briefs, stool kits, and personal feedback, then logged choices for forty straight patients aged fifty to seventy five.

Trained doctors were far more likely to have at least one patient take or plan the stool test. Yet when change was tracked within the same doctors over time, gains looked weaker and may reflect doctors who already offered the stool test offering it more widely. Choice aids help, but habit change takes more.
plos-pone-0351169:
Four medicines used for epilepsy and mood disorders were tracked through British family doctor records by Siti Watiqah Samsuddin and colleagues. Their 2026 PLOS One study covers 1995 to 2018, following how often doctors started patients on carbamazepine, lamotrigine, valproate, and lithium, split by age and sex.

Carbamazepine starts fell steeply after the early 2000s, while lamotrigine rose and by 2018 led among younger adults. Valproate starts dropped too, yet it stayed common in young men already taking it. Lithium remained the least used of the four. Prescribing ran consistently higher in poorer areas, a pattern the authors flag for attention.
plos-pone-0351469:
Guillermo Pérez Castro and four colleagues sharpen bicycle traffic simulation in this 2026 study. Planners use microscopic simulators to test street designs before building them. Those tools model free-riding speed poorly. Real cyclists speed up and slow down with slopes, curves, junctions, and wind. The team built three improved models inside a standard traffic simulator. One uses context-based speed distributions, one a regression, and one physics, calculating speed from rider power. Fifty-seven commuters in Sweden and Germany supplied trajectories.

All three models beat the built-in baselines at reproducing real speeds. The physics model matched observed riding most closely. Context proved not to be a luxury detail. Ignoring it produced much larger speed errors, especially climbing and descending hills. Junctions mattered too. For cities weighing bike lanes and signals, better speed realism means better predictions of travel time, bunching, and safety before a kerb is moved.
plos-pone-0351969:
Nora Salim and colleagues reviewed studies of what keeps parents of autistic children resilient. Caregiving demands run for years in these families. The review asked which factors travel with parents who cope well. Thirteen studies from recent years passed the quality checks. The team grouped the findings by theme rather than averaging numbers.

Five families of factors emerged. They covered the parents' social and economic footing. They covered traits of the child. They also covered the parents' own well-being and support. Resilience looks less like a gift of character than a balance of resources and strains. Services can change that balance with income help, rest breaks, and coaching.
plos-pone-0352169:
Abel Demeke and colleagues gathered every systematic review they could find on hepatitis B in Ethiopia, twelve reviews covering nearly a million people in all, and pooled them into one national estimate. The virus scars livers and causes cancer, yet earlier reviews disagreed with each other. An umbrella review, a review of reviews, was their way to settle the number and name the risk factors.

About six Ethiopians in a hundred carry the infection, a moderate level by world standards. Risk clustered around being male, multiple sexual partners, tattoos, shared sharp objects, tooth extraction, hospital stays, and blood transfusion, a list mixing private behavior with gaps in medical safety. The authors aim the findings at action: wider vaccination, safer blood, and stricter infection control in clinics and barbershops alike.
plos-pone-0352669:
Doni Dermawan and Nasser Alotaiq screened drug ideas on a computer for a rare red cell ill, pyruvate kinase deficiency. The first drug that lifts the weak enzyme helps, but the body clears it in ways that limit use. Their 2026 screen ran near two hundred kin of that drug through docking, shape checks, and long motion runs.

Two ideas rose to the top. One gripped the enzyme most tight in docking and held most steady in the runs, with the most hydrogen bonds kept. Both were set next to the known drug and a natural blocker. Checks on drug-like traits and ease of making came with the screen. The pair are leads for lab work, not drugs yet.
plos-pone-0352769:
Fuko Miyake and five colleagues report this 2026 PLOS One laboratory study on pancreatic cancer cells grown under physical pressure. Tumors press against the tissue around them, and that squeezing force pushes back on the cancer cells themselves. Earlier work had shown such pressure slows breast and colorectal cancer cells, but pancreatic cells had not been tested.

When the team compressed AsPC-1 pancreatic cancer cells, the cells grew more slowly than unpressed ones. Pressure lowered levels of Myc, a protein that drives cell growth, and that drop explained the slower growth. At the same time the cells raised Snail, a protein tied to worse outcomes for patients. The results suggest physical force inside a tumor can reshape cancer behavior in mixed ways.
plos-pone-0352869:
Sadik Abdulwehab, Duguma Debela Genati, and Frezer Kedir present this 2026 PLOS One review of delayed care-seeking by cancer patients in Ethiopia. Late arrival drives much of the country's cancer death toll. The authors pooled seven studies with more than twenty-six hundred patients. They estimated the overall scale of delay. They also identified the factors behind it.

Just over half of patients delayed seeking care. Living in the countryside tripled the odds of delay. Poor knowledge of cancer raised the odds nearly sevenfold. Having no pain tripled the odds too, since painless lumps are easy to ignore. Low awareness also played a part. The authors call for community teaching and rural outreach. Patients should arrive while cancers are still treatable.
plos-pone-0352969:
Min-Jung Kim, Hwan Sun Moon, and So-Hyun Paek present this 2026 PLOS One study checking whether ambulance crews and emergency departments grade patient urgency the same way. South Korea had just extended its five-level hospital triage scale nationwide to ambulances. The team linked ambulance and hospital records for nearly five thousand transported patients during the first implementation year, with special attention to children.

Crews and departments assigned the exact same level in only about half of adult cases and fewer child cases. Most disagreements sat at neighboring levels, especially around the middle of the scale. With children, crews tended to grade urgency higher than the department did, while adults showed the reverse lean. The authors suggest targeted training and feedback for pediatric triage, where the mismatch is widest.
plos-pone-0353069:
Md Muqtadir Fuad, Md Sajib Milki, and Ridwan Al Aziz build a forecasting framework for dengue in Bangladesh in this 2026 study. Dengue outbreaks there are usually predicted from weather alone, yet the circulating virus types also shape how outbreaks unfold. Their system pulls in time patterns, weather, population, and virus data at district level, then tests many kinds of forecasting models against each other.

No single model won everywhere. A classic statistical model gave the best early warnings for one-step-ahead outbreak alerts, while another tool forecast the size of outbreaks better over longer horizons. Simpler regression stayed competitive in certain outbreak regimes, and a deep learning model produced poorly calibrated uncertainty during surges. The authors conclude that forecasters should pick the model to match the decision at hand, short-term alerts or seasonal planning, rather than crown one method overall.
plos-pone-0353169:
Haviv Avrahami and Lindsay Zanno present a full skull anatomy of Fona herzogae, a small plant-eating dinosaur from Cretaceous Utah. The species is known from an unusually large pile of separate skull bones, rare for its early-diverging family. Their 2026 description uses high-resolution digital scanning to document each element from several angles.

The new detail sharpens how traits are scored across the dinosaur's family tree. Re-scoring a Korean relative from firsthand study moved it inside the same subfamily. Support also grew for including several Asian species in that group. A geographic split between Asian and North American members came out clearer. The authors say rich disarticulated material can anchor family-level questions.
plos-pone-0353269:
Omer Kursad Katirci, Diana Toderita, and Anthony Bull simulate switching on a hip muscle harder during walking, in this 2026 PLOS ONE modelling study. The muscle, gluteus medius, keeps the pelvis level with each step, and therapists already stimulate it electrically in some patients with nerve damage. Using gait data from thirty healthy adults, the team asked computer models of the body what would change if that muscle worked harder.

Peak forces shifted in seven muscles, total effort changed in eight, and the load through the hip joint moved too. The pattern fits better side-to-side pelvic control. The results are purely simulated, but they show therapists exactly which other muscles would share or shed work.
plos-pone-0353369:
Ji-Yong Sung, Jin-Hong Kim, and Yi-Jun Kim search the neighbourhood around sarcoma tumours for clues to immunotherapy success, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Sarcomas respond unevenly to immune-checkpoint drugs, and the fibroblast cells surrounding a tumour help decide who benefits. Using single-cell data from two patient groups plus tumour records for hundreds more, they sorted fibroblasts into three subtypes.

Gene signatures from the subtypes tracked with predicted drug response, but differently across sarcoma kinds. One small four-gene signature, active in the inflammatory subtype, stood out as a candidate for forecasting survival. The authors stress it is a lead for testing, not yet a clinical tool.
plos-pone-0353469:
Wang and colleagues tested a sound-based method for finding early pipe corrosion in a 2026 study. Pitting eats small holes in aluminum pipes carrying liquids and gas, and leaks can be destructive. Flexible ceramic strips sent guided sound waves along curved pipe walls, and the team extracted a harmonic signal created when waves meet corrosion.

Repeat tests also checked how temperature shifts the signal, a confounder in real plants. Catching pitting early, before it pierces the wall, is the prize. A sensor that hugs curved pipes and works at plant temperatures could join routine inspection kits for chemical and energy facilities.
plos-pone-0353569:
Ivaan Pitua and three colleagues published this 2026 PLOS One review combining evidence on wasting, a form of acute malnutrition, in African children being treated for cancer. Malnutrition can worsen cancer care, yet its overall scale across the continent had never been pulled together. The authors searched major medical databases for studies of patients up to age nineteen published since the year 2000.

Sixteen study groups covering about twenty-four hundred patients in eight countries were combined. Roughly two in five children were wasted, though rates varied widely between studies. How malnutrition was measured mattered greatly: arm circumference checks found far more cases than weight-based measures, which can miss children with large tumors. Wasting was also linked to more treatment side effects and worse survival where those outcomes were tracked.
plos-pone-0353769:
Ziller and colleagues, in a 2026 study, ask whether older women who eat little protein are hurt worse when they fall. Falls are a major cause of injury and death in old age, and diet is one lever families can actually move. The team drew on a large American women's health study, following more than six thousand women with fall calendars for over a year.

About one faller in three was injured, and a smaller share broke a bone. Women whose protein share of calories fell below a modest line had clearly higher odds of a fracture from a fall than women above it. A striking subgroup result linked low protein with any fall injury among women on diabetes medicines, though that group was small. The authors suggest clinics screen diet and medicines together when planning how to keep older women safe on their feet.
plos-pone-0353869:
Hajek and colleagues asked whether plant-based eating links to loneliness in a 2026 survey of adults in Germany. Five thousand people aged from late teens to mid seventies reported what they mostly eat and how connected they feel to others. The survey measured loneliness, weak social networks, and pulling away from social life.

People who ate mostly vegetarian food scored higher on feeling cut off and on withdrawal than meat eaters at first. Once mood and mental health were taken into account, those gaps faded away. Vegan eaters showed no clear lasting gap, which suggests mental health, not diet alone, explains much of the link.
plos-pone-0353969:
Bastola and Li, in a 2026 study, compare sixteen prediction algorithms for spotting malnourished children in Nepal, using national survey data rather than clinic visits. Finding underfed children door to door is slow, and remote areas are often missed. A model that flags risk from household survey answers could aim scarce help where it counts.

Stunting, wasting, and low weight were merged into one malnutrition label from a 2019 child survey. Deep learning, boosting, and classic methods were all tried and scored on ten measures, with weight on catching true cases, since missing a hungry child costs most. A tablet-shaped deep network, TabNet, won, likely thanks to its attention design. Mother's education, household wealth, and child's age were the strongest predictors, with place, vaccines, and meal frequency behind. The authors offer the framework as a template for other low-resource countries.
plos-pone-0354169:
Hiroshi Nonami led a team of seven authors on this 2026 moral psychology study. They split dilemmas into two kinds: ones where a judge decides only others' fate, and ones where the judge's own life hangs on the choice too. In two experiments, participants judged sacrificing one person to save many, and their empathy was measured.

People allowed the sacrifice more readily when their own life was among those saved. Yet empathic concern consistently pushed against such cold calculations in both dilemma types. Nonami argues the distinction matters for understanding everyday moral choices, including shared-resource problems.
plos-pone-0354369:
Embark and colleagues, in a 2026 laboratory study, test whether a platinum compound that can leak from cochlear implants harms hearing cells. The implants restore hearing for many people, but their platinum electrodes can corrode slowly, raising resistance and releasing metal products into the inner ear. What those products do to the ear's sensory cells was unclear.

Using a standard line of auditory cells, the team applied the compound at several strengths and times, recording the cells' electrical state and their energy-making activity. The compound pushed the cells' resting voltage upward in a dose- and time-dependent way, a shift that can trigger ion channels and upset the cells' salt balance. Energy activity also changed with dose, though not further between one and two days, hinting that repair efforts switch on alongside damage. The authors urge implant makers to weigh corrosion products, not just device electronics.
plos-pone-0354469:
Kambiré and colleagues, in a 2026 study, purify and profile an enzyme from the gut juice of palm weevil larvae, a notorious pest of palm trees. The enzyme, beta-galactosidase, breaks down milk sugar and related compounds and is prized in food and drug making. Insect guts are a little-explored source of hardy enzymes.

Using a yellow test substrate, the team measured the enzyme's sweet spots: a warm temperature just above human body heat, by their modeling, and mildly acidic conditions. They estimated the energy the reaction needs and identified the likely acid and base players in its active site from how activity changed with acidity. Speed measures placed it in a useful working range. The authors conclude that this pest's digestion hides a capable industrial enzyme, and that insect guts deserve a place in the search for new biocatalysts.
plos-pone-0354669:
Shuang Li and co-authors built a deep learning model that predicts how strongly a cancer cell line will respond to a drug. The response measure halves cell survival, and computing it well could cut costly screening. Older models ignore either the drug's three-dimensional chemistry or the cell's biological state. Their 2026 design feeds both through separate branches.

One branch reads the drug as a molecular graph through a graph isomorphism network. The other reads fifty pathway activity scores computed from the cell line's gene expression. Training used a major public pharmacogenomics collection spanning many cancer types. Li and colleagues argue joining structure with pathway context should generalise better across data sources than either input alone.
plos-pone-0354969:
Emile Nkurunziza and Robert Kogi published this 2026 case-control study of cholera in Rumonge Health District, southern Burundi. The district suffers repeat outbreaks despite control campaigns. Comparing fifty households where someone fell ill with twice as many nearby healthy households, they asked families about water, food, and washing habits.

Taking drinking water from lakes or rivers, using it untreated at home, and eating unwashed raw fruit all raised the risk sharply. Poor handwashing after using the toilet mattered too. Nkurunziza and Kogi recommend safe water supplies and stronger hygiene teaching as the practical route to breaking the outbreak cycle.
plos-pone-0355269: Lin and three co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on power grids and business tech in China. They asked whether building ultra-high voltage lines, which move power over long distances, spurs firms to develop artificial intelligence. The evidence came from China's big transmission projects. If energy builds shape tech growth, planners gain one more reason to weigh where and when lines are built.
plos-pone-0355369:
Katherine Van Koevering, Yiquan Hong, and Jon Kleinberg study how Reddit organized itself around COVID-19 almost overnight, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Most big discussion topics accrete communities over years; this one arrived abruptly and hundreds of forums formed within weeks. Using a nearly complete census of those communities, the authors ask what people talked about, who they talked with, and what shapes the self assembly took.

The new forums did not float free of older ones. They plugged into existing frames, political, skeptical, and geographic, and geography proved the single largest organizing theme, despite the crisis being planetary. Neighbors wanted to talk to neighbors about local rules, risks, and resources. The authors call the pattern social tectonics: under sudden pressure, online society snaps into plates along old fault lines, and any emergency communication strategy should expect local identity to dominate.
plos-pone-0355469:
Mei-Ping Zheng and co-authors mined gene data for cell-cycle markers that flag sepsis, the runaway infection response that shuts down organs. Disturbed cell cycles are increasingly blamed for sepsis immune failure. Their 2026 study overlapped genes changed in sepsis with cell-cycle genes, then let machine learning shortlist the strongest candidates.

Four genes survived screening and validation, all running more active in sepsis samples. Each separated patients from controls well on accuracy curves. Enrichment and immune profiling placed the markers inside sepsis biology, and drug prediction suggested compounds that might touch them. Single-cell data located the markers in specific immune cell types and traced their behaviour over cell development paths.
plos-pone-0355869:
Caitriona Murphy and co-authors compared a new nose-only swab against combined nose-and-throat swabs for flu and COVID testing. Good sampling decides whether a test finds the virus, and throat swabbing is unpleasant enough to deter people. Their 2026 study enrolled feverish outpatients at a Hong Kong clinic who gave both sample types for laboratory comparison.

Agreement between the two methods was very high for influenza A, influenza B, and the coronavirus alike, each around ninety-eight to ninety-nine percent. Viral signal strengths were also compared head to head. Murphy and colleagues conclude the gentler anterior nasal swab performs on par with the combined method in symptomatic patients, which could widen testing uptake.
plos-pone-0355969:
Catharina Latz and colleagues tested whether artificial intelligence can grade cataracts from eye scans without a doctor's grading. Cataracts cloud the lens, and grading guides surgery decisions. Their 2026 feasibility study trained a neural network on about eighteen hundred scan images from just over nine hundred eyes.

Human grades from a standard scale served as the reference. The system graded one cataract type, at the back of the lens, with fairly high accuracy. It graded clouding of the lens centre much less well, at about three in five correct. Most errors there landed in a neighbouring grade. Latz and colleagues call the results promising but preliminary, a base for larger and more careful validation.
plos-pone-0356269:
Oscar Emil Puntervold and seven colleagues test whether a commercial chemistry kit built for blood and other fluids can profile metabolites in dead heart tissue, in this 2026 forensic study. Forty hearts from autopsies in Denmark were sampled: donors with type 2 diabetes, with ischemic heart disease, and controls without heart pathology. The kit measures hundreds of small molecules at once using mass spectrometry.

About three quarters of the kit's targets could be quantified in heart tissue, with fat-related molecules measuring best and some other classes proving patchier. A few metabolite groups differed nominally between donor groups, but nothing survived strict statistical correction, and overall profiles did not separate the groups. The authors call the approach technically feasible and a promising standardized basis for future forensic and heart research, rather than a ready diagnostic.
plos-pone-0356469:
Karikalan Nagarajan and co-authors trained community volunteers in a remote tribal district of Manipur, India, to support tuberculosis control. Volunteers learned to spot symptoms, collect and move sputum samples, and support patients through treatment. The 2026 study measured knowledge, attitudes, and intended practice before and after the training.

More than seven hundred volunteers were trained, and about half completed the full course and both assessments. The share reaching the top knowledge band jumped from about one in ten to about two in three. Attitude scores rose only slightly, though more volunteers said they would seek care quickly for symptoms. The authors conclude that short, culturally fitting training can raise TB knowledge fast, even in hard-to-reach areas.
plos-pone-0356569:
Yujie Liu and coauthors published a 2026 evidence summary in PLOS ONE on helping family members care for a relative living with an enterostomy, a surgically created opening for waste. Family caregivers handle pouches, skin care, and daily routines, often with little training. The team systematically searched guideline networks, nursing societies, and major databases, keeping only sources that passed quality checks, then distilled the best advice.

Thirteen sources survived: clinical decision tools, guidelines, a systematic review, and expert consensuses. From them the authors drew sixteen pieces of evidence in four domains. Families need structured teaching of knowledge and hands-on skills; support through the care process; protection of the caregiver's own body and mind; and a wider support system around them. The summary is offered as a ready reference for nurses building caregiver training plans, reflecting published evidence rather than a new trial.
plos-pone-0356769:
Samuel Westaway and colleagues used the UK Renal Registry to follow 5,447 adults whose kidney transplants failed between 2012 and 2021. They asked who got what treatment in the first year. They also asked whether the answer was fair. Their 2026 cohort study tracked re-transplantation, dialysis choices, conservative care, and death. The results were broken down by age, sex, ethnicity, wealth, disease, and center.

Nearly half went onto hospital dialysis. Only about one in twenty received a new kidney within the year. Black and Asian patients were markedly less likely to be re-transplanted than white patients. Men were more likely than women. Each step of deprivation cut re-transplant chances by roughly a fifth. The registry's findings give the transplant system hard numbers on inequities to answer for.
plos-pone-0356869:
Nuray Alaca and three colleagues studied healthy aging in a PLOS ONE paper from 2026. They asked how two inner resources, kindness toward oneself and belief in one's own ability, relate to aging well. Their measures covered pain, health habits, posture awareness, and quality of life in older adults.

Alaca's team found links suggesting that these inner resources matter alongside physical ones. People who treat themselves with patience and trust their capacity may keep up habits that protect health. Programs for older adults often focus on exercise and diet alone. This study argues for adding mental skills training to that mix, since how people relate to themselves can shape the daily choices that add up to aging well.
plos-pone-0357369: Dingle and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE plan for a study at three Australian universities. The plan tests Tuned In Connect, a program meant to lift the success of neurodivergent students by supporting their wellbeing. The design is quasi-experimental, meaning groups are compared without full random assignment. Publishing the plan first lets other experts judge the methods before any results appear.
plos-pone-0357469:
Jordan E Hamden leads a team of eight asking whether the microbes parents carry can tune a newborn's stress hormones, in PLOS ONE in 2026. In baby mice, hormone levels inside immune organs run higher than in blood during the first two weeks of life, and gut microbes are suspected of helping set those levels. Instead of wiping microbes out, the team bred mice from two colonies whose gut communities differed modestly and measured hormones in five day old pups.

The parent colonies' microbes differed in makeup, though not in overall diversity. Pups from one line carried higher levels of corticosterone, the main mouse stress hormone, and a related hormone in blood and immune organs. The team also measured fatty acids made by gut bacteria as a possible messenger. Even gentle differences in inherited microbes, the results suggest, reach into a newborn's hormone settings.
plos-pone-0357569:
Leah Gordillo and six colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article about desert wildlife. It studies toads in the Great Basin desert and the Mojave and their presence at artificial water sites, tanks and troughs placed in dry country. The authors test what drives that presence.

Two drivers named in the title are accessibility, how easily toads can reach and enter the water, and surface area, how large the water is. In deserts, artificial water can decide whether amphibians survive dry years. Land managers who maintain or remove these sites need to know which features toads actually use, and this study supplies that link.
plos-pone-0357969:
A Z M Fahim Siddique and six co-authors, in a 2026 PLOS ONE study, look for genes shared by two heart conditions. One is hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, in which the heart muscle grows too thick. The other is atrial fibrillation, a fast and uneven heartbeat that strikes these patients unusually often. The team wanted the genetic links that might explain that overlap.

They pooled gene lists from five public databases and compared the two conditions, finding eleven genes in common. Three stood out as central connectors, including NPPA, which makes a hormone involved in blood pressure control. Checks in separate patient datasets and in clinical samples confirmed that NPPA activity runs high in the thickened heart condition, tying it to electrical changes in the upper heart chambers.
plos-pone-0358069:
Mohamed Ahmed El Maghawry led a team of seven authors reviewing seven years of plasma therapy in Egypt, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Therapeutic plasma exchange filters harmful substances from the blood and treats a surprising range of diseases, from nerve to kidney to blood disorders. The team studied its use across organ systems at an Egyptian tertiary center.

El Maghawry's real-world cohort shows what the therapy achieves outside controlled trials, in daily hospital practice over a long span. Such records reveal which conditions the center treats most, how patients fare, and where the therapy is stretched thin. Centers in similar settings can benchmark their own programs against it. Long local records are how expensive therapies earn continued funding: by proof, not habit.
plos-pone-0358269:
Jargalmaa Amarsanaa and colleagues published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE tracking loneliness in Japan through the COVID-19 years. They followed the same group of adults through five yearly online surveys, from 2020 to 2024, using a short three-question loneliness scale. Rather than taking a single snapshot, the team watched how individuals moved into or out of loneliness over time.

Loneliness peaked in 2021, eased in 2022, and then held fairly steady through 2024. Most people followed stable paths, either lonely at every wave or not lonely at any wave, while a smaller group felt lonely only during part of the pandemic. Stricter cutoffs for what counts as lonely did not change that overall picture. The authors caution that an online panel cannot give exact national rates, but the patterns show whose isolation lingered after restrictions ended.
plos-pone-0358469:
Juan Pablo Narváez-Herrera led a team of six authors measuring carbon and soil life on a Colombian cattle farm, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. The dual-purpose farm, in the Amazonian foothills, raises cattle for both milk and beef across several kinds of land use. The team compared soil carbon stocks, litter breakdown, and soil animal diversity across those uses.

Narváez-Herrera's comparison shows which practices keep carbon in the ground and support soil life, and which let both slip. Cattle farming in the Amazon foothills sits at the center of climate and forest debates. Farm-level evidence like this can guide land use that keeps production while storing carbon, instead of forcing a choice between the two.
plos-pone-0358569: Teka and five co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on a surgical training program in Ethiopia's Tigray region. The program trains non-physician surgeons to handle emergency operations where doctors are scarce. The team gathered views on how well the program fits into the wider health system. Their focus was the surgeons who are not physicians. Fit matters because a good program can still fail if the system resists it.
plos-pone-0358769:
Masaki Chujyo, Shu Liu, and Fujio Toriumi ask where a network is weakest when damage spreads outward from a single point, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Such localized attacks, a fire, a flood, a failure cascading to neighbors, threaten power grids and transport webs. Standard importance scores rank nodes by connections, but the authors suspected they miss how position shapes a spreading failure. They propose an index that simulates an attack starting at each node and counts the links severed along the way.

On synthetic and real world networks, their index tracked the actual loss of robustness more closely than the classic centrality measures of degree, closeness, and betweenness. Highly connected nodes were not always the dangerous seeds; shape and neighborhood layout mattered as much. For operators hardening real infrastructure, the index offers a sharper way to decide which single points deserve protection first.
plos-pone-0358869: Susanti and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE interview study set in Java, Indonesia. They asked local stakeholders how acceptable low-intensity psychological care would likely be before it starts. Such care uses brief, guided help rather than long therapy. Views gathered early, through a theory-based frame, can reveal doubts and support that planners must address before launch.
plos-pone-0358969:
Balram Yelamasetti leads a team of seven 3D printing honeycomb sandwich panels and weighing strength against lightness, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The panels, plastic faces over a honeycomb core, promise stiff parts from little material, but four geometry choices pull the design in different directions. Eighteen configurations, varying cell size, cell wall thickness, and the two face thicknesses, were printed in PLA plastic and bent until they failed, then weighed.

Cell size and wall thickness together explained most of the variation in bending strength, and the same pair dominated the mass results in swapped order. The catch is that the geometry favoring maximum strength was not the geometry favoring minimum weight. The authors therefore blend the two analyses into a compromise setting rather than crowning a single winner. Their method suits any printed structure, from drone frames to furniture, where grams and strength must be bought together.
plos-pone-0359069:
Zihong Chen leads a team of eight hunting genetic risk markers for myasthenia gravis, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The disease weakens muscles when the immune system attacks the junctions where nerves meet muscle. The authors focused on markers inside long noncoding RNA regions, an understudied corner of the genome. They screened candidates from large genetic datasets. Then they genotyped one hundred sixty-one patients and the same number of healthy controls.

Overall, marker frequencies looked alike in patients and controls. The signal appeared only in the generalized form of the disease, where several variants near a noncoding RNA called HCG27 were more common, including the marker named in the study's title. Laboratory work traced how that marker influences HCG27 levels in immune cells. The findings nominate a regulatory variant and its RNA partner for deeper study of disease susceptibility.
plos-pone-0359269: Callizot and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on a possible new drug for Parkinson's disease. The compound, called AZP2006, was tested in lab models of the disease. The title calls it a promising protective treatment for nerve cells. Its action involves lysosomes, the cell's cleanup units, and a protein pair named progranulin and prosaposin. New ways to slow Parkinson's are badly needed.
plos-pone-0360069:
Kiran Katari and co-authors designed in 2026 a smart controller for a device that shields machines from shaking. The device is made from a rubber like material whose stiffness can be changed with a magnet. Shaking that reaches such a shield varies in speed and strength, so the control system must adapt on the fly.

Their design joins two ideas. A small neural network learns how the device behaves, while a robust control method, called sliding mode control, keeps things steady when conditions shift. Tests used shaking that changed in both frequency and amplitude. Better shields of this kind serve cars, factory gear, and fine instruments that must stay still to work well.
pmc-10869269:
van Kempen, Kim, Tumescheit, and co-authors present Foldseek, a fast way to search by protein shape. Computer methods now predict millions of protein shapes, and that flood has made searching them slow. Knowing a protein's shape helps reveal what it does, so search speed matters.

Foldseek compares a query shape against huge databases by encoding how amino acids touch in three dimensions. That encoding lets it find matches far faster than older shape tools. Quick shape search helps scientists spot distant relatives of a protein and guess at roles for proteins never studied in a lab.
pmc-13235869:
Faulkner and colleagues chart the sickle cell burden in Sierra Leone across more than three decades. Sickle cell disease is a major killer of children in sub-Saharan Africa. Yet country-level numbers for high-burden West African states have been thin, so the team turned to Global Burden of Disease estimates for 1990 to 2023.

They describe trends over time, split by age and sex, and ask what drove changes in deaths, including population growth and ageing. Sierra Leone has one of the world's highest rates of the sickle cell trait. Local numbers, even modelled ones, give health planners a firmer base for screening and care programmes.
pmc-13238569:
Zhou and colleagues test a walnut oil extract for protecting the ageing liver. Ageing steadily wears down body functions, and the liver is a common casualty. The team used mice given a sugar, D-galactose, that speeds ageing-like damage, and fed them the oil's unsaponifiable matter, the fraction left after soap-making chemistry, over eight weeks.

They tracked liver injury and the gut microbes that talk to the liver along the gut and liver axis. A food-derived extract that shields the liver while shifting gut bacteria kindly would be doubly useful. The study is an early animal step toward dietary guards against age-related liver decline.
pmc-13240869:
Tasew and colleagues at Myungsung Medical College measured postpartum depression among mothers in Addis Ababa's Bole sub-city after the pandemic. Four hundred ten mothers attending five primary health centers took part in early 2024. All had delivered between two weeks and one year before. Screening used the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale.

One in five mothers screened positive for probable postpartum depression. First-time mothers faced markedly higher odds, as did women with unplanned pregnancies. Poor partner support carried the strongest association, with low social support and induced labor also raising risk. The authors recommend routine screening inside postnatal care plus stronger partner and community support.
pmc-13241369:
Chiriboga's team at Northwestern asked mixed-race adults about joining genetics studies, a group such work often skips. Fourteen adults who call themselves Multiracial sat for long interviews. The team coded what they said against the study aims and new themes. Talk covered group identity, fears about ancestry tests, and how they wish to be engaged.

The adults used widely differing, often unsure words for their shared community. Many doubted that standard genetics work could capture their mixed roots well. They asked to be brought in early, at design, sign-up, and when results are read. Signing up younger city adults was their plain tip. Their words shape the study's closing advice.
pmc-13241469:
Kumar and colleagues at the Los Angeles VA uncovered how glioblastoma dodges mTOR-blocking drugs. Tumors keep making growth proteins through a backup internal ribosome entry route. A screening assay fished out protein kinase A as partner to the methylation enzyme PRMT5. Cell and mouse-brain tumor experiments tested the partnership.

The kinase stamps PRMT5 with a phosphate that lets it grip and methylate its partner protein. That grip switches on the backup translation of cyclin and myc messages. Blocking kinase and mTOR together killed tumor cells and shrank grafted tumors. Kumar proposes the dual blockade as a resistance-breaking strategy.
pmc-13243869:
Asad Ali, Saman Jabbar, and Shahid Aziz typed the resistance cassettes carried by MRSA bacteria collected across Lahore, Pakistan. Their study appeared in the International Journal of Microbiology in 2026. The SCCmec cassette is the DNA package behind methicillin resistance, and its type hints at where a strain evolved and how much resistance it carries. The team gathered 295 isolates from hospital and community settings and ran standard lab confirmations plus gene tests.

About half the isolates were confirmed as MRSA by the mecA gene and disc testing. Multiplex PCR sorted their cassettes into the known types, letting the authors compare hospital and community profiles side by side. Multiresistant type III cassettes stood out as a growing burden. Worryingly, cassette types typical of community strains turned up inside hospitals, blurring the old boundary between the two worlds. The authors call for tighter infection control to slow severe MRSA spread.
pmc-13246469:
Toofaninejad and co-authors report two rare surgical complications in this 2026 Clinical Case Reports article. A coronary-cameral fistula is an abnormal channel between a coronary artery and a heart chamber, and it can be created accidentally during heart operations. Both of their patients developed one after unusual muscle-cutting procedures inside the heart.

The first, a fifty-year-old man, formed a small channel into the right ventricle's outflow tract after resection of overgrown muscle. The second, a forty-one-year-old woman, developed one from the septum into the left outflow tract after repeat surgery. Heart ultrasound found both; neither disturbed circulation, so both were simply watched, the usual course for small fistulas.
pmc-13246569:
Jiang, Ma, Liu, and co-authors tested a traditional plant extract against bone loss in this 2026 Journal of Molecular Histology paper. Cuscuta chinensis, a parasitic vine used in Chinese medicine, was given to mice whose ovaries had been removed, a standard model of postmenopausal osteoporosis. The team combined bone scans, blood markers, and stem-cell cultures to trace how the extract worked.

Treated mice kept denser, better-connected bone, and their stem cells built bone more readily. The extract worked by protecting a protein called METTL3 from destruction: it blocked a partner protein, VCP, that normally tags METTL3 for disposal. Keeping METTL3 raised chemical tagging of RNA in bone cells. Silencing METTL3 erased the benefit, confirming the pathway.
pmc-13246969:
Hasnain and Telange survey nanostructured drug delivery in this 2026 Discover Nano review. Conventional drugs often dissolve poorly, spread everywhere in the body, and cause dose-limiting side effects. Nanocarriers, particles engineered at the billionth-of-a-meter scale, promise finer control over a drug's size, surface, loading, and release, steering treatment toward diseased tissue.

The review compares carrier families, lipid-based, polymeric, inorganic, carbon-based, and biomimetic, against their design logic, strengths, and weaknesses. It examines how particles enter cells, where they travel inside them, and how coatings help them hide from the immune system or latch onto targets. The authors close on translation: what it will take to move elegant laboratory carriers into approved medicines that survive manufacturing and regulation.
pmc-13249669:
Carta and colleagues reviewed antibody drugs for chronic migraine, in a 2026 systematic review. Reid argues that belief in an outer world, and in other minds, rests on common sense built into human nature. Perception, on his account, reaches the world itself, not a screen of images.
