Psalms and Gospels alike carry the wording generations of Catholics prayed from memory. Traditionalists still favor it, and readers comparing English Bibles will find its differences from the King James Version instructive.

A shared, binding pact that bars the use or threat of nuclear arms, the Assembly argues, would help clear the nuclear threat away. It would set the stage for talks toward the full end of such arms. The vote keeps alive a long push, led by states with no nuclear arms of their own.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: Resolution 69/69, adopted by the General Assembly at its sixty-ninth session in 2014, returns to the proposed Convention on the Prohibition of the Use of Nuclear Weapons. Katanga's secession was met with forceful orders on 24 November 1961. The Congo's parliament had been restored, and a central government formed on 2 August 1961. The Council strongly deprecated Katanga's illegal secessionist acts and the armed attacks on United Nations forces. Such acts had to stop at once. The Secretary-General was authorized to take vigorous action, with the needed measure of force if it came to that. His task was to seize, hold, and expel every foreign military and advisory figure outside United Nations command, and all mercenaries. States were asked to stop arms and war material from reaching Katanga. No state was to back the secession by act or by silence.
un-sc-res-1769:
Adopting Resolution 1769 on 31 July 2007, the Council acted on Darfur. The war there had killed hundreds of thousands since 2003. A small African Union force could not stop the attacks on civilians. Sudan had at last agreed to a joint force with a mostly African character.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council creates the African Union-United Nations Hybrid Operation in Darfur, called UNAMID. It is authorized for an initial twelve months. Up to 19,555 troops and 3,772 police may deploy. The force takes over from the African Union mission by the end of 2007. It may use force to guard civilians, aid workers, and itself, and to back the peace deal.
un-sc-res-1869:
Bosnia and Herzegovina gained a new international overseer in March 2009. On 25 March 2009 the Security Council welcomed Valentin Inzko as High Representative. The Steering Board of the Peace Implementation Council had named him on 13 March. He succeeded Miroslav Lajčák in the post. The Council paid tribute to the outgoing holder's work. The job flows from the Dayton Peace Agreement of 1995.

The Council restated the weight it gives the High Representative's role. He guides the civilian side of the peace deal. He coordinates the agencies helping the parties carry it out. He also holds final authority on how the civilian annex is read on the ground. The appointment kept that structure in place.
un-sc-res-2669:
Action on Myanmar came with Resolution 2669, adopted on 21 December 2022. The military had seized power in February 2021 and still held the elected leaders in detention. Violence spread across the country, and activists had been executed that July. Displacement and poverty climbed fast, while aid workers faced tight limits.

The Council demands an immediate end to all forms of violence. It urges the military to free all prisoners held without cause, naming the detained president and state counsellor. Full aid access must open for everyone in need. The text backs the ASEAN peace plan and its special envoy. It also calls for conditions that let Rohingya refugees return home in safety and dignity.
un-sc-res-269:
South Africa would not leave Namibia, and the Council hardened its line in 1969. Pretoria had spurned resolution 264, which called its presence there illegal. On 12 August 1969 the Council condemned that refusal. It also condemned South Africa's defiance of the United Nations. A report on the Secretary-General's talks fed the vote. Four members held back, among them France and Britain.

Keeping troops in Namibia, the Council ruled, is an act of force. It strikes at the standing of the United Nations itself. It breaks the land's wholeness and denies its people a say in their rule. The Council backed the right of Namibia's people to fight for freedom. South Africa stayed for twenty more years all the same.
un-sc-res-369: Kept in the official record of the United Nations, Security Council Resolution 369 is catalogued here as dating from 1975. Voting in the Council requires support from its permanent members, so each adopted text marks a point of agreement. Readers will find the full wording here, taken from the English Wikisource transcription of the UN official record. The entry belongs to the library's DECLASSIFIED group of public official records.
un-sc-res-69:
Israel's bid for United Nations membership came before the Council in March 1949. On 4 March 1949 the Council judged the application on the Charter's terms. It decided that Israel is a peace-loving state. It also found Israel able and willing to carry out the Charter's duties. Those findings are the legal heart of the text. Few admission resolutions spell them out so fully.

On that basis the Council recommended Israel's admission to the General Assembly. The vote was nine to one, with one abstention. Egypt cast the no vote. Britain abstained. The Assembly admitted Israel that May. The decision gave the new state its seat while the first Arab-Israeli war was ending.
un-sc-res-869: UNPROFOR's mandate was extended by one day on 30 September 1993. The Council restated resolution 743 (1992) and later texts on the force. It repeated its resolve to guard the force's safety and freedom of movement in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, acting under Chapter VII to that end. The extension ran only to 1 October 1993. The Council stayed actively seized of the matter. The one-day term was a bridge, holding the force in place while the Council weighed a longer renewal, which followed in resolution 871 (1993).
un-sc-res-969: A formal decision of the United Nations Security Council, Resolution 969 is catalogued here under 1995. The Council's fifteen members vote on draft texts, and adopted ones enter the record as numbered resolutions. The library holds the complete text in the form transcribed for English Wikisource from the official UN record. As a public record, it has long been open to scholars and general readers alike.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Security Council resolution 1269, adopted unanimously on 19 October 1999, is the Council's general resolution on international terrorism, not tied to a single attack. Alarmed by the increase in terrorist acts worldwide, it unequivocally condemns all acts, methods and practices of terrorism as criminal and unjustifiable. That holds whatever their motivation, wherever and by whomever they are committed.

The Council calls on all states to carry out the anti-terrorist conventions they belong to and to join the rest as a priority. It sets out practical steps. States should cooperate to prevent attacks and bring perpetrators to justice. They should block the preparation and financing of terrorism at home. They should deny terrorists safe haven through arrest, prosecution or extradition. They should check that asylum seekers have not taken part in terrorist acts. They should share information to prevent attacks.

Resolution 1369, adopted unanimously on 14 September 2001, keeps the UN mission between Ethiopia and Eritrea for another six months. Both countries had signed the Algiers peace agreements in December 2000, ending their border war. The mission, UNMEE, patrolled a temporary security zone between them while a boundary commission prepared its ruling.

The Council renewed UNMEE's mandate into March 2002. It reaffirmed both parties' duty to meet their obligations under humanitarian, human rights, and refugee law, and to keep UN and Red Cross personnel safe. Support for the Secretary-General's good offices and for the African Union's role ran through the text. The border ruling itself arrived the following spring.

Two months of patience for the Sahara file came from this text of 2003. On 25 March, the Council adopted Resolution 1469 without dissent. The vote mission, MINURSO, was still waiting for a political opening. Morocco and the Polisario Front stayed locked in place. The Secretary-General had written to propose a report date in May.

The text extends MINURSO's mandate to 31 May 2003. The Secretary-General must report on the state of play by 19 May. That date was his own proposal. The short stretch was a holding move, nothing more. A bigger call came that summer. In Resolution 1495, the Council backed the envoy's peace plan for the territory.

In November 2004 the Security Council packed its bags for Africa. Resolution 1569, adopted unanimously on 26 October 2004, moved two days of meetings to Nairobi, Kenya. The sessions would run on 18 and 19 November. Their agenda was Sudan, then gripped by civil war and the Darfur crisis.

Members planned to discuss Sudan with the African Union. The regional bloc IGAD would also take part. Other peace efforts in the region were on the list. One rule was waived for the trip: meeting records could be issued later in New York. The move showed how seriously the Council took Sudan's wars.

Troops moved from one African mission to a twin in 2006. Burundi had just held sound polls. Its UN force, ONUB, had men to spare. Congo, next door, faced strain with polls of its own near. The chief wrote on 30 March 2006 with a plan to share the load. Resolution 1669 passed on 10 April 2006.

The chief could shift a set force for a short span. At most, one battalion of foot troops would go. A field hospital would move as well. Up to fifty men to watch and report could join them. The loan ran to 1 July 2006. It drew on a grant first made in December 2005. Fresh terms for both forces would let the Council judge if the loan should live on.

The Congo crisis and the breakaway province of Katanga are the subject of Resolution 169, adopted on 24 November 1961. Congo's parliament had been restored and a central government formed that August. Katanga's provincial leaders, backed by outside resources and foreign mercenaries, still claimed their province was a sovereign nation, a claim the Council flatly rejected. UN staff had faced violence in the fighting.

The Council insists that the secessionist activity in Katanga stop at once. It authorizes the Secretary-General to take vigorous action, including force if needed, to seize, detain, and deport foreign military staff, advisers, and mercenaries not under UN command. It asks states to block arms supplies that could serve warlike ends and to deny transport for them. It declares full support for the Central Government and urges all member states to back it.

Darfur's hybrid AU-UN mission is created in Resolution 1769, adopted on 31 July 2007. Sudan had accepted the hybrid operation at the June 2007 Addis Ababa consultations, the Darfur Peace Agreement remained unimplemented, and attacks on civilians and aid workers plus widespread sexual violence continued. The African Union's AMIS was to fold into the new force.

The Council authorizes the AU/UN Hybrid Operation in Darfur, UNAMID, for twelve months, at up to 19,555 military personnel and 3,772 police plus nineteen formed police units. UNAMID must take over authority from AMIS no later than 31 December 2007, with UN-provided command and backstopping and a predominantly African character. Acting under Chapter VII, the Council authorizes UNAMID to protect its personnel and humanitarian workers, support Darfur Peace Agreement implementation, prevent armed attacks, and protect civilians. UNAMID must also monitor whether arms are present in Darfur in violation of Resolution 1556 (2004).

Bosnia still had a foreign overseer in 2009. The war there had ended almost fourteen years before. The peace deal was signed at Dayton. Under Resolution 1869, passed on 25 March 2009, the Council backed a change at the top. Valentin Inzko of Austria would be the new High Representative. He took over from Miroslav Lajcak.

The Council praised the work Lajcak had done. It stressed that the High Representative has the last word on the peace deal's civil side. It also noted a list of goals Bosnia still had to meet. Five goals and two terms stood in the way. Once met, the overseer's office could close. A European Union envoy would take its place.

Myanmar's crisis reaches the Council's agenda in Resolution 2669, adopted on 21 December 2022. The military's state of emergency of 1 February 2021, violence against civilians and infrastructure, the July 2022 execution of activists, and mass arbitrary detention had deepened humanitarian need and displacement. ASEAN's Five Point Consensus of April 2021 had seen limited implementation.

The Council demands an immediate end to all forms of violence across the country. It urges the military to release arbitrarily detained prisoners, naming the detained State Counsellor Aung San Suu Kyi and President Win Myint. It calls for implementation of ASEAN's Five Point Consensus, with the Secretary-General or his Special Envoy to report orally by 15 March 2023. The Council backs coordination between the UN and ASEAN envoys. It also demands full, safe, unhindered humanitarian access and action on the root causes in Rakhine State so Rohingya refugees can return voluntarily and safely.

South Africa's hold on Namibia drew a sharp rebuke in Resolution 269, adopted on 12 August 1969 by eleven votes to none with four abstentions. Pretoria had refused to obey an earlier resolution demanding it end its administration of the territory, which the UN regarded as held illegally. The Council framed the defiance as a challenge to its authority under the Charter.

The resolution condemns South Africa and declares that keeping its administration in Namibia amounts to an aggressive encroachment on UN authority and a denial of the Namibian people's sovereignty. It backs the legitimacy of the Namibians' struggle against that presence. Above all, it orders South Africa to withdraw its administration right away, with 4 October 1969 set as the last possible day.

The observer force on the Golan Heights received a new term on 28 May 1975, under Resolution 369. The force, called UNDOF, watches the separation of Israeli and Syrian forces. Two disengagement agreements had been signed after the October war of 1973. Tension in the area still ran high.

The Council repeated that the two disengagement agreements were only a step. The real goal was to carry out Resolution 338 of 1973, which demanded a cease-fire and peace talks. The parties were called on to put that resolution into effect at once. The observer force's mandate was renewed for another six months. At the end of that period, the Secretary-General had to report on developments. His report also had to cover the steps taken toward Resolution 338.

Israel applied for UN membership less than a year after independence. War with its Arab neighbors had only just paused. Resolution 69 was adopted on 4 March 1949. Nine members voted in favor. Egypt voted against. Britain abstained. Few admission votes have carried such political charge.

The Council formally judged Israel a peace-loving state. It found Israel able and willing to honor the Charter. On that basis, it recommended admission to the General Assembly. The Assembly admitted Israel that May. Supporters saw the vote as completing the UN's own 1947 partition decision. Opponents saw disputed questions left unresolved. The short text remains a founding document of Israel's international status.

Resolution 869, passed on 30 September 1993, may hold the record for the shortest grant in the Council's life. It stretched the term of UNPROFOR, the guard force in Croatia and Bosnia, by one day. The new end date was 1 October 1993. The lines that back old texts are all but as long as the grant itself. Care for the force's safety, and its free range on all its tasks, is the cause the text gives for its act, under the Charter's hard chapter.

A one-day term was a bridge, not a plan. Talks on the force's fate were stuck mid-stream, as safe zones and air strikes split the hall. The Council kept its grip on the file, and a long grant came days later.

Thirty years after it was created, the Cyprus peacekeeping force came up for renewal again in December 1994. A report from the Secretary-General, dated 12 December, recommended six more months. Cyprus's government agreed the force should stay beyond the end of the year. Patrols still met interference near the buffer zone, which worried the Council. Resolution 969 was adopted unanimously on 21 December 1994.

The Council extended the force's stationing until 30 June 1995. It pressed both sides to cut the number of foreign troops on the island and to reduce defense spending. An agreement of 1989, under which posts along the cease-fire lines were left unmanned, was to be extended. The leaders of both communities were also urged to promote tolerance between Greek Cypriots and Turkish Cypriots. The text set a path of small, practical steps, while the island's division itself remained unresolved.
wagstaffe-question-of-witchcraft-debated:
John Wagstaffe published The Question of Witchcraft Debated in 1669, in the confident early years of the Royal Society. His discourse argues outright against the very opinion of witches. Wagstaffe does not hedge or qualify; he denies the whole business, which made his tract the boldest skeptical sortie of the Restoration.

He attacks the evidence, the confessions, and the theology that supports them. Glanvill's circle answered him hotly, since much turned on the outcome. A landmark of English unbelief, his book shows skepticism leaving private doubt for open print. Wagstaffe wrote before it was safe, and his daring still gives the tract its charge.
wallace-malay-archipelago-1869:
Alfred Russel Wallace spent eight years in the islands of Malaysia and Indonesia collecting birds, insects, and mammals. His 1869 book The Malay Archipelago tells that journey in full. He supported himself by selling specimens to museums and collectors back home. He wrote it after he and Darwin had jointly announced natural selection.

Wallace describes volcanoes, jungles, rare birds of paradise, and the peoples who guided and fed him. He also notes a sharp line dividing the islands' animal life, still called Wallace's Line by scientists. The narrative mixes danger, illness, and wonder with calm, exact observation. The book remains a founding story of biogeography, the study of where species live and why.
wallace-malay-archipelago-vol-1-1869:
Alfred Russel Wallace published Volume 1 of The Malay Archipelago in 1869, after eight years of travel in the islands between Asia and Australia. Wallace earned his living by collecting specimens for sale. At the same time he formed, on his own, the theory of natural selection that Charles Darwin also reached.

Volume 1 follows Wallace through Singapore, Malaya, and the great islands of the west, describing forests, volcanoes, and peoples. He logged birds, insects, and mammals, and noted sharp changes in species from island to island. Those changes led to the line now called the Wallace Line. The book mixes adventure, sharp observation, and science of the first rank.
wallace-malay-archipelago-vol-2-1869:
Volume 2 of Wallace's Malay Archipelago appeared in 1869, completing his account of eight years in the islands of Southeast Asia and New Guinea. Alfred Russel Wallace had collected more than a hundred thousand specimens on the trip. The second volume moves east, toward the lands of birds of paradise.

Wallace described the Aru Islands, New Guinea, and the Moluccas, with their rare birds and distinct peoples. He compared island species on each side of a deep divide now called the Wallace Line. His notes on the bird of paradise hunts remain famous. The volume closes a travel book that is also a founding work of the study of how species are spread across the earth.
